News.title: How to make pinhole projector to view solar eclipse as special glasses sell out
News.content:
How to make pinhole projector to view solar eclipse as special glasses sell out

The UK will experience a partial solar eclipse on Wednesday, (12th August) and as specialised glasses start selling out online, here's an easy way to ensure you can still see the spectacle

View Image You must use proper protection when viewing a solar eclipse (Image: john finney photography via Getty Images)

UK skies are set to put on a remarkable show this week, with a stunning partial solar eclipse scheduled to take place, and you really won't want to miss it.

‌



On Wednesday (12th August), the UK will see a deep, partial eclipse that will be the closest to totality we have witnessed since 1999. Parts of Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain will be plunged into complete darkness as they pass through the path of totality, while sky-watchers across the UK will be treated to a deep partial eclipse, with roughly 90% of the sun covered by the moon. And Brits are already gearing up to watch the spectacle, as solar eclipse glasses are already selling out on sites like Amazon.

‌



The UK last saw a total eclipse almost 30 years ago, when Cornwall and parts of Devon found themselves in the path of totality. These events are extraordinarily rare, as any given spot on Earth can expect to see a total solar eclipse only once every 360 to 410 years. With the next total eclipse set to be visible from the UK not arriving until 2090, this week's event represents a once-in-a-lifetime chance to witness something truly special.

‌



A solar eclipse happens when the moon moves directly between the Earth and the sun, casting a shadow that blocks the sun's light either completely or in part. What's crucial to understand is that even when the sun appears largely hidden, it is still extremely dangerous to look at it directly without the right kind of eye protection.

Eclipse glasses are widely considered one of the best ways to view the event safely, as they are built with far more powerful UV protection than standard sunglasses, enabling you to look straight at the sun without risking damage to your eyesight. However, with demand soaring ahead of Wednesday's event, many retailers are already running low on stock.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



The good news is that there's a brilliantly simple alternative you can put together at home. A DIY pinhole projector allows you to watch the eclipse indirectly, meaning no specialist equipment is required. You only need three basic items to get started: a cardboard box, a sheet of kitchen foil and a pair of scissors.

Educational platform Twinkl Resources shared a step-by-step video guide on TikTok showing exactly how to assemble your own pinhole projector. It's an easy and enjoyable project - and with the summer holidays in full swing, it's a fantastic way to keep the kids engaged and excited about the wonders of the natural world.

How to make a pinhole projector

Making a pinhole projector is easy. You want to begin by opening up your cardboard box and taping a strip of white paper down one side of it. It doesn't matter which side, but the opposite side must be suitable for cutting holes into.

‌



Once your paper is secured, you need to cut out two squares from the opposite side of the cardboard box. Cover one square with a sheet of kitchen foil, and secure it with tape. Then, use a pin to make a small hole in the centre of the foil.

Make sure the box is completely sealed at the top, so the only gaps are the pin hole and the empty square. Your pinhole projector is now complete and ready to use so that you can enjoy the eclipse safely.

How to use a pinhole projector

When eclipse day arrives, take your projector outside and stand with your back facing the sun. Angle yourself so the sunlight shines directly onto the kitchen foil end of the box, letting the light pass through the tiny pinhole.

‌



Bring the box up to your face and look through the square viewing hole. On the white paper lining the inside of the box, you should see an image of the sun projected - and as the eclipse progresses, you'll be able to watch the moon's shadow move gradually across it.

Other ways to safely watch a solar eclipse

If you'd prefer to use eclipse glasses rather than a projector, make sure any pair you purchase or dig out from storage meets the required safety standards. Royal Museums Greenwich advises that glasses must display a safety certification of either 'ISO 12312-2' or 'ISO 12312-2:2015' on the frame or packaging.

Be wary of using an old pair you may have kept from a previous eclipse, as if the lenses show any signs of scratching or creasing, they should not be used, as they could be damaged and have reduced protection.

Article continues below

And if getting outside on the day isn't an option, the Royal Observatory will be broadcasting a free live stream of the eclipse from London on 12 August, so you can take in the whole event from the comfort of your sofa.

News.title: British couple jailed in Iran over espionage claims end hunger strike as worried son says it's a cry for help
News.content:
British couple jailed in Iran over espionage claims end hunger strike as worried son says it's a cry for help

Craig and Lindsay Foreman, who were detained in Iran's notorious Evin jail last year, embarked on three-month hunger strikes together in a bid to speak with their families again

View 4 Images Lindsay and Craig Foreman have been locked up in Tehran's hellhole Evin prison since January 2025 (Image: PA)

A Brit couple accused of espionage and imprisoned in a notorious Iranian jail have ended a three-month-long hunger strike in a "cry for help", their concerned son has said.

‌



Craig and Lindsay Foreman, both aged 53, embarked on concurrent hunger strikes this year as a means of protest against the treatment they received at the Tehran's notorious Evin jail, where they have been detailed since 2025. The pair were jailed on suspicion of espionage as they passed through the nation during a motorcycle journey from Europe to Australia, and sentenced to a decade behind bars in January.

‌



They went on gruelling 93 and 84-day hunger strikes together in protest, which their son said they closed this week with a five-day water fast.

‌



Brit jailed in Iran given extra prison sentence, family claim READ MORE :

View 4 Images Craig and Lindsay Foreman were jailed in 2025 (Image: PA)

Speaking to the BBC, Lindsay's son Joe Bennett said that he and four other unnamed people helped the couple close out their protest on Saturday with a five-day fast. They teamed up with other prisoners at the Evin jail, he added, in a bid to create something "bigger than themselves".

He said: "My mum and Craig have spent months on hunger strike, and even at the point of bringing it to an end they wanted to make it about something bigger than themselves.

‌



"Those final five days became about people standing together around values that should be universal: Truth, justice, kindness, peace and unity." Speaking to Sky News, Mr Bennett added that, while the strike was their "only agency to rebel" his family had been "begging" them to come off it over fears of damage to their bodies.

View 4 Images The couple went on a three-month hunger strike (Image: PA)

He said: "It was an act of defiance. It was their only agency to rebel, essentially. Their concern spread further than themselves, and I think that speaks volumes.

‌



"But as a family we've been begging for months for them to come off because it was a real worry for us all - especially the length of time that passed and we got a message through that we would join them in a five-day fast towards the end of their hunger strike - which we've now completed - that they would end their hunger strike."

The strike had an particularly severe impact on Mr Bennett's mum Lindsay, who he said was hospitalised with low blood sugar, something he learned while being drip-fed information in recent months.

View 4 Images Craig and Lindsay Foreman were travelling through Iran during an around-the-world motorcycle trip (Image: FAMILY HANDOUT/AFP via Getty Ima)

Article continues below

A family spokesperson said the couple had ultimately agreed to end their strike after negotiating with prison guards to speak directly to their loved ones again. He said: "The hardest part is the lack of information, we've had no calls with them, so you can never really check in on a daily or even weekly basis.

"I haven't spoken to my mum for almost three months. The five-day water fast at the end of the 90 days was a real hardship on their bodies. I know that my mum had very, very low blood sugar. She was in hospital."

Mr Bennett is now hoping to have a conversation about his mum and stepdad's incarceration with new Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, having spoken with the UK's first envoy for complex consular cases, Alistair Burt, and Stephen Doughty, the new minister for the Middle East.

News.title: More than two-thirds of England now in drought
News.content:
Last month, England and Wales saw the driest July since records began in 1836 - while for southern England, it was the driest month ever recorded.

South-east England received 1% of the expected average rainfall for July, while some parts of Hampshire, Isle of Wight and West Sussex have not had a rain day for 59 days.

All of England is experiencing pressure on water resources, the National Drought Group said.

Farmers have reported reduced output after their earliest harvests in 20 years, with the National Farmers Union (NFU) warning that continued dry weather could lead to some food shortages.

NFU president Tom Bradshaw said yields of wheat and oats were "very, very poor" this year and warned livestock farmers have had to use their winter feed rations because they have been unable to grow grass.

Water Minister Emma Hardy said the government is working to make it easier for farmers to build more on-site irrigation reservoirs, which capture and hold water.

Only 14% of England's rivers are considered to be at normal levels, while 22% are "exceptionally low" - including the River Avon in south-west England and the River Ely Ouse in eastern England.

The Environment Agency has warned that low water levels have resulted in potential navigation issues for boats on the Thames, Lark and Ouse.

Reservoir levels have also continued to decline, with almost all across England below normal and five classed as "exceptionally low", according to the agency.

Warmer water is putting fish under "severe stress," Head of Fisheries at the Angling Trust Mark Owen said, as it holds less dissolved oxygen.

Emma Pinchbeck, chief executive of the Climate Change Committee, said the UK is "not prepared at all" for the prolonged dry weather.

"We're seeing right now with the impacts on farming from this drought and the extreme heat we're experiencing, our infrastructure, our agricultural sector and lots of areas of the economy are not really ready for the weather we now have and how that weather will change up to 2050," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

News.title: Record 230 people cross Channel in one small boat
News.content:
A small boat has crossed the English Channel carrying 230 people, the largest number to make the journey in a single vessel.

It breaks the previous record set in July, when 165 people made the crossing on a single vessel.

The boat arrived in the UK in the early hours of Monday.

A picture taken off the coast of northern France showed the inflatable boat was so full many passengers had to dangle their legs in the water as it entered the busy shipping route.

A Home Office spokesperson said this latest incident demonstrated the "reckless and dangerous tactics employed by criminal gangs... who continue to put lives at risk by cramming ever greater numbers of people onto unseaworthy vessels".

French rescuers said the 15m (49ft) boat was "buckling" in the water and could have led to a "tragedy".

The boat was already carrying about 50 people when it was seen heading towards a beach to pick more passengers up, the crew in Berck-sur-Mer added.

French maritime officials said 30 migrants were left stranded by the tide during a boarding attempt at Berck beach in northern France.

They were brought to safety by maritime and land-based rescue services, the statement from France's Channel and North Sea Maritime Prefecture said.

The boat carrying 232 people continued its journey, before two passengers requested assistance and were taken to Calais by a French Navy rescue ship, the statement added.

News.title: 30 years later, a former rival will stand trial for Tupac's murder
News.content:
It's been three decades filled with mystery, conspiracies - and anger.

The drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996 changed the trajectory of hip-hop and elevated the rapper from the face of the genre to a cultural icon.

His killing became one of popular culture's great mysteries, with countless theories but no arrests until 2023, when Duane "Keffe D" Davis was unexpectedly charged with murdering the famous rapper.

The 63-year-old former gang boss is due to stand trial in Las Vegas, where he is accused of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang. He's pleaded not guilty. If convicted, he faces life in prison without parole.

The trial is likely to unravel the intricacies of the bitter and deadly East Coast vs West Coast rap rivalries AND turf wars between the Bloods and the Crips street gangs that were immortalised in rap lyrics and news reports in the 1990s.

It could also include several celebrity witnesses - including Suge Knight, the former CEO of Death Row Records, who has been thought of as the last surviving witness to Shakur's death.

But the complicated case hinges almost exclusively on one key piece of evidence: a book co-authored by Davis that he has argued is partially a piece of fiction.

Jury selection in the case began on Monday, with opening arguments slated to start on 17 August.

News.title: Consortium including Jeff Bezos advances talks for stake in Liverpool FC
News.content:
A consortium including billionaire Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has advanced its talks to buy about a 30% stake in Liverpool, BBC Sport has been told.

The group is led by British-Indian millionaire businessman Amit Bhatia and also includes Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin.

Owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG) confirmed last month that the group had "expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club".

Bhatia is the son-in-law of Indian billionaire businessman Lakshmi Mittal and had been a director and co-owner of Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before relinquishing his stake in the club last month.

American businessman Bezos, founder of e-commerce giant Amazon, is the fourth-richest person in the world.

According to Forbes, the 62-year-old has an estimated net worth of $256bn (Â£192bn).

FSG, who bought Liverpool in a Â£300m deal in 2010, previously sold a minority stake in the Anfield side to global sports investment firm Dynasty Equity.

BBC Sport contacted FSG about the latest developments, but they had no further comment.

In January, Liverpool became the top-earning Premier League club for the first time, according to analysis from financial firm Deloitte.

The following month the club announced record revenues of Â£703m for 2024-25 financial year.

News.title: We are chasing Ebola virus - it is ahead of us, WHO warns
News.content:
The latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo began at least three months before it was officially declared - meaning the health authorities are still playing catch-up, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned.

More than 1,900 people have died from the virus since that declaration on 15 May, making this the second-worst Ebola outbreak ever.

Infection rates are still high, adding to the concern that the authorities are struggling to get to grips with the spread of the disease.

The epicentre of this outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, is in the east of DR Congo where insecurity has hampered control efforts.

There is also no approved vaccine or any recognised therapeutic drugs, making treating Bundibugyo harder.

"We are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us," WHO Africa director Dr Mohamed Janabi said at a news conference in the city of Bunia, which is at the heart of this outbreak.

He cited research showing that the virus started spreading in February and was initially misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid.

Janabi also said that, in part because of insecurity, health workers are only reaching about 30% of the cases with the rest dying at home.

Traditional burial practices â where mourners touch the deceased's body - and a suspicion of health authorities in some communities have also made things difficult.

But there are now several dedicated treatment centres in the east of DR Congo and people are getting diagnosed much more quickly.

So far there have been 4,294 confirmed cases and 1,960 deaths, DR Congo's health ministry has said.

The largest recorded outbreak was in West Africa between 2014 and 2016 when 11,325 people died.

News.title: Nigel Farage says incident at his home 'directly linked' to Ann Widdecombe murder
News.content:
Nigel Farage said an incident at his London home last year was "directly linked" to the murder of Ann Widdecombe, after counter-terror police reopened an inquiry into it last week.

It relates to what Farage described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025, the BBC understands.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation was handled.

At a Monday press conference, the Reform UK leader said: "I understand this is a completely unprecedented move, and yes, this is directly linked to the murder of Ann Widdecombe, and I'm afraid I just can't tell you any more than that at this stage."

News.title: New weight loss pill approved for use in UK
News.content:
A daily weight-loss pill made by the drug firm behind the Mounjaro jab has been approved for use in the UK - the first country in Europe to do so.

Foundayo, made by Eli Lilly, is for treating obesity and type 2 diabetes.

But while people will be able to buy it privately with a prescription, the approval by the Medicines and Healthcare productors Regulatory Agency does not automatically mean it will be made available on the NHS.

Foundayo is a form of GLP-1 medication that blunts appetite, and comes after the MHRA approved a pill version of a similar weight-loss drug, Wegovy, in June.

Eli Lilly said while it could immediately be used by the NHS for type 2 diabetes, it would be making an application to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence in England for it to be recommended as a weight loss treatment as well.

Dr Simon Cork, from Anglia Ruskin University, said while the weight-loss benefits of Foundayo were less than other treatments, patients could still expect to see "significant, clinically meaningful changes to their weight".

And he said a key advantage was that it was likely to be cheaper than other weight-loss treatments, which have tended to be tightly restricted by the NHS.

University of Glasgow expert Prof Naveed Sattar agreed it was "good news".

He said another benefit was its convenience, pointing out that unlike the Wegovy pill, which has to be taken on an empty stomach, this pill could be taken at any time of the day.

"The arrival of another effective oral option is a positive development and should help more people access treatment that best suits their needs and preferences," he added.

Experts believe it could help people coming off weight-loss jabs remain slim.

Trials found that patients who had used weight loss jabs and then been given the tablet, also called orforglipron, every day for a year avoided regaining much of the weight they had lost - a known risk when coming off GLP-1 injections.

People on weight loss medication are also advised to eat a healthy diet and get enough exercise.

And, like any medication, there can be side effects to using Foundayo, including nausea, diarrhoea, constipation and vomiting.

News.title: MSP apologises for hurt caused by rape 'demonisation' comments
News.content:
A newly-elected MSP has apologised for the hurt caused by comments in which they talked of the "demonisation" of rape.

Scottish Green Party politician Q Manivannan has also faced criticism for suggesting rape is a "spectrum of things" during a podcast recorded before they were elected to the Scottish Parliament.

Earlier, the Scottish Rape Crisis Alliance (SRCA) - which represents four rape crisis centres - said there is "no hierarchy of rape" and warned the MSP not to minimise sexual violence.

In a statement, Manivannan said clips from the podcast had been "selectively edited" but said they were "sorry" for the upset, and insisted they would never seek to diminish a rape survivor's experience.

The comments, which were made during The Subjective Space podcast , externalrecorded last year, sparked fury after they re-emerged online at the weekend.

News.title: Six arrested after woman found dead in north London
News.content:
Six people have been arrested on suspicion of murder following the death of a 23-year-old woman in north London.

Police were called at 09:33 BST on Thursday, following concerns for the welfare of a woman at a residential address on Bollinder Place, Clerkenwell.

Officers attended alongside the London Ambulance Service and found an unresponsive woman, who was pronounced dead at the scene.

Four women, aged 20, 21, 23, and 26, and two men, aged 21 and 24 were arrested at the scene. All six have since been released on bail while enquiries continue.

Work is ongoing to trace the woman's next-of-kin, who will be supported by specially trained officers once identified.

Ch Supt Jason Stewart said: "This is a tragic incident and our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the young woman who has lost her life.

"We understand that news of an incident like this will cause concern within the local community."

News.title: Hope of finding mum's body 'lost if killer released'
News.content:
The court heard evidence from a domestic abuse report Linda made to police before her death, which showed she feared he would kill her.

Linda said that when she confronted Razzell about an affair he had with a 19-year-old in 2000, he threw her so hard she cracked a rib. He also made threats to kill her, she had told officers.

Razzell was tried and acquitted of two counts of domestic abuse a few months before he killed Linda.

However, a Parole Board hearing in 2023 concluded on the balance of probabilities that he was abusive.

In a victim statement played in court, Linda's cousin Westmore said a "huge chunk of happiness and joy" had been taken from her family's lives.

Linda's mother had died when she was eight and she went to live with Judy, meaning the pair grew up like sisters.

Westmore continued: "The major impact on myself and our family would be a loss of trust in the justice system of this country if he [Razzell] is released without saying where Linda's remains are.

"It's chilling that Glyn Razzell can calmly present as an innocent trustworthy man.

"If Glyn is released, all hope of ever finding Linda's remains will be lost."

Razzell, who wore a black suit in court, has applied for parole four times. When his application was refused in 2021, he became the first prisoner to be denied parole under Helen's Law.

The law requires the Parole Board to take into consideration a killer's refusal to disclose where they hid their victim's body.

The court also heard that he contributes to a website, easily found online, which claims he is innocent.

News.title: Asylum seeker who groomed and raped girl, 13, jailed
News.content:
An asylum seeker who raped a 13-year-old girl after pretending to be a teenager on Snapchat has been jailed.

Abdul Khan attacked the girl in a nature reserve in Clifton, Nottingham, on 14 May last year.

Khan arrived in the UK in the back of a lorry in 2015, Nottingham Crown Court heard, and faces automatic deportation to Afghanistan after he has served two thirds of his sentence.

He was jailed for nine and a half years on Monday after he was convicted of two counts of rape, one count of sexual activity with a child, sexual communication with a child, meeting a child following grooming and perverting the course of justice.

A four-day trial was told Khan, who is believed to be 28 and already serving a 23-month sentence for sexual communication with a different child in Derbyshire, arranged to meet his victim in woodland after telling her on the Snapchat messaging app he was a 14-year-old boy.

When they met in person and it was clear he was not 14, he tried to appease her by claiming to be 16, the court heard.

After activity that jurors found had been consensual, Khan, of HMP Nottingham, twice raped the girl.

Judge Mark Watson said the victim told her father what had happened and he contacted police.

Khan was then linked to the rapes by a mobile phone seized during his arrest over his contact with the child in Derbyshire.

Yet despite DNA evidence subsequently linking him to the attack, Nottinghamshire Police said he continued to deny having met the victim.

Addressing Khan, the judge said: "You deliberately concealed your true identity. She thought she was communicating with a child of her own age.

"It was a lie you have persisted with throughout these proceedings."

News.title: Two more Thetford disorder arrests takes total to 15
News.content:
Two more arrests have been made following three nights of unrest in a Norfolk town.

Disorder linked to anti-immigration protests took place in Thetford in Norfolk on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, with a police presence in the area ever since.

Norfolk Police said a man in his 20s, arrested on Sunday on suspicion of assaulting an emergency worker and being in possession of a Class B drug, remains in custody.

A teenage boy, arrested on suspicion of assaulting an emergency worker, was taken to Bury St Edmunds Police Investigation Centre and has since been released on bail until 4 October.

The force has made 15 arrests in total since the disorder started last week.

News.title: British couple held in Iran end hunger strike
News.content:
A British couple jailed in Iran after being accused of espionage have ended their hunger strikes after 93 and 84 days respectively.

Craig and Lindsay Foreman were arrested in January 2025 while passing through Iran on a motorcycle journey from Europe to Australia. They were both sentenced to 10 years in jail in February, but Craig Foreman's family said his punishment had been extended by two years after speaking to the media.

The couple from East Sussex, who both deny espionage, went on hunger strike in May when prison authorities prevented them from calling their families.

The family of the couple said they had been protesting against how they and other prisoners were being treated.

A spokesperson for the family said the couple agreed with prison guards to end their strike to be able to speak directly to their loved ones again.

However, the family said contact was yet to be re-established, as of Monday afternoon.

The family had also previously called for the couple to end their hunger strike.

Five people outside the prison joined the pair on their hunger strike for the final five days from Tuesday to Saturday as an act of solidarity, the family added.

Lindsay Foreman's son Joe Bennett and four unnamed others took part in the UK, as well as other prisoners inside Tehran's Evin jail, the family said.

"My mum and Craig have spent months on hunger strike, and even at the point of bringing it to an end they wanted to make it about something bigger than themselves," Bennett, from Folkestone in Kent, said.

"Those final five days became about people standing together around values that should be universal: Truth, justice, kindness, peace and unity."

By the end of the protest, Craig Foreman had been on hunger strike for 93 days, and Lindsay Foreman for 84 days, the family added.

Although they said they were unaware of the condition of the pair, who had consumed just milk and either honey or salt in water during their strikes.

Bennett said the couple also went on a separate hunger striker back in November as a "cry out for help".

News.title: Owner of 250-year-old Grade II-listed windmill gave it colourful makeover without permission
News.content:
Dr Eiddwen Jones, 85, is the great-great-great-great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Jones, who she said was the first miller at Llynon mill in 1776.

He managed the property in the village of Llanddeusant, Anglesey, until he died in his nineties.

She said the windmill should be repainted in whitewash as it is a historical building, and traditionally "that's how the mills were".

The author, whose family moved from Anglesey to Flintshire 150 years ago, said she did not agree that the windmill was painted in the first place to celebrate the Eisteddfod.

She has visited the windmill several times throughout her life where Thomas Jones' name is painted inside, and said he "would have turned in his grave, I believe," if he had known about its new appearance.

Jones added that it looked "very impressive in its original colour" when driving towards it.

"It's been made fun of now rather than kept the fact that it was a historical building and that people have been working there for a couple of centuries," she said.

Holt said the mill can be hard to find for visitors, as it is not close to the A55 road.

But the new colours have sparked a lot of interest.

With winters especially proving difficult with fewer people coming, he added: "I have a duty to ensure the future of the mill for the next generation."

He apologised to the local authority, saying he "realises that they [the council] are only doing their job and I know that I have broken the rules".

But he added: "I'm struggling and the winter is hard, but painting the mill has attracted more visitors here and helped me pay the bills."

He is gathering the opinions of visitors to the mill this summer to make a case to the council.

News.title: Suffolk heathland fire stood down as major incident
News.content:
A heathland fire which engulfed an area the size of 210 football pitches in Suffolk has been stood down as a major incident, almost two weeks after the blaze broke out.

Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said the decision followed a fire risk assessment of Dunwich Heath and RSPB Minsmere.

The service stressed "the incident itself is not over" and said people must stay away from the heathland, where firefighters remained to dampen down, monitor for hotspots, and any further fire activity.

Jon Lacey, the county's chief fire officer, said the decision to stand down the major incident reflected the "significant progress made by our crews and everyone who has supported this response".

News.title: Ex-Cambridge professor Jason Arday cancels live event after plagiarism row
News.content:
Jason Arday has cancelled an appearance in London next month, following his resignation as a Cambridge professor in the wake of allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements.

Arday's talk at the Royal Geographical Society's conference has been "cancelled at the request of the speaker", the organisation said.

He is also no longer listed on the websites of two other scheduled events in the coming months.

Arday - who became Cambridge's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - has admitted errors in his early work, but said he was not a "liar" and that the recent furore had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

He had been due to take part in a "fireside chat" at the Royal Geographical Society's conference in London on 2 September.

Arday's appearance at Topping & Company book shop in Edinburgh on 18 September is no longer listed on the website and has reportedly also been cancelled. The shop declined to comment.

He was also announced as a guest for the Arizona Women's Board Authors' Luncheon on 24 October, but is no longer listed on the event's website.

He is still listed as a speaker for the Stroud Book Festival in Gloucestershire in November.

News.content:

Moscow appears to be adopting increasingly aggressive strategies to recruit fresh troops for its war of attrition in Ukraine, as Vladimir Putin looks to make up for heavy battlefield losses.

Men are reportedly being snatched off Russian streets and students offered significant financial incentives to join drone units as Moscow looks to avoid another forced mobilisation.

Local officials have been issued recruitment quotas by the Kremlin and Moscow’s defence ministry as it looks to meet this year’s 409,000 target, sources familiar with the matter told the Financial Times.

Russians are given referral bonuses for encouraging others to sign up while officials exploit knowledge of potential recruits’ debts and legal problems to pressure them into signing up, the FT adds.

It comes as Putin seeks to regain the initiative in Moscow’s stalling four-and-a-half year invasion, after Kyiv's increased long-range attack capability has seen it inflict major damage on Russia’s energy industry.

open image in gallery Russia has driven up its recruitment as it suffers heavy battlefield losses (file photo) ( AFP/Getty )

The Russian army has suffered 1.4 million casualties including 450,000 deaths since its invasion began in February 2022, according to data from the Centre for Strategic & International Studies (CSIS).

According to Ukrainian estimates, Russian recruitment rates are not keeping up with casualty rates, with 222,500 troops lost - including 131,000 killed - but only 221,000 recruited so far in 2026.

“Year by year and month by month, it’s harder for the Russian army to find people,” Grigory Sverdlin, director of a charity helping Russian troops desert called Get Lost, told the FT.

“Putin is evidently putting off a new wave of mobilization, so the defence ministry has to put more pressure on all sorts of people to sign contracts.”

Human rights campaigners say police have raided workplaces and snatched people off the street to take them to military recruitment offices, where they were forced to sign contracts in several incidents in recent months.

Raids in Russian cities and towns like Penza, Kamenka and Kuznetsk saw men being rounded up by police officers and other military enlistment officials, it is claimed.

open image in gallery Ukrainian soldiers drive in a military truck along a road in the Kharkiv region ( AFP/Getty )

“In Penza, they're taking everyone indiscriminately, stopping cars and public transport, rounding up men and taking them away to sign contracts. Raids are happening across the entire city," one local resident told human rights group Idite Lesom, according to Ukrainska Pravda.

The raids have intensified since the authorities began “catching men” in January, a Penza resident told the Mobilizatsiya channel, according to the outlet.

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelensky has claimed that the Kremlin is preparing to carry out a “significant” wave of involuntary reserve call ups this autumn.

The Institute for the Study of War reports that Russia has been preparing conditions to conduct rolling partial reserve call-ups since October last year, and has passed bills to expand the pool of criminals who may be recruited.

Targeting sign ups from students also suggests that Moscow is keen to pour more skilled human resources into its drone forces which - like those of Ukraine - are playing an increasingly vital role in the war.

open image in gallery A Russian FPV-drone hits a car, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in the frontline town of Kramatorsk. The recruitment of troops to become skilled drone operators is now critical for Russia and Ukraine ( Press Service of the 93rd Kholodnyi Yar Separate Mechanized Brigade of the Ukrainian Armed Forces )

Drone operators typically work some distance from the front line, but they are regarded as high-value targets who are hunted down and killed if their positions are revealed.

Russia has denied that any kind of general mobilisation drive is on the agenda, and says it is not running short of recruits despite Ukrainian claims.

Similar recruitment tactics have been reported in Ukraine, where footage from October 2024 purportedly showed Ukrainian military recruitment officers raiding restaurants, bars and a concert hall in Kyiv in search of men not registered for conscription.

Officers positioned outside the doors of the capital city’s Palace of Sports were seen carrying out checks as people left a concert by Ukrainian rock band Okean Elzy on Friday night, local media and witnesses said.

Moscow has also sought to bring in thousands of foreign troops to help fight in its war. Zelensky said on Sunday that up to 50,000 North Koreans were set to be deployed on Russian territory.

It has used a network of online recruiters to deceptively “funnel thousands of Africans from nearly every country on the continent into the frontlines, according to the Africa Centre for Strategic Studies.

Cuba and Colombia have also been targeted by Moscow for recruitment to the Russian army, according to a report published in April by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH).

Shoppers have been warned they can expect to pay more for their food shop “come the later part of this year”, as extreme heat and drought bring farming to the brink.

The chair of the House of Commons’ Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee, Alistair Carmichael, has said consumers can expect to see the impact of this summer’s record-breaking weather in six to 12 months, as growers have warned that this year’s barley and wheat yield is expected to be lower than previous years.

“The problems for farmers today will be the problems for consumers in six or 12 months’ time because you see massively decreased yield for wheat and for barley,” said Mr Carmichael, the Liberal Democrat MP for Orkney and Shetland, on BBC Radio 4’s The World At One.

“And you’re seeing increasingly sort of concerned noises coming from vegetable producers as well.”

He added that shoppers will not be able to rely on imports to buy cheaper food because of the extreme heat throughout Europe.

open image in gallery Experts warn this is one of the most severe droughts farmers have experienced ( Getty )

“We can’t look to some of the alternative markets that we might have done in continental Europe in recent years because they are experiencing the same problems that we are,” he said.

“If you decrease the supply but you maintain the demand, then you’re going to pick the price up, so we will be seeing further food price inflation shocks for everybody come the later part of the year.”

Experts in the food industry have warned that UK food security is growing more fragile due to the extreme weather after England and Wales experienced their driest July since records began, while the south of England saw the driest month ever recorded.

Analysis from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) last week estimated that the hot and dry conditions that have plagued spring and summer could cut the country’s cereals and oilseed harvest by 2.5 million tonnes compared to earlier projections.

The National Drought Group revealed on Monday that almost three-quarters – 71.3 per cent – of England is now in drought. The National Farmers’ Union president Tom Bradshaw said conditions had left the agricultural sector struggling.

“This is one of the most severe droughts many farmers and growers have lived through,” Mr Bradshaw said. “Harvest yields are looking poor, farmers are struggling to access water to irrigate fruit and vegetables, and livestock farmers are having to use grass they cut this spring for their stores of winter feed for cattle as there’s very little grass growing now.

open image in gallery England and Wales experienced their driest July since records began ( AFP/Getty )

“The picture is even worse when we look across Europe to many of the countries we import food from, with huge wildfires across France and Spain. While retailers are used to managing variations in global supply, we’re not going to be able to trade our way through this potential crisis.

“If this summer teaches us anything, it is that we must prioritise food production. We have taken food production for granted for too long; we must create a more resilient food system to feed the 29 million households across the country, and we can’t produce food without water. This means urgent action to bolster our water security and ensuring our food security is treated as a vital part of our nation’s critical infrastructure.

“Central to this will be fast-tracking investment and planning changes, meaning we can build new reservoirs on farms. We need a common sense approach to water use, with water access prioritised for livestock, particularly poultry and pigs. More flexible abstraction rules are also needed so farmers can access water for irrigation. This would enable us to grow more of the food we can and should produce here ourselves, especially fruit and vegetables.”

News.title: Met police detective stalked former partner and ‘persistently’ sent her messages
News.content:

A detective constable persistently sent his former partner messages and followed her at an event during an eight-week period of stalking, a court heard.

Timothy Fory, of the Metropolitan Police’s directorate of professional standards, was convicted of stalking Stephanie Lane, who was also a detective at the force, from July to September 2024.

The pair had a brief relationship, but they broke up as Ms Lane thought Fory was not respecting her boundaries, Westminster Magistrates’ Court heard on Monday.

Fory, 34, who had been serving in the force for four years, then “persistently” sent her messages on WhatsApp, before he was blocked and he turned to Instagram and Facebook.

In one message, Fory sent Ms Lane a link to Ann Summers lingerie, the court heard.

Ms Lane replied to the message saying: “I’m starting to think you’ve not registered that we’re not seeing each other anymore.”

Fory replied that he was still “going to imagine you in stockings”.

In another message, Fory asked Ms Lane “Why are you looking so sexy?”, and added: “I want to put my arms around you.”

Fory also followed her at a social event in which “everywhere she went he followed”, prosecutor George Crivelli said.

After he was blocked on social media, the defendant found Ms Lane’s ex-partner Joshua Gray on Instagram and “out of pure spitefulness and perhaps desperation” sent him a message about him being in a relationship with her, the court heard.

Ms Lane said in a victim impact statement read to the court that Fory was “spiteful” and “vindictive” and his actions left her “anxious, nervous and on edge”.

open image in gallery Timothy Fory was handed a 12-month community order and must carry out 150 hours of unpaid work and 15 days of a rehabilitation requirement ( PA )

She said she has struggled sleeping, has lost weight and now constantly looks over her shoulder.

Ms Lane also said the stalking has “affected” her work, especially when cases “similar” to her own come up.

Fory had denied stalking without fear, alarm or distress in March of last year, but was convicted of the offence after a trial last month.

The defendant was spared jail and handed a 12-month community order and must carry out 150 hours of unpaid work and 15 days of a rehabilitation requirement.

A five-year restraining order was put in place, meaning he cannot contact Ms Lane directly or indirectly.

He was also made to pay £775 and a statutory surcharge of £114.

District Judge Caroline Jackson said Fory was in a “position of trust”, saying: “You of all people ought to be fully aware and appreciate the impact your actions have on people”.

The judge told the defendant: “I am saddened that you still don’t appreciate and understand the impact of your conduct.”

She also said a pre-sentence report showed he still believed that Ms Lane sent him “mixed messages”.

She added his “worrying” behaviour only stopped because he was blocked on the platforms.

The court heard Fory was suspended from duty on full pay.

Miranda Zeffman, defending, said Fory, who has no previous convictions, will now look to work in the construction industry.

The Met said Fory was suspended from duty when he was charged in February 2025, and now faces an accelerated misconduct hearing as soon as possible.

Detective Chief Superintendent Iain Keating of professional standards said: “DC Fory’s behaviour is a discredit to the thousands of Met officers who are committed to tackling offences against women and girls in London.

“His actions are even more concerning given he is attached to the Met’s directorate of professional standards, a unit directly responsible for investigating misconduct and upholding high standards across the Met.

“This court result, off the back of a swift investigation by officers, is a welcome one that I hope reassures women and girls, including the victim in this case, that the kind of conduct shown by DC Fory will not be tolerated.”

At least 77 people have been killed after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia, tearing down buildings across several cities and leaving others trapped in the rubble.

The 7.4 magnitude quake struck near San José del Palmar, some 150 miles west of Bogotá, at 7.34am local time on Monday, with tremors felt in major cities nationwide.

The highest reported death toll was in the western province of Risaralda in Colombia's coffee-growing region, where authorities reported 42 fatalities.

Britain’s foreign office advised against all but essential travel to parts of Colombia, reporting the closure of six airports and warning of the possibility of aftershocks.

Have you been affected? Contact james.reynolds@independent.co.uk

The quake struck just days after far-right populist Abelardo De La Espriella was sworn in as president, thrusting the new administration into its first major crisis.

open image in gallery Residents dig through the debris of a collapsed building after an earthquake, in Cali on Monday ( Reuters )

At least 18 people were killed in Pereira, mayor Mauricio Salazar told Caracol Radio, while others continue to remain trapped in collapsed buildings.

Two others were killed in Manizales, mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas said in an interview with Blu Radio. The number of people injured is yet to be confirmed.

One person died in Buenaventura, Colombia's main Pacific port, when a building collapsed, trapping several people, authorities said.

And people remained trapped in Cali, one of Colombia's largest cities, after more than two dozen structures collapsed, mayor Alejandro Eder said.

open image in gallery People look for survivors amid the rubble of a collapsed building after an earthquake in Cali, Colombia ( AFP/Getty )

He added that the city had asked authorities in Bogota and Medellin to send disaster teams to support rescue efforts.

“At this point, two people have already been rescued alive, one elderly woman and one young girl. There are more people trapped,” Eder told Blu Radio.

“We have at least 12 critical points and 25 collapsed structures that we are responding to.”

De La Espriella said in a video filmed while flying to Bogota that he was suspending his planned activities to lead emergency coordination efforts out of the capital.

open image in gallery The Manizales Cathedral was among the buildings damaged by the tremors ( AFP/Getty )

Colombia's civil aviation authority said flights were suspended at airports in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura while inspectors checked for structural damage.

Initial statements suggested that the quake’s depth was 79km before this was upgraded to 96km (60 miles) with the tremor magnitude increased to 7.4.

Witnesses in the Venezuelan border state of Tachira and the central-western city of Barquisimeto reported the quake had been felt there.

No tsunami warning was issued in the aftermath of the incident, the US tsunami warning system confirmed.

Reports from nine departments and all 32 departmental capitals where the quake was experienced were received by Colombia’s disaster agency triggering evacuations and damage reports.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management in Colombia said it is in communication with local officials to evaluate potential damage but no major destruction has been reported in the capital.

open image in gallery People look for survivors amid the rubble of a collapsed building after the earthquake hit Cali ( AFP/Getty )

The region was hit by devastating twin earthquakes near Caracas in Venezuela in June, which killed over 6,000 people. Witnesses told Reuters that they felt the tremors in the border state of Tachira and the central-western city of Barquisimeto.

Colombia’s location on the Pacific Ring of Fire makes it highly susceptible to earthquakes. The Ring of Fire is a belt where the Earth’s tectonic plates meet, with around 90 per cent of the planet’s largest earthquakes occurring here.

The country’s most devastating quake occurred in August 1868, killing around 70,000 people.

News.title: Tucker Carlson will not be running for president despite rumors, Marjorie Taylor Greene says
News.content:

Tucker Carlson will not run for president despite rumors to the contrary, former GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene has said.

Speculation about the conservative podcaster’s political ambitions intensified earlier this month after Greene posted a photo of herself with Carlson and a collection of MAGA dissidents, announcing the birth of a new movement.

The group — which included former Trump official Joe Kent and Rep. Thomas Massie — has publicly broken with President Donald Trump over the ongoing war in Iran. Some members have also strongly opposed the administration’s handling of the Epstein files.

“We said no more foreign wars and we meant it and supported Donald Trump because he made that promise,” Greene wrote in the August 1 post. “But he’s betrayed us all. Our commitment is America First for all Americans, right, left, and center,” she continued…The movement has begun.”

Greene, who resigned from Congress in January after Trump threatened to support a primary challenger, told Politico that enthusiasm for the still-amorphous political project has been “overwhelming”— and claimed that her phone has been ringing off the hook.

open image in gallery Tucker Carlson will not be running for president despite the rumors, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene said ( AFP via Getty Images )

“Our argument is the two-party system is a complete and total failure,” Greene told the outlet, saying the group was still discussing its next steps. “I am 100 percent totally completely disgusted with both parties.”

But Carlson, she insisted, will not mount a White House bid.

“Tucker, he’s not running for president,” Greene told the outlet. “He said that publicly. He said that privately.”

Earlier this summer, after declaring that he no longer supported the GOP, Carlson said in an interview that he was “of course” not planning to run for president.

open image in gallery Earlier this month, Marjorie Taylor Greene announced a new political 'movement' with a host of MAGA renegades, including Tucker Carlson and Thomas Massie ( @FmrRepMTG, X )

Still, two people familiar with the matter told Politico that the former Fox News host’s calculation could shift under the right circumstances.

“He won’t run against JD Vance. He will very likely run if Trump endorses [Marco] Rubio,” one unnamed source said. Carlson has publicly said that he likes the vice president and counts him as a friend.

Kent, the former director of the National Counterterrorism Center, said earlier this month that he and others urged Carlson to throw his hat in the ring. “All of us at one point in time told Tucker he needs to run, and Tucker’s been pretty public that he’s not going to run,” Kent said on The Young Turks.

Some close to the White House, however, appear unfazed by the prospect of Carlson joining the 2028 field. As one put it to Politico: “He’s not building a new party, he’s building a new subscription model.”

Multiple recent polls indicate that the Iran war remains deeply unpopular. Even among MAGA voters, support has dropped substantially, according to a July Politico survey.

Whether that frustration can be converted into enduring support for a new third party, however, remains an open question. Historically, third-party movements have fared poorly in national U.S. elections.

Nottingham Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis has filed a defamation lawsuit against Crystal Palace after fans unfurled a banner which showed him holding a gun to player Morgan Gibbs-White’s head.

Marinakis’ legal team lodged the claim on Monday, nearly a year on from the banner’s display during the Premier League clash between the two clubs at Selhurst Park.

The banner, raised in the Holmesdale Road End where the club ultras are situated, referenced Forest talisman Gibbs-White’s sudden transfer U-turn and the awkward interview he subsequently did with the club, during which Marinakis was anchored to his side.

The banner also included unsubstantiated claims against Marinakis, a Greek shipping magnate, who has repeatedly, vehemently denied the allegations.

He is now suing in the High Court, with his defamation claim against Crystal Palace and “Persons Unknown”.

Marinakis’ lawyers, Nottingham Forest and Crystal Palace have been approached for comment by The Independent.

It is the latest action to be taken against Palace as a result of the banner, after the FA charged the club in November with failing “to ensure its spectators and/or supporters (and anyone purporting to be supporters or followers) didn’t behave in an improper, offensive, abusive, insulting and/or provocative way at this match”.

Palace were fined £50,000 four months later, with the FA adding: “The fact that Crystal Palace had a policy to prevent banners being smuggled into the stadium demonstrates that it was aware of the risk.”

The game on 24 August last year took place amid heightened tensions between Palace and Forest after the Eagles were demoted from the Europa League due to a breach of multi-ownership regulations.

Forest voiced their concerns over this to Uefa and were then the beneficiaries of Palace’s removal, which lifted them into Europe’s second-tier competition.
