World.title: At least 13 killed in Ukrainian drone strike deep into Russia
World.content:
At least 13 people have been killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, local officials have said.

They confirmed one child was among those killed, with 75 more people injured as drones hit Nizhnekamsk, more than 1,100 kilometres (680m) from the Ukrainian border. Ukraine's Armed Forces said the city's Tanevo oil refinery had been hit.

It is one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of Moscow's full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022.

Kyiv has recently stepped up its long-range strikes on facilities it says contribute revenue and logistics to Russia's war on Ukraine.

The strike on Nizhnekamsk lasted several hours overnight and into the morning, according to local sources.

Verified images on social media show large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background.

The Uzkbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan.

According to Russian news agency RIA, most of the victims had been staying in a hostel at the time of the attack, and Russia's Investigative Committee said that "civilian individuals who were not involved in any military operations were present" where the drones struck.

The BBC has not independently verified this information. Moscow said that "all those involved in the attacks" would "face inevitable and severe punishment".

Oil refineries in Nizhnekamsk had already been hit once - on 12 June.

"The facilities Ukraine targets are used to carry out attacks against Ukraine, manufacture weapons, support Russia's war effort," said Andriy Kovalenko, head of the Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation.

World.title: World's oceans hit record-high July temperatures
World.content:
The world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, partly fuelled by developing El NiÃ±o conditions in the Pacific, according to the EU's climate monitoring service.

The average sea surface temperature (SST) outside the world's polar regions - between 60 degrees north and 60 degrees south - was 20.96C last month, beating the previous high of 20.89C, set in 2023.

Last month was the joint second-warmest July globally on record, with temperatures 1.47C above the estimated pre-industrial average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.

Meanwhile, Western Europe experienced its hottest ever June and July, with prolonged hot and dry conditions fuelling extreme wildfires across the region.

Elsewhere, the UK is braced for its fifth heatwave of the year this week, as persistent dry weather puts further pressure on water supplies and could see more areas officially declared in drought.

World.title: Netanyahu's rejection of Trump's 15-point Gaza plan unlikely to be final word
World.content:
In July, after months of delicate negotiations, Trump announced a "major milestone" in the implementation of his plan to end Israel's war in Gaza.

Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump said that the Board of Peace had reached an agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups in the territory.

The deal is meant to be carried out in phases, with all weapons decommissioned and stored by a new Palestinian administration in Gaza â which reports to the Board of Peace - and Israeli forces withdrawing from the more than 60% of Gaza they currently control.

Senior Hamas officials confirmed that they had agreed to the new framework, conditioning it on mutual compliance by Israel. This was widely viewed as a major potential breakthrough in the conflict. The UK welcomed it and the European Union hailed it as a "crucial step".

However, for more than a week, Israel did not give its formal response.

An Israeli spokesman said only that the roadmap did not "reflect Israel's positions." A far-right member of the government, Itamar Ben-Gvir, wrote on X that the deal was "unacceptable."

Increasingly, mainstream Israeli opposition politicians also raised doubts. They questioned whether all small arms would be decommissioned and the sequencing of the plan.

Finally on Sunday, Netanyahu told his cabinet, "I wish to be precise here: Israel does not accept the 15-point document."

He added: "The IDF [Israel Defense Forces] will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament."

In the same statement, the prime minister described President Trump as "the greatest of our friends in the White House" but said that Israel knew "how to stand firm" against unacceptable ideas.

In Israel, there is widespread scepticism that Hamas intends to follow through on its commitments.

The Islamist movement has long seen "armed struggle" as a core precept, its legitimate response to Israeli occupation of Palestinian lands. In recent months, there had been signs of it reasserting its authority in Gaza.

"Israel can certainly never agree to retreating anywhere where the terrorist group that caused the worst massacres since the Holocaust is still there and is still ruling the Strip," Fleur Hassan-Nahoum, an Israeli commentator and former deputy mayor of Jerusalem told the BBC.

She stressed that the "trauma of the Israeli people" from the deadly Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023, which ignited the devastating Gaza war, should not be underestimated.

World.title: 'Total incinerated destruction': Canada wildfire evacuees wonder if they still have homes
World.content:
Earl Kurz and his wife have lived in Peachland, a town overlooking Okanagan Lake in Canada's British Columbia, for 30 years. In the last 10, he said he has grown used to wildfires threatening his community.

But this is the first time he's been forced to flee, and surveying the damage left behind by the Bald Range wildfire, which broke out on Friday and grew in a matter of hours to 53 sq miles (136 sq km) in size, has been difficult.

"It's total incinerated destruction," Kurz said. "The hot spots are just barren areas of nothing except 12 inches of ash."

Officials in British Columbia are still trying to determine how many homes were lost to the fire, which remains out of control as of Monday.

World.title: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
World.content:
The case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive.

It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017.

Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks.

Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government.

We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond.

Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia.

Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia.

The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction.

We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment.

When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence.

He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police.

He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg.

The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do.

The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible.

World.title: Former Thai MP allegedly kills official and confesses on YouTube
World.content:
A former Thai MP allegedly shot dead a local official near Bangkok, then dialled into a YouTube livestream to inform the host - a political pundit - of what he had done.

Former Nonthaburi MP Chalong Reawraeng told the shocked host, Anchalee Paireerak, that he had shot Thongchai Yenprasert, a former police official, outside Thongchai's office on the northern outskirts of the capital.

Thongchai, who was hit in the neck, died in hospital. His driver was shot in the arm and hand.

Chalong was arrested but then allowed to hold a press conference at a police station where he attempted to explain what had happened while smoking a cigarette.

Police say they granted the unusual request so that Chalong could apologise to the victim's family - but once behind the microphone he described his actions in detail for over six minutes.

He told reporters that Thongchai was "angry" at him, but did not explain why. He also said he did not intend to shoot Thongchai, whom he described as a "good friend".

Chalong said he told Thongchai that he wanted to talk to him. According to local media reports, the two were involved in a personal dispute.

"He [Thongchai] then pushed me, saying 'I don't want to talk, I don't want to talk.'"

Chalong said he then followed Thongchai towards his car.

"When I pulled the gun out, I didn't intend to shoot him. But then [Thongchai's driver] pulled his gun out and pointed it at me, so I fired."

Thongchai, a retired police colonel, was president of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organisation or PAO, a local government body.

World.title: Alleged rebel leader killed in Colombia as president targets armed groups
World.content:
Military intelligence officers said that Forero led a group known as Frente 28, which is one of the many dissident factions to have sprung forth from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).

The Farc, Colombia's largest left-wing rebel group, signed a peace deal with the government in 2016 but some of its members did not agree to the terms of the deal and refused to lay down their arms.

These dissidents groups, which are now mainly involved in cocaine trafficking and illegal mining, are among the main driving forces behind the resurgence in violence in the country.

De la Espriella said he would take a radically different approach to defeating criminal groups in the country than his predecessor in office, Gustavo Petro.

Petro, the first left-wing politician to be elected president of Colombia, advocated what he called a "total peace" strategy, which prioritised negotiation over confrontation.

His attempts to negotiate with a number of armed groups, however, failed as members of the illegal organisations repeatedly broke ceasefires and walked away from the talks.

De la Espriella's combative approach has been met with defiance by dissident rebel groups.

On Saturday, just a day after the was sworn into office, two explosive devices went off.

In Cauca province, a car bomb exploded at a tollbooth, injuring two security guards, and in Cesar province, a police officer was killed by explosives dropped from a drone.

In a video uploaded to social media, de la Espriella praised the military for killing Forero, who was also known as "El ruso" (The Russian), and whom he described as an explosives expert.

He added that three more alleged members of the dissident group had been killed in the military operation in a rural area in Meta province.

The president also said that soldiers had killed two alleged members of another criminal group, the Gulf Clan, in a separate offensive in Antioquia province.

De la Espriella has the backing of US President Donald Trump, who endorsed his candidacy.

On Friday, the US state department said it planned to provide $1bn (Â£740m) in security assistance to de la Espriella's government.

It also welcomed Colombia into the US-led group dubbed "Shield of the Americas" - an alliance of Western Hemisphere countries which have pledged to co-operate in their fight against drug trafficking gangs and transnational crime.

World.title: China evacuates one million from homes as massive storm arrives
World.content:
Chinese authorities have evacuated more than a million people from their homes in eastern China including the financial capital Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall.

The typhoon brought heavy rain and halted transportation across the region. Nearly 1,000 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone on Monday.

While authorities have downgraded Dolphin to a tropical storm, they continue to warn of torrential rains, severe flooding and the risk of landslides through to Wednesday as the storm moves north.

Chinese authorities had earlier issued their highest-level red alert for Dolphin, which is the strongest storm to hit China this year.

It packed maximum wind speeds of 150km/h (94mph) when it first slammed into Yuhuan in the Zhejiang province at 17:30 (09:30 GMT) on Sunday before making a second landfall in the city of Wenzhou about an hour later, meteorological authorities said.

Heavy rain was forecast on Monday for the provinces of Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and the city of Shanghai.

World.title: Lassa Fever: 53 health workers infected as cases hit 1,000 in 2026
World.content:
Nigeria has recorded 1,000 confirmed cases of Lassa fever, with 237 deaths in 2026, according to the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC).

The figure includes 53 healthcare workers who have been infected with the disease, highlighting the continued risk faced by frontline health workers responding to the outbreak.

The agency released its situation reports for epidemiological weeks 29 and 30 on Monday, covering 13 to 19 July and 20 to 26 July, respectively.

According to the Week 30 report, Nigeria recorded 17 new confirmed cases and six deaths during the week, bringing the cumulative figures to 1,000 confirmed cases and 237 deaths.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

More details

According to the NCDC, the case fatality rate increased slightly from 23.5 per cent in Week 29 to 23.7 per cent in Week 30.

The NCDC said 23 states have now reported at least one confirmed case across 116 local government areas (LGAs).

Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue accounted for 86 per cent of all confirmed cases, with Ondo recording the highest proportion at 32 per cent, followed by Bauchi with 25 per cent. Taraba accounted for 13 per cent; Edo, 10 per cent and Benue, six per cent.

Health workers remain at risk

The NCDC reported one new healthcare worker infection in Week 30, bringing the number of healthcare workers infected with Lassa fever in 2026 to 53.

The agency said infections among healthcare workers remain one of the challenges in controlling the outbreak.

It said it had developed a 30-day Healthcare Worker Protection Plan to reduce infections among frontline health workers in high-burden states, with support from the World Health Organisation (WHO) and the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The agency also reported training frontline healthcare workers, strengthening infection prevention and control programmes, pre-positioning personal protective equipment and providing technical support to investigate and mitigate healthcare worker infections.

Challenges

The NCDC identified late presentation of patients as one of the challenges contributing to the high case fatality rate.

It also cited poor health-seeking behaviour linked to the high cost of Lassa fever treatment and clinical management.

Other challenges identified by the agency include poor environmental sanitation, limited awareness in high-burden communities and infections among healthcare workers.

The NCDC recommended year-round community engagement on Lassa fever prevention and urged healthcare workers to maintain a high level of suspicion for the disease, ensure timely referral and treatment, and adhere to standard infection prevention and control procedures.

About Lassa Fever

Lassa fever is a viral haemorrhagic disease transmitted primarily through contact with food or household items contaminated by the urine or faeces of infected rodents.

Human-to-human transmission can also occur through contact with bodily fluids.

Symptoms typically begin with fever, weakness and headache but can progress to severe complications, including bleeding, respiratory distress and organ failure if not treated early.

World.title: Standing Still: No surprises, the Falcons have fallen
World.content:
The signs have been there since last year, when the collective strength of the players, not any masterplan from the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF), dragged the team to a 10th WAFCON title in Rabat.

With twelve months to restrategise and rebuild a squad capable of surviving an increasingly competitive women’s football landscape, the Falcons, led by coach Justin Madugu, and the NFF instead stood still. So, there was no real surprise on Sunday when a 19th-minute free-kick from Cameroon’s Myriam Nyadjou was enough to end Nigeria’s title defence at the quarter-final stage in Casablanca, the earliest continental exit for the Falcons in recent memory, and one that leaves their automatic ticket to the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil gone.

Like the biblical Samson, who did not know his strength had left him, the Falcons arrived in Morocco believing that ten stars on the badge and a rich history would be enough to waltz through. It wasn’t. Nigeria stumbled through the group stage. They lost to WAFCON debutants Malawi, scraped past Zambia 1-0, and needed a fortuitous 6-2 rout of Egypt to survive on goal difference.

In Nigerian parlance, they wobbled and fumbled their way into the quarter-finals, where Cameroon shut them out entirely. Only the four WAFCON semi-finalists earn automatic World Cup places. Under Gusau’s NFF, both of Nigeria’s flagship national teams, the Super Eagles and the Super Falcons, have now failed to qualify for their respective World Cups through the front door. That is not misfortune. That is the cumulative cost of two decades of drift.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

What should have happened

Twenty years ago, Nigeria’s advantage in African women’s football was so overwhelming that a serious, funded, long-term plan could realistically have produced a World Cup semi-finalist by now. Three things were needed, and none were sustained.

A real domestic league, treated as infrastructure rather than charity. The Nigeria Women’s Football League has survived on the goodwill of state governments and sporadic sponsorship rather than a coherent commercial and broadcast strategy. Compare that to Morocco, which five years ago launched a deliberate national women’s football strategy, based on youth academies, a professionalised league, coaching pipelines, and is now reaping continental finals and automatic World Cup qualification as a direct result. Nigeria had a decade’s head start in talent and squandered it in administration.

A structured pathway from Flamingos and Falconets to the senior team. Nigeria’s women’s youth sides have consistently reached the latter stages of global finals, proving that raw talent has never been the problem. What has been missing is a federation-run bridge, a clear coaching philosophy, sports science, and fitness benchmarks that translate youth promise into senior-team readiness, rather than leaving each generation to rediscover form from scratch under a new coach.

A proper diaspora and welfare strategy

Nigeria’s biggest asset is the number of Falcons playing in Europe and the United States. But scouting, integration, and camp welfare have too often been reactive. Players called up close to tournaments, bonus disputes resurfacing at the worst possible moments, and preparation windows compressed instead of planned years in advance. A federation serious about semi-finals and beyond would have built year-round data on every eligible player abroad and resolved welfare issues long before they became distractions at major tournaments.

None of this required extraordinary money. It required continuity of leadership and a plan that outlived any single NFF administration, something Nigerian football has rarely had.

How the damage can be reversed

The damage is not irreversible, but it will not be undone by the rhetoric of the kind Amaju Pinnick’s era was known for or by another four years of ad hoc tournament preparation.

First, whoever wins September’s NFF election must present, before the vote, a costed and time-bound women’s football strategy, not a manifesto line but a document with named milestones, the way Morocco’s federation did.

Second, the domestic league needs a broadcast and sponsorship overhaul that makes playing in Nigeria financially viable again, so talent isn’t lost to obscurity before it can be scouted. Third, a full-time technical department should track every Nigerian-eligible player abroad from the youth level, so squad-building for major tournaments starts years, not months, in advance.

Fourth, welfare and bonus structures need to be settled in contract terms and made permanent, removing the recurring off-field distractions that have dogged the team at major tournaments.

Let me be clear. For the Super Falcons, the playoff route to Brazil isn’t just a path; it’s the only door left standing. Miss it, and this generation watches the World Cup from home for the first time. That alone should be unthinkable.

But here’s the painful truth: even qualification won’t erase two decades of stagnation. It will only delay the reckoning. Yet if the Falcons fail to make it to Brazil entirely? That missing presence would make the case for reform in September undeniable, not by choice, but by the sheer weight of humiliation.

And perhaps, heartbreakingly, that might be the only silver lining left: a crisis so loud that even the deaf finally hear the call for change. Also, much more painful is that instead of resigning their posts, the administrators, collectively, are seeking another team in office—for what?

Nigeria has never lacked players capable of reaching a World Cup semi-final. What it has lacked, for two decades, is a federation willing to build the system around them. September’s election is the clearest chance in years to change that.

World.title: Groups urge Tinubu to reject tobacco control amendment, demand fresh legislative review
World.content:
Civil society and public health organisations have urged President Bola Tinubu to withhold assent to a proposed amendment to Nigeria’s tobacco control law, warning that some provisions could weaken existing safeguards against tobacco and nicotine addiction, particularly among young people.

The groups made the call at a press conference in Abuja on Monday, titled “Why Nigeria Must Reject Harmful Amendments to the National Tobacco Control Act.”

The event was organised by the Nigeria Tobacco Control Alliance (NTCA), in collaboration with Corporate Accountability and Public Participation Africa (CAPPA) and other tobacco control organisations.

Beyond asking Mr Tinubu to withhold assent, the coalition called on the National Assembly to recall the consolidated National Tobacco Control (Amendment) Bill, 2025, and subject it to what it described as a transparent, public health-led review.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The demand followed the Senate’s approval of the bill after its earlier passage by the House of Representatives, bringing the proposed legislation closer to presidential consideration.

‘Reject the bill’

Reading the coalition’s statement, CAPPA Executive Director Akinbode Oluwafemi said the organisations supported updating the National Tobacco Control Act, 2015, and its 2019 regulations to reflect changes in the tobacco and nicotine markets.

He, however, said such changes should not come at the expense of existing public health safeguards.

Mr Oluwafemi acknowledged provisions the coalition considered positive, including the proposed extension of smoke-free zones to within 30 metres of schools and health facilities, and the inclusion of the Nigeria Police Force and the ministry responsible for youth development in the National Tobacco Control Committee.

He argued, however, that these provisions did not outweigh other changes the coalition considered potentially harmful.

The coalition, therefore, urged Mr Tinubu to withhold assent if the bill reaches his desk.

It also asked the National Assembly to publish the committee reports, voting records and stakeholder submissions that informed the consolidated version of the bill.

The groups further called on the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare to clarify its position on the legislation and demand its recall if it was not adequately consulted during the legislative process.

Questions over consolidated bill

The Country Coordinator of the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids (CTFK), Michael Olaniyan, questioned how the consolidated version of the bill was produced, claiming it contained provisions not included in documents presented at the House of Representatives’ public hearing in November 2024.

According to him, the earlier documents totalled four pages, while the consolidated version runs to 31 pages.

“What we have now is a 31-page new document that suddenly emanated from a four-page combined document,” he said.

Mr Olaniyan questioned how the additional provisions were introduced and which public health institutions were consulted before they were incorporated.

Advertising loopholes

Mr Oluwafemi also raised concerns about provisions the coalition said would relax existing restrictions on tobacco advertising, promotion and sponsorship.

He said the bill would permit the promotion of non-combustible products through adult publications, point-of-sale materials, and online platforms, as well as the sponsorship of cultural, social, and recreational events targeted at adults.

He particularly criticised the proposed definition of an “adult publication” as one with a readership of at least 50 per cent adults.

According to him, such a threshold could allow publications with substantial numbers of younger readers to carry s for tobacco and nicotine products.

Smaller packs, weaker enforcement

The Executive Director of A New Thing International Foundation, Kenneth Anetot, said provisions allowing tobacco and nicotine products to be displayed at points of sale and sold in smaller packs could increase their visibility and accessibility among young people.

Mr Anetot said adolescents were particularly vulnerable to addictive substances because their brains were still developing, including areas involved in decision-making and impulse control.

He urged the National Assembly to recall the bill and allow wider stakeholder participation in its review.

READ ALSO: Group warns against tobacco industry still targeting Nigerian youths despite control laws

Nigeria’s tobacco burden

The coalition’s concerns come as tobacco control advocates warn that tobacco use and nicotine addiction continue to impose a significant health and economic burden on Nigeria.

The WHO describes tobacco as a major risk factor for cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, more than 20 types of cancer and other debilitating health conditions. It also states that tobacco kills more than seven million people globally each year.

In Nigeria, the NTCA has previously cited estimates that tobacco-related illnesses cost the country more than N211 billion annually, including healthcare expenses and productivity losses, while nearly 30,000 people died from tobacco-related causes in 2021.

The alliance said young Nigerians were being exposed to smoking, vaping and shisha imagery through music videos, fashion and digital platforms.

A recent study also raised concerns about tobacco marketing targeting women and girls in Nigeria, suggesting that the industry is expanding its marketing strategies to reach new groups of potential consumers.

The health and economic burden of tobacco has also heightened concerns about weakening the safeguards Nigeria has built over the years.

Speaking at Monday’s event, NTCA Coordinator Olawale Makanjuola said Nigeria had made significant progress in tobacco control and argued that some of its regulatory approaches had become reference points for other African countries.

He cited efforts to regulate tobacco imagery in entertainment as one area in which Nigeria had made progress.

Mr Makanjuola warned that provisions in the proposed amendment could reverse some of those gains.

He urged the government and lawmakers to ensure that any changes to the National Tobacco Control Act strengthen, rather than weaken, protections against tobacco and nicotine-related harm.

World.title: After years of delay, Niger begins gratuity payment
World.content:
The Niger State Pension Board has begun paying gratuities to state and local government retirees and death benefits to the next of kin of deceased beneficiaries, as part of efforts to reduce the backlog of benefits in the state.

The Director-General of the Board, Nasiru Namaska, flagged off the payment in Minna, where he commended Governor Mohammed Bago for releasing funds to settle outstanding gratuity liabilities owed to retirees.

Mr Namaska said that some beneficiaries had retired more than 10 years ago without receiving their gratuity.

He said the Bago administration inherited a huge backlog of liabilities and had been releasing funds in batches to address the outstanding obligations.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to him, the government has so far released about ₦7 billion towards the settlement of gratuity liabilities.

The director-general said eligible beneficiaries in the current batch would receive 100 per cent of their approved gratuity, in accordance with the governor’s directive.

Payments are being made through cheques.

Mr Namaska urged retirees whose names were not included in the current batch not to panic, assuring them that their cases would be reviewed and that affected beneficiaries would be considered in subsequent batches.

He also appealed to beneficiaries to remain patient as the Board continue the process of clearing the outstanding liabilities.

Death benefits

On death gratuity, Mr Namaska said the next of kin of deceased beneficiaries must present a Letter of Administration or a court declaration before payment can be processed.

He added that where there are two beneficiaries, both must be present before the cheque can be released.

The director-general urged beneficiaries to collect their cheques and lodge them in their respective bank accounts before the end of the day.

He also commended the Commissioner for Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs, Mu’azu Jantabo, for providing the modalities that facilitated the payment to local government retirees.

The Permanent Secretary, Establishment, Joanna Pada, also commended Mr Bago for approving the release of funds and urged the beneficiaries to use their entitlements judiciously.

Retirees’ long wait

The latest payment comes against the background of years of concern over unpaid gratuities and retirement benefits in Niger State.

In May 2024, Governor Bago announced approval of ₦25 billion to pay outstanding pensions and gratuities owed to retired civil servants.

The announcement followed years of complaints and pressure from retirees over the delay after retirement.

An investigation published by The ICIR in February 2024 documented the difficulties faced by retirees over unpaid benefits and reported their protests.

The government subsequently flagged off payment to an initial batch of 335 retirees in July 2024.

By November 2024, the Pension Board said it had paid more than ₦4 billion in eight batches.

However, the payment process later faced interruptions. In December 2025, the Niger State Council of the Nigeria Union of Pensioners said gratuity payments had stopped at Batch 11 for state retirees, while local government retirees had not received payments beyond Batch 2. The Union called for the resumption of payments.

In January 2026, Governor Bago announced plans to resume gratuity payments and directed relevant authorities to reinvest the funds further to ensure payments go to genuine beneficiaries.

He also said the state had no outstanding pension or salary arrears at the time.

Archives verification

Before the commencement of the latest payment exercise, Mr Namaska took members of the media on a tour of the Pension Board’s archives.

He explained that the board retrieves, sorts, and verifies beneficiaries’ files and records before processing payments.

He said the verification process is intended to ensure accuracy and prevent irregularities in the payment of public funds.

Beneficiaries speak

For some beneficiaries, the payment represents relief after years of waiting.

Tukura Kwaliki, one of the beneficiaries, described the payment as a significant moment after years of uncertainty.

“This is not just money to me. It is the reward for many years of service and sacrifice. After waiting so long, receiving this gratuity has brought relief to my family and me. I am grateful that the government has finally remembered people like us.”

For Zainab Suleiman, who came to receive the death benefit on behalf of her family, the payment was particularly significant given the circumstances of the claim.

“Losing a loved one is painful enough, and waiting for an entitlement after that loss makes it even harder. Today, we have received some relief. We sincerely appreciate everyone who made this possible, and we hope other families, still waiting, will also receive their entitlements.”

The latest exercise is expected to be part of the Niger State Government’s ongoing efforts to clear liabilities owed to retired state and local government workers and the families of deceased beneficiaries.

World.title: Funke Akindele sets another December box-office test with ‘The Four’
World.content:
Nollywood actress and filmmaker Funke Akindele is set to return to cinemas in December with her latest feature film, The Four: No One Fights Alone.

The film is scheduled for a cinema release on 11 December, with FilmOne Entertainment handling its theatrical distribution. It is produced by Funke Akindele Network (FAAN TV).

Akindele, who wrote, directed and produced the film, unveiled its cast on Monday, with the project featuring Richard Mofe-Damijo (RMD), Bisola Aiyeola, Chioma Akpotha, Waje, Timini Egbuson, Lateef Adedimeji, Ali Nuhu, Uzor Arukwe and Wunmi Toriola, among others.

Other members of the ensemble include John Ekanem, Ireoluwa Olaniyan, Omotunde Adebowale David, popularly known as Lolo1, Mide Iwasokun, Kolapo Omotosho, Shoday, Ogbolor, Ronke Oshodi Oke, Antar Laniyan, Samuel Banks and Ayomide Iwasokun.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The December release extends what has become a significant year-end cinema run for Akindele, whose last three December films have successively raised the bar at the Nigerian box office.

The Four

The Four is described as an emotionally driven drama centred on friendship, motherhood, resilience and the strength of ordinary women.

The story follows Esosa and three fiercely loyal women whose determination to secure the future of a young man they care about puts their friendship, courage, faith and loyalty to the test.

The film also explores themes of hope, sacrifice and unity, while incorporating music, fashion, language and tradition to reflect aspects of Nigeria’s cultural identity.

Unveiling the film on her X page, Akindele said the project was conceived around relationships and experiences audiences could recognise in their own lives.

“Audiences have grown with us over the years, and they expect stories that entertain while reflecting who we are.

“With The Four, we are exploring the relationships that shape us, challenge us and stay with us. I think audiences will find a part of themselves in this story,” she said.

Another box-office test

The Four arrives on the back of three successive December releases that have strengthened Ms Akindele’s position as one of Nigeria’s most commercially successful filmmakers.

A Tribe Called Judah, released in 2023, became the first Nigerian film to surpass the ₦1 billion mark and eventually ended its theatrical run with about ₦1.4 billion.

A year later, Everybody Loves Jenifa surpassed that performance, grossing about ₦1.88 billion.

Akindele raised the benchmark again with Behind The Scenes, released in December 2025, which recorded a reported gross of approximately ₦2.76 billion.

Her other commercially successful productions include Omo Ghetto: The Saga and Battle on Buka Street.

The 11 December release of The Four will test whether Akindele can sustain the box-office momentum of her recent December releases and extend a run that has repeatedly rewritten Nigerian cinema records.

World.title: WAFCON 2026: Madugu takes responsibility as Super Falcons face World Cup playoff after Cameroon defeat
World.content:
Super Falcons head coach Justin Madugu has apologised to Nigerians and taken responsibility for Nigeria’s disappointing quarter-final defeat to Cameroon at the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations, insisting the team will fight to secure a place at next year’s FIFA Women’s World Cup through the playoffs.

Nigeria’s hopes of securing an automatic ticket to the 2027 World Cup were dashed after Cameroon claimed a 1-0 victory in Casablanca, with Maéva Nyadjou’s free-kick proving decisive.

The defeat means the Super Falcons must now navigate the African playoff route for one of the remaining opportunities to qualify for the tournament in Brazil.

Speaking after the game, a visibly disappointed Madugu apologised for failing to deliver the result Nigeria needed.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“First of all, I want to apologise to Nigerians over our inability to win today’s game, which would have qualified us for the World Cup. It was not our intention,” Madugu said.

“The ladies did the best that they could, but that’s the way the game was destined to go.

“We apologise, and I take responsibility for that. We still have a second chance, and we will do our best to see what comes out of it.”

Madugu denies division in Super Falcons camp

Madugu was also questioned about Nigeria’s late substitutions and the incident involving Esther Okoronkwo and Asisat Oshoala towards the end of the match.

Okoronkwo had an opportunity to equalise and opted to go for goal instead of passing to Oshoala, who appeared to be in a better position to score. The decision prompted a visible reaction from the experienced forward.

Asked whether there was any division within the squad or whether incentives reportedly promised to the players by the National Sports Commission had influenced their decisions, Madugu dismissed the suggestion.

“To the best of my mind, the girls, there’s no problem in the camp. There are no camps within the girls,” he said.

“They are all on the same page. They have been working together, cooperating. It’s just one of those things that can happen in the course of a game.

“I’m sure she felt she could score. That was why she made the attempt and probably would have passed the ball to Asisat, who was in a better position to score. But that is not to say there is any division amongst them.

“There is no division in the team. And again, well, I wouldn’t attribute that to the promises made by the National Sports Commission.”

Madugu instead blamed Nigeria’s failure to take their chances, insisting the Super Falcons created more opportunities against Cameroon than in their previous matches.

“In all the games they played, they never created the kind of chances they created today,” he said.

“But it’s just that the conversion was not right, and we were not precise and clinical with our finishing. And that accounted for why we couldn’t score the goals from the chances that were created. It’s just one of those things that happen in football.”

Super Falcons refuse to give up on World Cup dream

With Nigeria’s direct qualification opportunity gone, Madugu acknowledged the disappointment surrounding the result but promised that the team would make the most of its second chance.

“I quite understand the pains everybody is going through. We all know what it means for all of us as a country. And as I said, I apologise and take responsibility for that,” he said.

“But we still have a second chance, and we’ll give it our all to make sure that we do not disappoint and go the same way that the men took.

“We will do our best and try to get it right to make sure that we go through the playoffs.”

Madugu gives Cameroon credit

The Super Falcons coach also praised Cameroon for their defensive organisation and overall performance, while maintaining that Nigeria had enough opportunities to win the contest.

“I would like to give the Cameroonian team credit. I would like to congratulate the Cameroon team. They won their game today,” Madugu said.

“They came in via sort of the highest, one of the best-ranked teams in the tournament. And for their group, they won their two games and drew with Cape Verde in a match that did not really matter for their position.

“And for today, they did the best they could. They defended very well. But in spite of all that, we still created a lot of chances, which, if we had converted, the result would have been different.

“But that is not to say you take anything out from the effort, the energy they also expended in trying to make sure they had the game and get the result we didn’t get.

“So I give them credit for it, and we see how it goes.”

Nigeria will now turn their attention to the playoff, where South Africa await as another major hurdle in their quest to reach the 2027 World Cup.

Madugu said the coaching staff would conduct a detailed assessment before preparing for the crucial encounter.

“Yeah, we get another game, playoff of a second chance against South Africa. We go back, watch all the games still and then come up with a plan where we know it can help us because we cannot afford to drop that second opportunity.

“We have to give it all our best.”

Madugu admits changes could be considered

The coach also admitted that the quarter-final defeat would force the technical crew to assess every aspect of the team, including the possibility of introducing new players.

“It’s quite natural that when things like this happen, you have to do an overall assessment of the team. What went wrong? What did we do well? Where did we get it wrong?” he said.

“We have to do an overall assessment and then see what we can do within the shortest possible time before the next game against South Africa.

“There’s nothing bad in exploring other players.”

Madugu also defended goalkeeper Chiamaka Nnadozie despite her involvement in the decisive moment, insisting that one mistake should not define her quality.

“Chiamaka has been a wonderful goalkeeper, not only in the national team, but even in a club. But like you are saying, anybody can make mistakes at any time, and then it could be costly, just as it was costly for us today.

“But that is not to say she’s a bad goalkeeper. It’s just one of those things that’s meant to be.”

Plumptre’s absence still a concern

Madugu also returned to Nigeria’s defensive struggles and pointed to the absence of Ashleigh Plumptre as one factor the team has had to contend with.

“It’s the same players that played last year that were not conceding goals. It’s the same players, the same group of players. Only one person is missing.

“Only Ashleigh Plumptre. And Ashleigh was playing from even the left fullback position. It was only Ashleigh.

“So, I mean, it’s something that we’ve been bothered, we’ve worried about it. We’ve been doing a lot to try and fix all this. But like I said, it’s just one of those things and we still have to continue to work.

“It’s still a work in progress.”

Madugu: Super Falcons must keep fighting

Despite the disappointment of losing their quarter-final, Madugu insisted Nigeria’s attacking approach was not entirely to blame, arguing that chances can come from different areas of the pitch.

“They got a goal from a set-piece, and it ended the game. So, chances can come from different aspects of the game, not necessarily just through build-up play,” he explained.

“We still had chances, a few chances that were created through the middle, but they had a good plan of trying to ensure that they block the central area, which assisted them.

“We equally had our own plan of ensuring that we go through the wings, and we were still creating chances from those wings. It’s not as if we didn’t have a plan to ensure that we could also go through the middle.”

He pointed specifically to Okoronkwo’s late opportunity as evidence that Nigeria were still capable of creating chances centrally.

“The chance Esther got, the final ball that came, it was not from the wing. It came through the middle,” Madugu said.

“So, sometimes when games go like this, it has a different way of interpretation, and then you just have to take it the way it is.

“It was not our intention that the game should go the way it went. If we had been more clinical, the result would have been different.”

With Nigeria’s World Cup hopes now resting on the playoff route, Madugu knows the margin for error has become even smaller.

“Going forward, like I said, as long as there is still an opportunity, we cannot afford to drop our guard,” he said.

“We will learn from this and go back and continue to work to make sure that we exploit the second chance that we have.

“We cannot give up. We must continue the fight.”

World.title: ‘I’m definitely not finding any woman, ever’ — Frank Edoho
World.content:
Veteran television host Frank Edoho has ruled out finding another partner, saying he has discovered a “superpower” in being alone.

The 54-year-old made the declaration on X in response to reactions to his appearance at the wedding of content creators Peller and Jarvis, where he declined to offer the newlyweds marital advice.

When asked during the ceremony to advise the couple, Edoho questioned his suitability for the task and chose instead to offer them his good wishes.

“You’re asking me, who knows nothing about marriage, to advise the couple? I am going to give my wishes instead.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I wish Peller the happiest of lives, the best of blessings and the utmost of peace,” he said.

His response prompted an X userX user to praise him for declining to give marital advice, while suggesting that his experiences with marriage could make Nigerians reluctant to accept his advice.

The user also expressed hope that Edoho would eventually meet a woman who would show him “true love”.

Edoho agreed with much of the user’s comment but rejected the suggestion that another relationship was in his future.

“How wise of you. You are absolutely right about everything but that last part.

“There’s a superpower that comes with being alone, and it’s beautiful. I’m definitely not finding any woman. Not ever,” he wrote.

His declaration generated reactions online, with some social media users linking it to his previous comments about marriage and relationships.

‘Never getting committed again’

The television personality’s latest statement is not the first time he has publicly ruled out another relationship.

In May, when asked about his relationship status, Edoho said he was single and had no intention of committing to another relationship.

“Yes. I have had my share. Never getting committed again. Ever,” he said.

He also said during an appearance on the Tea With Tay podcast that “maybe” he was not good at marriage.

The broadcaster has spoken about the emotional impact of his failed relationships and his decision to prioritise his personal peace.

Two marriages

Edoho was previously married to broadcaster and actress Katherine Obiang, with whom he has three children.

The marriage, which began in the early 2000s, ended after about seven years. Edoho has previously described the relationship as a mismatch and acknowledged that he was young when he got married.

The separation later became controversial, with Ms Obiang making allegations of physical abuse, which Edoho denied.

Edoho subsequently married Sandra Onyenucheya, an interior designer associated with Vivabella Designs, around 2013. They had two children together, bringing the broadcaster’s total to five children from both marriages.

He later said the marriage effectively ended in December 2022 and confirmed that they were undergoing divorce proceedings, describing the experience as devastating and saying he dealt with much of the pain privately.

The breakdown of the marriage subsequently became public, with Edoho and Sandra making allegations and counter-allegations concerning infidelity and other circumstances surrounding their separation.

Edoho alleged that his former wife had an affair with singer Chike, while Sandra disputed his account and levelled her own allegations against him, including claims concerning infidelity, emotional abuse and financial disagreements.

Both parties have disputed aspects of the other’s account.

Broadcasting career

Born in Kano, Edoho studied Animal Science at the University of Calabar before beginning his broadcasting career.

He later moved to Lagos and rose to national prominence as the host of the Nigerian edition of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? in 2004.

He hosted the game show for 13 years, becoming known for his calm presentation style, wit and the programme’s signature question, “Is that your final answer?”

After leaving the show in 2017, he later hosted The Price Is Right Nigeria and returned to Who Wants to Be a Millionaire when the programme was revived in 2022.

World.title: #OsunDecides2026: What Osun residents say about Governor Adeleke’s stewardship
World.content:
During the campaigns for the 2022 Osun State governorship election, Governor Ademola Adeleke repeatedly assured residents that his administration would chart a different course if elected.

Running as the candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), he promised improved welfare, economic growth, infrastructure development and people-centred policies, arguing that Osun deserved better governance.

Addressing thousands of supporters at a rally in Osogbo on 14 May 2022, Mr Adeleke unveiled a five-point agenda as the blueprint for his administration from 2022 to 2026.

Mr Adeleke’s agenda promised improved welfare for workers and pensioners, economic expansion through business partnerships and support for enterprises, and a homegrown infrastructure policy aimed at ensuring “Osun money serves Osun people.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The agenda also prioritised people-focused social policies centred on skill-based education, affordable healthcare, security, and social protection, alongside agro-based industrialisation to create jobs and wealth for the youth and women.

Barely two months later, he defeated the incumbent governor, Gboyega Oyetola, the All Progressive Congress (APC)’s flagbearer, in the 16 July 2022 governorship election by more than 28,000 votes.

Four years after

Nearly four years into his administration, Mr Adeleke, who was inaugurated on 27 November 2022, maintained that his government has delivered on its campaign promises.

Last month, he said his administration had recorded achievements across key sectors, including the construction of more than 300 kilometres of roads, the rehabilitation of over 200 primary healthcare centres and more than 150 public schools, as well as the continued payment of salary arrears and pension debts.

He also cited the disbursement of nearly N2 billion in cooperative financing, the provision of tractors and other farm inputs to support agricultural production, and the ongoing development of a standard stadium.

The administration had earlier, in November 2024, announced that it had cleared more than N47 billion in inherited pension liabilities within two years in office.

The government also stated that it approved the implementation of the N75,000 minimum wage for state workers as part of its commitment to improving workers’ welfare.

Mr Adeleke, who is seeking a second term under the Accord Party umbrella in Saturday’s election, said his administration fulfilled its pledge to make the University of Ilesa fully operational through the commissioning of several landmark projects.

He also pointed to investments in infrastructure at Osun State University (UNIOSUN), the advancement of the state’s ICT and digital economy agenda, and initiatives aimed at improving education and student welfare.

What Osun people say

Some residents of the South-west state, in separate interviews with PREMIUM TIMES, evaluated the government’s performance in the last three years and nine months.

While some praised the Adeleke administration for its performance, particularly in workers’ welfare, infrastructure and education, others said it fell short of their expectations in areas such as healthcare, security, tourism, investment and equitable distribution of infrastructure.

Maryam Adaranijo, a private-sector worker residing in Osogbo, the state capital, acknowledged the administration’s efforts on workers’ welfare but said she had seen little difference between the Adeleke-led government and its predecessors in overall performance.

“However, three and a half years down the line, I cannot see much of a difference. He did a lot for workers’ welfare and payments of pensioners; I’ll give him that. It’s just that there’s too much bias and nepotism in his style of governance.

“He focused too much on his hometown (Ede) in terms of infrastructure. Obviously, that should be expected, but it shouldn’t be at the detriment of the state capital (Osogbo). The only two projects he commissioned in Osogbo, Lameco Flyover and Oke-Fia Flyover, were unnecessary in my opinion when there are roads that need urgent intervention,” she said.

Ms Adaranijo specifically criticised the condition of the road linking Orisumbare Market, Station Road, Oja-Oba, Ayepe and Ilesha Garage, saying the route was narrow and in poor condition despite connecting Osogbo to Ilesha, one of the state’s major towns.

She also said the government should have paid greater attention to tourism and maintained projects inherited from previous administrations, arguing that such projects were funded by taxpayers.

“The annual Osun Osogbo festival is in a couple of days, yet the road leading to the groove is nothing to write home about. Mind you, this is a globally recognised festival by UNESCO. We should not still be clamouring for more investments in tourism in 2026.

“A lot of schools also built by APC have also been abandoned. It is taxpayers’ money, and they should be maintained,” Ms Adaranijo added.

However, Abdulmujeeb Tadese, a resident of Iwo in Osun West Senatorial District, gave the administration a more positive assessment. He commended its record on workers’ welfare and infrastructure, although he said his expectations were initially low because of what he described as “the maladministration of the previous Aregbesola-led government.”

“However, Adeleke came on board and not only cleared the half salaries for virtually all the workers but also increased the salaries being earned by the workers significantly. Promotion in Osun used to be merely on paper, without commensurate funding.

“On infrastructure, he did remarkably well, touching all 30 local governments in no small measure. Iwo, Ila, Ilesha and Ede now have their first-ever dual carriage roads, amongst several others,” Mr Tadese explained.

On concerns over the concentration of infrastructure projects in Ede, the governor’s hometown, Mr Tadese said other parts of the state had also benefited from the administration.

“The rest of us in other parts of the state are not left out at all. We are all beneficiaries, but we demand more. I will score him 85 per cent.”

Workers’ welfare, infrastructure

Abiola Oyetade, a sales representative residing in Modakeke, also praised the administration for its handling of workers’ welfare.

Having two civil servants as parents, he said he had personally witnessed the difficulties faced by workers under the previous administrations.

“Both my parents were civil servants, and I remember vividly what happened to civil servants during the regime of Governor Aregbesola. To cut a long story short, I think this present government is doing well. They have started paying all those outstanding debts,” Mr Oyetade said.

He also credited the administration with improving education in the state, particularly its position in education rankings and students’ performance.

“And talking about education, I think education in Osun State has really improved. Some years back, Osun would be rated between 28th, 30th or 31st, but I think now we are in the first five in the country. The students from Osun State also came, if not first or second, in the just-concluded UTME,” Mr Oyetade stated.

For AbdulJelili Oyebola, from Irepodun Local Government Area, the administration’s infrastructure efforts were noticeable, but he rated its overall performance as average. He said more attention should have been given to public education and healthcare, particularly at the grassroots level.

“What mostly concerns us at the grassroots, especially in Irepodun Local Government Area, is the provision of adequate healthcare facilities in our hospital, and ensuring enough teachers are available to our children in public schools,” he said.

Mr Oyebola also urged the state government to strengthen its agricultural support programmes by providing farmers across the state with inputs and equipment.

“Looking at the current Nigerian economy, it’s obvious we need to all go back to farming, so he should help us with farming inputs like tractors in our various local government areas; this will make living easy for us here,” he said.

He further called for closer monitoring of contractors handling government projects to ensure that infrastructure delivered across the state meets the required standards.

“I remember during the regime of Aregbosola, we heard he used to visit infrastructural projects after contractors left sites, even at night. If those contractors know their superiors will inspect their work closely, they will deliver quality projects,” Mr Oyebola added.

Ifeoluwa Olagbaju, a resident of Ife East Local Government Area, similarly acknowledged the administration’s efforts on infrastructure, workers’ and pensioners’ welfare, as well as agricultural support. However, he criticised its performance in healthcare.

“I don’t think he has done well in the health sector. If you go to Asubiaro, the patients there surpassed the number of doctors that should attend to them, which delayed the required time to attend to the patients, which really needs to be worked on; the available healthcare for patients is not so encouraging,” Mr Olagbaju said.

Bosede Omolara, a civil servant from Ikirun, offered a different assessment of the administration’s record on workers’ welfare, saying timely salary and gratuity payments had improved workers’ morale and productivity.

“He fulfilled all his promises to us, civil servants, regarding our salaries and gratuity. We receive all these payments as and when due. And these have improved our rate and quality of work to the state as a whole; we work appropriately,” Ms Omolara said.

Taiwo Onayemi, a resident of Ipetu-Modu in Ife North Local Government Area, also praised the administration’s record on workers’ welfare but said it needed to do more on security.

“He has tried his best. On his five-point agenda, I will score him high in workers’ welfare, but practically, he does not seem to have figured it out, as the chief security officer of the state. Maybe it’s out of his jurisdiction.

“With the implementation of state police in the country, we hope governors will have their say on security in the state and protect their state further. We look forward to a better Osun in the near future,” Mr Onayemi stated.

Adeyemi Waheed, from Ede Local Government Area, said that the administration’s prioritisation of workers’ welfare had produced wider effects on other sectors of the state.

He said timely payment of salaries had improved workers’ morale, particularly among teachers, while putting more money in the hands of workers to support economic activity. He also linked the improved road network to easier movement of agricultural produce.

“We used to hear half salary, but he cleared all previous administration debts. Now, Osun State salary scale is far better, and it adopted the minimum wage ahead of any state in Nigeria. This has helped other sectors like education and the economy,” Mr Waheed said.

Business investment, job creation

For David Ojo, a cement retailer in the Power Line area of Osogbo, the government needs to do more to create an environment where businesses and young people can thrive.

The entrepreneur said the administration had made progress in workers’ welfare but should place greater emphasis on agriculture, industrialisation and support for small businesses.

“As an entrepreneur, I look at things from the angle of how much the government is helping businesses and creating opportunities for people to make money for themselves. In that area, I think there is still a lot more to be done.

“I expected to see more support for small businesses, more investment in agriculture and more industries that can create jobs for young people. So, I would say the government has made progress, but I don’t think it has fully met my expectations yet. I would give him 65 per cent on performance,” Mr Ojo said.

Zainab Fatiu, a university student in Kwara State but resident in Osogbo, also acknowledged improvements in road construction, workers’ salaries and infrastructure, but said the administration had yet to meet all expectations.

“Overall, I will say he has done well, but not all expectations have been fully met. I think the governor has made some progress in delivering on the promises he made before the 2022 election, especially in road construction and workers’ welfare. On a scale of one to 10, I would rate his performance seven,” Ms Fatiu said.

The Osogbo-based undergraduate said the government should now focus more on employment opportunities for young people, healthcare, education and security.
