World.title: Discovering Mexico: Puebla
World.content:
Listen to this article

Puebla is for you if you like: Colonial history, sweeping mountains, racing while holding tortillas

Mexico’s fourth-largest city, Puebla, has more going on beneath its colonial facades than most visitors realize. Its historic center, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, holds 2,619 monuments — more than any other city in the Americas — plus the tallest cathedral bell towers in the country. The city’s well-preserved architecture has also made it a go-to filming location, standing in for 18th- and 19th-century Mexico and Spain in productions including “Frida” and “Man on Fire.”

All of this is before you get out into the wider state, where sweeping mountain ranges, active volcanoes and enormous cacti dot the landscape. The state is one of the last stops in southern Mexico before the jungle claims the country. We’ve collected some of our best pieces from the last few years, to help you experience one of Mexico’s most genuine — and stunning — regions.

Puebla’s capital — also, conveniently, called Puebla — is filled with the sort of magic that only Mexico’s oldest cities can really offer. Many of the nation’s most definining moments and people have filled these streets (and the tunnels underneath them).

Puebla’s identity is tied up in origin stories, although some more verifiable than others. Its early name, Puebla de los Ángeles, traces to a 1531 account of a bishop’s vision guiding Spanish settlers to the site. Its signature dish, mole poblano, is said to have been improvised by nuns at the Convent of Santa Rosa in 1680 when an archbishop arrived unannounced and the kitchen had little to offer but chilis, chocolate, nuts and stale bread. And on Nov. 18, 1910, the Serdán family home became the site of the first armed clash of the Mexican Revolution, two days before Francisco Madero formally launched the uprising; the bullet-scarred house is now a museum.

While its days of defining Mexico’s future are probably behind it, Puebla remains a fascinating destination for anyone who wants to understand how the modern country truly came to be.

While Oaxaca, Sonora and Yucatán often vie for the title of Mexico’s gastronomic heart, it’s really Puebla that deserves the credit for much of the nation’s great cuisine.

Puebla’s culinary reputation rests on three dishes with stories as rich as their flavors. Mole poblano, which rumour claims is a single flash of nun-driven inspiration, remains the most famous of Mexico’s 300-plus regional moles. Chiles en nogada, with its patriotic red, white and green color scheme, traces back to a 1821 feast honoring independence figure Agustín de Iturbide. Tacos árabes, born from Middle Eastern shawarma techniques brought by 1930s immigrants, is the progenitor of the iconic pastor.

The state is quite a bit more than just colonial architecture and great food, though. Just outside Tehuacán, Puebla’s second-largest city, sits a landscape that looks like it belongs on another planet.

The Tehuacán-Cuicatlán Biosphere sprawls across 145,255 hectares of protected desert, home to more than 2,500 species of cacti — tall and candle-thin, round as beach balls, or shaped like something out of a sci-fi set. A day inside it turns into a full sensory tour of the region: 2,000-year-old salt flats still worked by hand at Zapotitlán Salinas, a lunch built around cactus flowers and hibiscus water (with insects on offer for the adventurous) and a pottery workshop in Los Reyes Metzontla where clay deposits — leftovers from an ancient sea — get shaped into earthy, hand-thrown crockery.

In a small Puebla town two hours north of the city, an entire industry is built on Christmas spirit. Chignahuapan produces an estimated 70 million hand-blown ornaments a year, and inside the country’s largest esfera factory, the process starts with nothing more than a glowing-hot glass tube and a steady breath. From there, silver coatings, hand-mixed paint and careful dabs of glitter transform each piece into something ready for the tree — some ornaments even take a year to master.

Step inside the traditional workshop where trompos, Nativity scenes and piñata-shaped baubles come to life, one painstaking layer at a time.

In the days before Day of the Dead, the Puebla town of Huaquechula holds a tradition unlike anywhere else: the trueque, an ancient barter market where locals swap goods — peanuts, sugar cane, homemade bread — for everything needed to build their altars. Families trade for marigolds and cockscomb flowers, while vendors carry stacks of pan de muerto in its many forms, from bone-topped loaves to body-shaped muertitos dusted in red sugar.

Beyond the market, the town runs on hospitality: cooks prepare meals for hundreds of festival participants around the clock, and visitors are waved into strangers’ homes to see their altars up close. Huaquechula offers a rare, local variation on Mexico’s most iconic holiday — equal parts market day, family reunion and open-door celebration of the dead.

Our glimpse into Puebla ends on a unique note. The annual Carrera de la Tortilla, a 5-km race through Tehuacán that retraces the daily walk local women make to market, tortillas and all. Most runners came from Santa María Coapan, the self-proclaimed “Tortilla Capital” of Mexico, who run decked out in traditional Mixtec dress.

Part sporting event, part tribute to the women who keep the tradition alive, it’s one of Puebla’s more charming annual customs.

Puebla, Where Magic Lives in Every Journey / Sub English

Watch this video on YouTube

How to get there

When it comes to arriving in Puebla, it really only makes sense to arrive from Mexico City.

By air

Puebla International Airport: 45 minutes from the city center, the airport offers connections to almost every major Mexican destination, plus Newark, Houston and Los Angeles.

Mexico City Benito Juarez (AICM): The big one. About 2 hours (traffic permitting) from central Puebal. Available from everywhere in Mexico, and almost every major global airport besides.

Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA): The eternally troubled AIFA is finally beginning to come into it’s own. 2.5 hours away, it offers similar domestic connectivity to AICM and flights in from Colombia, Venezuela, the Dominican Republic and Cuba.

By road

Mexico City: 135km (83 miles) somewhere between 90 minutes and 3 hours, depending on when you travel. National holidays often lead to enormous tailbacks, but tackling the drive early on a weekday often means you can get there in less than two hours.

World.title: Ohuira Bay communities weigh federal plan for Sinaloa ammonia plant
World.content:
TOPOLOBAMPO, Mexico — When federal officials finally unveiled a plan last week to address the 12-year conflict over a nearly completed ammonia plant beside Ohuira Bay, Indigenous Yoreme activist, rural sociologist and law student Melina Maldonado did not feel relieved.

She felt crushed.

After six days of roundtable discussions, she had begun to feel hopeful; it seemed they were really taking in new information and seeing a different side to the debate. The proposal led her to believe otherwise.

“They didn’t listen to our reasons for saying no,” Maldonado said. “They listened for a way to make it a yes.”

The federal proposal promises environmental safeguards, community monitoring and public investment around the German-backed GPO-Proman plant in northern Sinaloa state. But it leaves the project’s operation largely intact — and that has exposed the fundamental divide at the heart of the conflict: The government is offering ways to make the plant safer, while the communities closest to the bay are still adamant that it should not operate at all.

Those communities must now take the proposal into their own assemblies and, using their traditional Indigenous consensus-based governance model, decide whether to accept it. Until then, the blockade outside the gate to the plant — now in its 72nd day — remains in place.

A proposal, not an agreement

The plan emerged after six days of talks involving federal and state officials, representatives of GPO-Proman and members of the ¡Aquí No! (Not Here!) collective, which is led by Yoreme-Mayo communities surrounding Ohuira Bay and has become the principal force opposing the plant.

Federal officials presented the proposal as a path toward resolving a conflict that has become one of Mexico’s longest-running and most contentious environmental battles. But movement leaders emphasized that no agreement has been reached and that they do not have the authority to accept the plan on behalf of their communities.

The proposal must first be explained and discussed in assemblies in Ohuira, Paredones, Lázaro Cárdenas and Topolobampo. These communities surround the Santa María-Topolobampo-Ohuira lagoon system, a Ramsar wetland of international importance, and would bear the plant’s most direct impacts.

Community response to the proposal

“We have to hold our own internal assemblies,” said Claudia Susana Quintero, a Yoreme educator, resident of the village of Ohuira and one of the leaders of ¡Aquí No! “We have to explain it to the community, analyze it and decide how we are going to reach consensus.”

The representatives’ role is to take the proposal home and return with a decision reached collectively — not to accept it on their communities’ behalf.

The US $1.6 billion plant, designed to produce 2,200 metric tons (2,425 tons) of ammonia a day, is reportedly about 88% complete. Opposition began soon after the project was approved in 2014 and has centered on threats to fishing, the lagoon ecosystem, industrial safety and what Yoreme communities describe as a deeply flawed Indigenous consultation.

The current protest began in late May, when residents tried to block the movement of massive absorption towers from the port. Protesters later shifted their encampment to the plant entrance, where they have remained through extreme heat and intense storms.

A project the government considers strategic

President Claudia Sheinbaum has defended the plant as important to Mexico’s goal of achieving greater food sovereignty. Ammonia is a principal raw material in nitrogen fertilizers, and Sheinbaum has said Mexico currently imports nearly all the fertilizer it uses, apart from production by state-owned company Fertinal.

She has also emphasized that the plant is nearly finished, and that it underwent an environmental review and received majority support in the government-led Indigenous consultation — a process the four communities closest to Ohuira Bay continue to dispute.

The Economy Ministry says the GPO plant could reduce Mexico’s fertilizer imports by as much as 70% and keep approximately US $500 million now spent on imports within the Mexican economy.

For the federal government, the plant is part of a broader strategy to reduce dependence on imported agricultural inputs. Opponents say that national goal does not justify concentrating the risks in their communities.

What the government put on the table

The proposal leaves the ammonia plant in place, but would significantly alter how it operates. Among its most significant provisions, the plan calls for GPO-Proman to stop drawing water directly from Ohuira Bay and instead use water discharged through a nearby Federal Electricity Commission canal.

Opponents have long warned that the plant’s authorized system would pull large volumes of seawater from the lagoon and return warmer, saltier water, potentially disrupting fish and shrimp nurseries. Under the new plan, wastewater would instead be carried offshore rather than released back into the lagoon system.

The plan also proposes a new environmental baseline study, continuous water-quality monitoring and an oversight body made up of community members, scientists, government officials and company representatives. Additional measures would address sewage and agricultural runoff already entering the bay, as well as emergency preparedness and civil protection.

Other commitments focus on longstanding community needs, including housing, education, fishing infrastructure and assistance in certifying local shrimp and crab products so they can command higher prices.

Economic development plans in Topolobampo

Federal commissioner Mauricio Rodríguez Alonso, who has led the talks, stressed at a Tuesday news conference that the plan grew out of dialogue among the communities, GPO-Proman and government agencies. He said the company had agreed in principle to its commitments.

Ulises Pinzón, Topolobampo’s municipal representative, said the package could bring meaningful benefits. He was particularly encouraged by provisions giving communities a voice over future petrochemical development.

That is especially significant in Topolobampo, which the federal government has designated as an economic development hub where chemical and petrochemical industries are among the priority sectors. The plan would also keep proposed methanol and urea plants and a port terminal on hold unless the communities agree to them.

But Pinzón noted that many of the promises involve responsibilities the government should already be fulfilling, rather than concessions from GPO-Proman itself.

“On paper, honestly, I see an attractive proposal,” he said. “The question is how we can ensure that these commitments are actually fulfilled.”

That distinction — between a promising announcement and a binding, enforceable agreement — is now one of the central questions confronting the communities.

The risk that remains

For opponents of the plant, the most troubling unresolved issue is the danger of a catastrophic ammonia release. The government proposal does include new safeguards: an emergency-response center, joint industrial-risk monitoring, water curtains around pipelines and storage tanks, and a regional civil-protection plan — something Rodríguez acknowledged does not currently exist.

But movement leaders say emergency planning and mitigation cannot eliminate the underlying danger documented in the company’s own risk assessment.

According to that assessment, a five-minute leak could create a high-impact zone extending roughly 15 kilometers (9 miles) from the plant, encompassing Topolobampo and nearby Yoreme communities. A broader impact zone could extend as far as 45 kilometers (28 miles), reaching toward Los Mochis and other surrounding communities.

“That risk is still there, and it is still not clear to us,” Pinzón said. “The first people affected would be those of us who live in Topolobampo.”

Loss of life is not remediable

Company project documents show the plant is designed to store up to 75,000 metric tons (82,670 tons) of anhydrous ammonia near populated communities. Quintero said the proposal may reduce certain environmental impacts, but it cannot eliminate the consequences of a major industrial accident.

“You can remediate many things,” she said. “What you cannot remediate is the loss of life.”

For Maldonado, this is where the government’s proposal misses the point. Her own community, the Yoreme fishing village of Lázaro Cárdenas, looks across the bay at the plant every day.

The communities’ opposition has never been limited to the plant’s effects on water quality or fisheries, she said. It is rooted in the belief that a facility carrying such risks should not operate near people’s homes. She pointed to the company’s brightly colored risk map.

“This is the risk zone the company itself identified,” she said. “And now they are minimizing it or pushing it into the background.”

A decision made under threat

The communities will not consider the proposal in a political vacuum. Several of the movement’s most visible leaders have received threats related to their opposition to the plant and now live under government protection measures.

Four of ¡Aquí No!’s most visible leaders, including Maldonado, Quintero and Ohuira traditional governor Felipe Montaño, have been enrolled in Mexico’s federal protection mechanism for human rights defenders and journalists. Protection measures can include bulletproof vests and government-issued panic buttons intended to summon help in an emergency.

But Quintero said such equipment offers little comfort as the communities prepare to deliver an answer that government officials and project supporters may not want to hear.

“I know my community is going to say no,” she said. “But now the government is putting us in the line of fire against the rest of society that says yes.”

She worries that the plan could recast defenders as obstacles to jobs and economic development, increasing the pressure on people who have already spent years facing intimidation for speaking publicly.

“A bulletproof vest and a panic button are not going to help me much if someone decides to act tomorrow,” Quintero said.

The experience, she added, has gradually consumed the rest of their identities.

“We are no longer mothers, daughters or sisters,” she said. “We are nothing more than defenders.”

From shock to strategy

By Thursday evening, the mood inside the movement had begun to shift.

Enrique Ayala, a longtime activist staying at the blockade, said movement leaders spent six hours Thursday with scientists and lawyers analyzing the proposal and plotting their next steps.

“The government proposal is one-sided,” Ayala said. “They are pushing ahead with their project.”

But after years of being ignored, Ayala sees the government’s willingness to sit down with them as progress.

“We have to get up, keep going and make proposals of our own,” he said. “After 12 years when they paid us no attention, now we have them sitting at the table.”

And despite the government’s apparent intention to move the plant toward operation, Ayala said the movement has not abandoned its original goal.

“We still believe we can get the company to leave,” he said. “Sometimes you have to dream.”

Tracy L. Barnett is a Guadalajara-based freelance writer and the founder of The Esperanza Project.

World.title: From the archive: A guide to Mexican nicknames and how they’re given
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in February 2025 — is a perfect example, offering humorous insight into the fine art of giving nicknames in Mexico.

If you’ve spent much time among Mexicans, you’ve probably realized something. They love to give each other — and consistently use — nicknames.

I’m not just talking about diminutives of names, though these are also popular. Guillermo, for example, is Memo for short, the same way Bob is a diminutive of Robert.

How nicknames work in Mexico

There’s Alex for both Alejandro and Alejandra, Chio for Rocío, Lalo for Eduardo, Lola for Dolores and Chava for Salvador. There’s also short versions of double names, like Mafer for María Fernanda, Majo for María José and my favorite, Lucifer for Lucía Fernanda, a name most people do not give their kids. And of course, the classic “-ito” and “-ita” can go at the end of many names. So sometimes people call me Sarita, and my partner Juanito. Careful with using these, though, as they’re often infantilizing, and as you very likely know, some people do not like being infantilized.

So you get the idea: most names here have a shortened version. But Mexicans don’t stop there!

My nicknames

I’ll admit that this makes me very happy. As a kid, I never had a nickname, and I was jealous that I didn’t. Thinking back, it’s probably better; it wouldn’t have necessarily been a nice one, as I was both a crybaby and a showoff. Come to think of it, I might still be both of those things. Thankfully, I don’t currently have any nicknames related to either of those characteristics. Yet.

I do have some other fun ones though. “Sirena polar” — polar mermaid — might be the most creative, given to me by a friend of my ex-husband who was amazed that I insisted on swimming in ice-cold water after a hike. For reasons unknown to me, this same friend also often called me “cara de nutria”: otter face. Maybe because otters swim in cold water, too? Another friend, not quite as creative, simply calls me “mi gringa favorita.” I’d be more flattered if I weren’t one of the only gringos she knows.

The futility of protesting against your nickname

Many nicknames are purposefully funny, and sometimes shocking. And from what I can tell, people don’t seem to be insulted by them. Sometimes I wonder if they actually are bothered but know that trying to fight back against the Mexican urge to make fun of everything is futile.

So when you get a name like “El Frijol” because you’re very dark-skinned, you just go along with it, I guess?

In the particular case of another acquaintance, the guy was tall and good-looking. He was married, but seemed to have no shortage of women interested in him, or of self-esteem.

I always wanted to ask him if the nickname bothered him, but we were never close, so the opportunity was lost. But I did get to ask my ex-husband, who his friends had nicknamed “el bello camello” — the beautiful camel — supposedly because they thought he looked Arab.

The new generation of nicknames

Could this be one of those cultural things that’s dying out with more socially conscious and sensitive younger generations? I don’t think it is, as my daughter, age 11, has several nicknames herself. At school, her friends sometimes call her Plana, which means flat. It’s a synonym of her name, Lisa, which means “smooth” in Spanish and is often featured on hair conditioner bottles. And in her Scout troop, every kid has a nickname, each one the name of a bird. She’ll also respond to “Mona,” which is kind of nice. “Mona” is more of a Spanish-from-Spain word for “pretty,” but in this case, of course it’s about the Mona Lisa.

So perhaps the tradition will continue?

Don’t take yourself too seriously

After several years of watching the issue of how people address them being taken very, very seriously north of Mexico, I’ll admit that I find the ability to joke around with silly nicknames refreshing. Like all humor, though, it’s very culturally specific; there are plenty of unspoken rules regarding when it’s funny and good-humored and when it’s not.

It’s not that I want the freedom to be gratuitously mean, which is something very different. But I do think that it’s always worth it to not take ourselves so seriously all the time, something most of us can agree makes us generally unlikable.

So if you get a nickname here, try to go with it. Because people don’t get nicknames when they’re not being included in a group. Even if it’s not one you’d have chosen for yourself, it’s a signal that you are part of a community; people know you.

They might be making fun, but it’s affectionate fun. Try to take it that way.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

Europe – The Record, and What Sits Underneath It

Warmest June and July ever measured

Western Europe averaged 21.62 degrees across June and July, the European Union’s climate service reported on Monday, 2.79 degrees above the 1991 to 2020 mean and above the previous record set in 2022. Its records run back to 1950.

The region has now had four separate heatwaves since May, which the service describes as exceptional. Eastern Europe and Scandinavia were markedly cooler, and for the continent as a whole July was only the eleventh warmest on record.

The soil is the number that matters

Surface soil moisture in Western Europe was clearly lower in July than during the drought July of 2022, with parts of Iberia, France, Germany, Austria, Hungary and Britain drier than average. The world’s oceans meanwhile recorded their warmest July on record at 20.96 degrees.

The service’s climate lead put the mechanism plainly, saying that when soils dry out they lose their ability to cool naturally, so heat builds more easily. Heat and drought, she said, are increasingly reinforcing each other.

The Rivers – Three Arteries Running Low

Shipping, irrigation and power at once

Levels on the Rhine, the Danube and the Seine are unusually low. Several countries have reported disruption to inland shipping, to irrigation and to electricity generation.

These are the arteries that move German chemicals, Dutch grain and Central European steel. When barges load light, freight costs rise across the whole corridor.

A continent discovering its own fragility

Europe has spent two decades treating its inland waterways as settled infrastructure. Three summers in five years have now shown that assumption to be wrong.

The mood is not alarm so much as a grudging recalculation. This is a continent adding a line to its cost base that was never there before.

Germany – Where the Weather Reaches the Accounts

Farms under pressure, output falling

Drought and heat are squeezing German agricultural businesses, and the farmers’ association is demanding faster action from government. German meat production has fallen again, with the decline particularly clear in poultry.

June was almost three degrees above average in Germany, with the southwest markedly warmer than the northeast. A second consecutive summer of this kind stops being weather and starts being a supply forecast.

Two numbers about German labour and tax

The trade union federation calculates that around two million employees are underpaid relative to the minimum wage each year, putting the cumulative shortfall since 2015 at roughly 64 billion euros against a statutory floor of 13.90 euros an hour. Separately, the finance minister has withdrawn a plan to tax associations more heavily after sustained criticism, striking the provision from the bill.

He said the intention had never been to reach small clubs but business associations and federations. A government retreating from a revenue measure it had just drafted says something about how little room it has.

Western Europe has just recorded its warmest June and July since measurements began, its soils are drier than in the drought of 2022, and the Rhine, Danube and Seine are all low enough to disrupt shipping — the summer has become a line in the cost base.

Spain – Two Hundred Thousand Hectares and a Revised Number

The fire season moves north

Nearly 200,000 hectares have burned in Spain since the start of the year. The European climate service notes that the fire season is extending northward, and that larger fires send smoke higher and further, affecting air quality thousands of kilometres away.

Spain is the European Union’s largest producer of olive oil and a major supplier of fruit and vegetables. What burns there is felt in food prices across the bloc.

Madrid revises Ceuta upward

The government now estimates that around 80,000 people entered the North African enclave of Ceuta irregularly during the surge of late July, up from a previous figure of 72,000. The territorial policy minister gave the revised number during a visit to the exclave on Monday.

Most of those who crossed returned to Morocco within 24 to 48 hours, and the surge occurred mainly on 30 July. Revising a figure upward by eight thousand two weeks later tells you how uncertain the counting was.

Three Continents – One Harvest Tightening

The same story from Lusaka to Seoul

The World Food Programme warned last week that a strengthening El Niño could push nearly 49 million more people into acute hunger by the end of 2027, with Southern Africa among the hardest hit. In Asia, China’s own state newspaper reported economies facing food security risks while Korean employers shortened the working day for heat.

Europe has now added its own record. Three continents are tightening their agricultural output within the same fortnight.

What that means for Latin America

This is not a weather story for Latin American readers, it is a price story. Simultaneous supply pressure across Europe, Africa and Asia points to firmer markets for soy, corn, beef, coffee, sugar and wheat.

Brazilian and Argentine exporters are the residual supplier when three other continents come up short. The risk sits on the other side of the same coin, since the weather system driving all of it does not stop at the Atlantic.

Energy – The Second Cost Line

Low water meets high fuel

The same low river levels disrupting freight are also affecting electricity generation, at a moment when European energy costs remain politically sensitive. Two constraints are arriving in the same quarter.

On the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran’s stated conditions continue to increase pressure on Washington, and nothing has been settled. Any resolution would ease European input costs immediately.

The quiet week that is not quiet

France, Italy and Britain produced nothing of substance on Monday, deep in the European holiday. That silence is seasonal rather than significant.

The costs accumulating in the meantime are not seasonal at all. Europe will return to its desks in September with a harvest, a freight bill and an energy question all worse than when it left.

The Bigger Picture Western Europe has recorded its warmest June and July since measurements began in 1950, averaging 21.62 degrees, 2.79 degrees above the long-run mean and beating the record set in 2022. Four heatwaves since May, soils drier than in the drought of 2022, and the Rhine, Danube and Seine all low enough to disrupt shipping, irrigation and power. In Germany the effect is already visible in the accounts, with farms under pressure and meat production falling again. In Spain nearly 200,000 hectares have burned this year, in a country that supplies much of the bloc’s olive oil, fruit and vegetables. For Latin American readers the significance is not the heat but the coincidence. Africa, Asia and Europe are all tightening agricultural supply within the same fortnight, which points to firmer prices for the region’s soy, corn, beef, coffee and sugar, and to a weather system that will not stop at the Atlantic. A magnitude 7.4 quake tore through western Colombia on Monday morning, killing dozens and handing a president just three days in office his first national emergency.

The Colombia earthquake that hit on Monday, 10 August 2026 was one of the strongest the country has felt in years. It struck at around 7:34 a.m. local time, and by midday the death toll had passed five dozen.

The tremor was centered about 5 kilometers east of San José del Palmar, a small town in the jungle department of Chocó. The United States Geological Survey put it at magnitude 7.4.

Because the quake was so powerful, it was felt across much of the country and into neighboring Ecuador and Panama. Buildings swayed hundreds of kilometers from the epicenter, and frightened residents ran into the streets.

What we know about the Colombia earthquake

The USGS measured the quake at magnitude 7.4 and placed its focus 107 kilometers below the surface. The European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre logged a slightly smaller magnitude of 7.2 at a similar depth.

That depth matters more than it sounds. A shallow quake concentrates its violence at the surface, while a deep one like this spreads the shaking over a much wider area but does less damage directly above.

It is the reason a monster 7.4 was felt from Quito to Panama City yet did not level whole towns. It is also why the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center ruled out any tsunami, saying the quake was too deep inside the Earth to move the sea.

The human toll

By the middle of Monday, local officials reported at least 69 deaths, and the number kept climbing as rescuers reached collapsed buildings. The dead included 40 in Risaralda, 27 in Valle del Cauca and two in Manizales.

Many more people were injured, and more than 20 municipalities reported damage. Collapsed or cracked buildings were confirmed in Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdó.

Six airports suspended operations, including those in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura. The closures cut off some of the fastest routes into the worst-hit areas just as help was most needed.

A president three days into the job

The disaster is the first major test for Abelardo de la Espriella, who was sworn in as president on Friday, 7 August 2026. He took office in Cali, breaking with tradition, and now that same city counts damaged buildings.

De la Espriella said he would take personal charge of the response and ordered a Unified Command Post, the body Colombia uses to coordinate agencies in a crisis. He suspended his agenda in Bogotá and said he would travel to Pereira, near the epicenter.

De la Espriella told Colombians they were “not alone” and that “the state is present and taking action.” He had campaigned on a hard line on security, not on a natural disaster in his first week.

He succeeded Gustavo Petro only this month, and the quake now frames the opening of his term. How his young government handles the rescue and the rebuilding will shape early opinion of it.

Help from abroad

The United States was quick to respond. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the Trump administration “stands ready to support the people of Colombia” and was closely monitoring the disaster.

The tremor was also felt in Ecuador and Panama, though both reported only minor damage. For a region that sits on the restless edge of the Nazca and South American plates, Monday was a reminder of how quickly the ground can turn.

What it means for residents and travelers

For anyone in the region, the first effect was on travel. Six airports were shut, grounding flights into Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura and cutting the quickest routes into the disaster zone.

Big quakes are almost always followed by aftershocks, which can bring down walls already cracked by the first jolt. In the hardest-hit towns, damaged and leaning buildings were the main danger once the shaking stopped.

Colombia sits where the Nazca plate grinds beneath South America, which makes it one of the most seismically active countries in the region. A focus 107 kilometers down let the energy travel far, which is why the shaking reached Quito and Panama City.

Frequently Asked Questions

How big was the Colombia earthquake and where did it hit?

The United States Geological Survey measured it at magnitude 7.4, centered about 5 kilometers east of San José del Palmar in Chocó, at a depth of 107 kilometers. It struck at around 7:34 a.m. local time on Monday, 10 August 2026.

How many people died in the Colombia earthquake?

Local officials reported at least 69 deaths by midday Monday, with 40 in Risaralda, 27 in Valle del Cauca and two in Manizales. The toll was still rising as rescue teams reached collapsed buildings.

Which airports closed after the earthquake?

Six airports suspended operations, including those in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura. The closures disrupted travel across western and central Colombia.

Did the earthquake cause a tsunami?

No. The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center said there was no tsunami threat because the quake was too deep inside the Earth.

Sources: U.S. Geological Survey; European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre; Pacific Tsunami Warning Center; Colombian departmental officials via The Associated Press; France 24; El Tiempo; Infobae; Portafolio; U.S. Department of State (Secretary Marco Rubio).

Four of its governments are bidding for the same factories Mexico and Brazil want, and the money is moving faster than the heat allows anyone to work.

Southeast Asia – Bidding for the Factories You Want

Four national plans in three weeks

Thailand has unveiled a national plan to become a regional semiconductor hub, and Malaysia has committed more than 45 million dollars to advanced chip packaging. Vietnam has deepened cooperation with the regional semiconductor association, and the Philippines is debating the terms of a large chip and computing project.

These are national industrial strategies announced within three weeks of each other. The ambition across the region is unmistakable and unusually coordinated in its timing.

What it means for Latin America

This is a direct contest for the same nearshoring capital that Mexico and Brazil are courting. Every incentive package announced in Bangkok or Kuala Lumpur is one a board will weigh against Querétaro or Campinas.

The regional mood here is impatient ambition, a set of governments unwilling to be left as assembly floors. Their honest constraint was named in Bangkok last week, where the AI drive was described as limited by shortages of skilled people and access to data.

China – Building Machines, Buying Nothing

Two numbers that do not belong together

China’s artificial-intelligence industry reached 176.7 billion dollars in 2025, growing 40% in a year. Its consumer prices fell 0.1% in July and rose just 0.5% over twelve months, half the pace of June, while factory-gate prices fell 0.7% on the month.

A country can pour money into computing power and still not persuade its own households to spend. Its main large-company index fell 0.4% on Monday while most of Asia rose.

Read the demand picture carefully

Beijing’s statisticians attribute the weakness to imported international factors and note that core prices rose 0.3% on the month, while foreign analysts read the same figures as households declining to spend. Both readings come from the same release and the argument is unresolved.

For Latin American exporters this is the number that matters most this week. Copper, iron ore and soybean demand ultimately rests on whether Chinese consumption is pausing or contracting, and Monday’s data did not settle it.

The Region – El Niño Reaches the Order Book

A warning from Beijing’s own paper

China Daily reported last week that Asian economies face growing risks to food security. Southeast Asia is bracing for hot, dry conditions and heightened haze as El Niño strengthens, and Indonesia has already seen an early surge in wildfires.

In South Korea, heat illness cases have hit a record with two further deaths, the highest-level warning has been issued for greater Seoul, and workplaces are lengthening lunch breaks and adding rest periods. That is a heat that has started shortening the working day.

The same weather system, two continents

This is the El Niño the World Food Programme warned about days ago, when it said nearly 49 million more people could face acute hunger by the end of 2027. Asia and Latin America are exposed to the same event from opposite sides of the trade.

A tighter Asian harvest means a larger Asian import bill for soy, corn, beef, coffee and sugar. For Latin American producers that is a price story rather than a weather story.

Four Southeast Asian governments announced semiconductor strategies within three weeks, and in the same fortnight Korean employers began shortening the working day because of the heat — a region investing in 2030 while negotiating with 2026.

Japan – Cutting Tax and Capping Spending at Once

Ten trillion yen, and no named source

Tokyo has locked in a cut to the consumption tax on food, from 8% to 1% for two years from April 2027, at a cost of roughly 10 trillion yen. Its own press is asking the obvious question of how the lost revenue will be covered.

In the same week the government moved to rein in supplementary budgets, seeking to lift growth while reducing debt. Those two decisions pull in opposite directions and both were taken deliberately.

Why a Tokyo budget matters in São Paulo

Japan is a creditor nation and a long-standing direct investor across Latin America, in mining, autos and infrastructure. Its bond yields and its currency shape how much of that capital travels.

The temperament on display is a government trying to be generous and disciplined in the same breath. Its market closed 2.08% higher on Monday on American employment data rather than on anything it decided itself.

Japan, China and Korea – One Paper, Two Protests

A document nobody liked

China’s foreign ministry said last week that it deplores Japan’s latest defence white paper. Days earlier Seoul had lodged its own formal protest against the same document, over its restatement of a territorial claim.

Tokyo has managed to antagonise both neighbours with a single publication. It has withdrawn nothing.

Fragmentation is the whole reason nearshoring exists

Since Japan’s prime minister linked a Taiwan contingency to Japanese military action, Beijing has suspended cultural exchanges, halted Japanese seafood imports and restricted rare earths and dual-use goods. None of it has been lifted.

This is the environment that makes boards look for production sites outside North Asia altogether. Every month these measures stay in place strengthens the argument for Mexican and Brazilian capacity.

Energy – Asia Is the Gauge for What You Pay

Where the fuel bill is already visible

Thai AirAsia has suspended nine routes from Bangkok’s main airport because of fuel costs, and the Laotian government is acting to soften pump-price rises. Both the regional bloc and Beijing have called publicly for safe transit through the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran said on Sunday that an agreement with Oman on new shipping lanes was in its final stages, while adding that the waterway reopens only once further conditions are met. Nothing about that is settled.

The number on your own screen

Asia imports most of its energy and shows the strain first, in cancelled routes and subsidised pumps. Latin American importers read the same barrel at a delay.

Brent was trading around 83 dollars and West Texas near 78 as this brief was written. What Bangkok cancels this month is what São Paulo pays for next quarter.

The Bigger Picture Asia is committing to the next decade while struggling with this one. Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam and the Philippines have all moved on semiconductors within three weeks, and China’s artificial-intelligence industry has reached 176.7 billion dollars while its consumer prices fall outright. Against that, the immediate environment is getting harder. El Niño is strengthening, food security warnings are coming from Beijing’s own newspaper, Korean employers are shortening the working day for heat, and airlines are cancelling routes over fuel. For Latin American readers there are three practical reads. Southeast Asia is competing for the same factories, Chinese household demand remains the swing factor for copper, iron ore and soy, and a tighter Asian harvest points to firmer prices for the region’s agricultural exporters. Frequently Asked Questions

Which Southeast Asian countries are bidding for semiconductor investment?

Thailand unveiled a national plan in late July to build a regional chip hub, Malaysia committed more than 45 million United States dollars to advanced chip packaging, Vietnam deepened cooperation with the Southeast Asia Semiconductor Association, and the Philippines is publicly debating the terms of a large computing project. Thai officials have also acknowledged that the country’s artificial-intelligence drive is constrained by shortages of skilled workers and limited access to data.

What did China’s July inflation data show?

Consumer prices fell 0.1% from June and rose 0.5% from a year earlier, down from 1.0% in June, while core prices excluding food and energy rose 0.3% on the month and producer prices fell 0.7% on the month while remaining 3.5% higher than a year ago. China’s statistics bureau attributed the softness to international imported factors, while foreign analysts read the same release as evidence of weak household demand.

How is El Niño affecting Asian economies?

China Daily reported last week that Asian economies face growing risks to food security, Southeast Asia is bracing for hot and dry conditions with heightened haze risk, and Indonesia has recorded an early surge in wildfires. In South Korea heat illness cases have reached a record with two further deaths, the highest-level warning has been issued for the greater Seoul area, and employers have begun extending lunch breaks and adding rest periods.

Why did both China and South Korea protest Japan’s defence white paper?

Seoul lodged a formal protest over the document’s restatement of Japan’s claim to disputed islets, and China’s foreign ministry subsequently said it deplores the paper. The wider context is that Beijing has maintained trade measures against Japan since November, including suspended cultural exchanges, a halt to Japanese seafood imports and restrictions on rare earths and dual-use goods, after Japan’s prime minister linked a possible Taiwan contingency to Japanese military action.

Sources: Asia News Network, National Bureau of Statistics via Sina Finance, The Japan Times, Kabutan via Yahoo Finance Japan

World.title: El Niño Puts 756 Latin American Hospitals at Risk as Dengue Cases Top 624,000
World.content:
Health: Latin America

Key Facts —Dengue surge. In epidemiological week 12 of 2026, the Americas reported 624,085 suspected dengue cases, a cumulative incidence of 62 per 100,000 population — a 64% decrease from the same period in 2025 but still elevated. —El Niño threat. PAHO’s July 2026 analysis warns that the 2026–2027 El Niño event could expose 756 emergency hospitals in the Americas to coastal-flooding risks and disrupt supply chains for medicines and medical supplies. —2025 baseline. The Americas recorded 4.46 million suspected dengue cases in 2025, down 66% from the record 13 million in 2024 but still above the pre-pandemic average. All four serotypes circulated simultaneously in Brazil, Colombia and Mexico. —Brazil lead. Brazil reported 1.66 million probable dengue cases in 2025, with an incidence rate of 775.7 per 100,000. In early 2026, 62,707 suspected cases were reported through epidemiological week 5. —Vaccine access. PAHO is advising member states on newly approved dengue vaccines and has expanded clinical-training networks, while warning that climate-related disruptions could delay immunization campaigns.

Latin America is entering the 2026–2027 El Niño cycle with dengue still circulating at scale and its health infrastructure — including hundreds of coastal hospitals — newly exposed to climate-driven flooding risks.

The Scale of the Dengue Burden in 2025–2026

The Americas experienced its largest dengue epidemic on record in 2024, with more than 13 million cases reported to the Pan American Health Organization. In 2025, the numbers fell but remained high: 4.46 million suspected cases and 1.68 million confirmed cases across the region, according to PAHO’s February 2026 epidemiological update. The decline of 66% from 2024 was partly seasonal, but the underlying transmission potential remains.

Brazil accounted for the largest share. In 2025, the country reported 1.66 million probable cases, 1.45 million of them confirmed, with 1,793 deaths. The incidence rate was 775.7 per 100,000 population. Colombia reported 125,119 suspected cases in 2025, including 86,881 confirmed and 124 deaths. All four dengue virus serotypes — DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4 — circulated simultaneously in Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Mexico, Panama and Puerto Rico.

In the first weeks of 2026, the pattern continued. Through epidemiological week 12, PAHO reported 624,085 suspected cases across the Americas. Brazil alone added 62,707 suspected cases in the first five weeks of the year. The figures represent a 64% decrease from the same period in 2025, but PAHO warned that the seasonal uptrend is consistent with expected behavior and that health systems should prepare for potential increases.

What El Niño Adds to the Health Risk

In July 2026, PAHO published a public-health situation analysis specifically on the El Niño climate event for 2026–2027. The document is not a forecast of certainty but a mapping of vulnerabilities. It identifies the same set of climate-sensitive diseases — dengue, Zika, chikungunya, malaria, cholera — and adds a new layer of infrastructure risk.

The analysis examined 756 emergency hospitals across the Americas and found them exposed to coastal flooding associated with sea-level rise, which El Niño can amplify through storm-surge and extreme-rainfall events. The risk is not theoretical: disruptions to supply chains for medicines, vaccines and medical equipment have already occurred during past climate emergencies in the region.

The report also notes that drought conditions can paradoxically increase dengue transmission. When water becomes scarce, households store it in open containers, creating breeding sites for the Aedes aegypti mosquito. The 2023–2024 El Niño contributed to severe drought in the Brazilian Amazon, disrupting healthcare access and increasing malaria incidence in states such as Rondônia. The same dynamics could recur.

Climate emergency response in the Americas. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

How Countries Are Responding

PAHO’s response has three pillars: surveillance, vector control and clinical training. The organization has deployed expert teams to affected countries, expanded its online clinical-diagnosis course for dengue, and established national networks of clinical specialists in arboviral diseases. In August 2025, PAHO held a workshop to update its Integrated Management Strategy for Arboviral Disease Prevention and Control, setting a roadmap for 2026–2030.

On the vaccine front, PAHO is advising member states on newly approved dengue vaccines, though access remains uneven. The organization emphasizes that vaccination is a complement to, not a replacement for, vector control and early clinical management. It also warns that climate-related disruptions could delay routine immunization campaigns, widening existing immunity gaps.

The bottom line is that Latin America’s health systems are facing a converging threat: endemic arboviral diseases that never fully receded, a new El Niño cycle that amplifies both drought and flood risks, and infrastructure that was not designed for either. The 756 hospitals in the flood-risk zone are a concrete measure of that vulnerability.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many dengue cases were reported in the Americas in 2025?

The Americas reported 4.46 million suspected dengue cases in 2025, including 1.68 million confirmed cases, 8,966 severe cases and 2,207 deaths. This was a 66% decrease from the record 13 million cases in 2024.

What does El Niño mean for healthcare in Latin America?

PAHO’s July 2026 analysis warns that El Niño could expose 756 emergency hospitals to coastal-flooding risks, disrupt medicine supply chains, and increase transmission of dengue, malaria and waterborne diseases through both flooding and drought-driven water-storage practices.

Which countries are most affected by dengue?

Brazil leads in absolute numbers (1.66 million probable cases in 2025), followed by Colombia, Mexico, Guatemala and Panama. All four dengue serotypes circulated simultaneously in Brazil, Colombia, Mexico and several Central American countries in 2025.

One country is counting its votes on whether copper has paid off, and the other is counting, for the first time, what has been leaving alongside it.

DR Congo – The Uranium in the Cobalt

A state that starts measuring

The Democratic Republic of Congo said on Friday it will test its cobalt exports for uranium. The decision follows research published on 30 July in the journal Nature Communications, examined by the Financial Times and Lighthouse Reports, which estimated that thousands of tonnes of the radioactive metal left the country as a by-product over roughly two decades.

Kinshasa will set up a working group, consult the International Atomic Energy Agency about a technical mission, and assess health and environmental risks within sixty days. It also plans to install radiation detectors on trucks leaving the country.

Contested, and taken seriously anyway

The government disputes the method, saying the estimates rest on modelling rather than direct measurements of exported material, and that uranium occurring alongside copper and cobalt in the region is natural and well documented. Chinese mining companies operating in the country reject the claims outright.

The head of the Congolese nuclear energy agency told the Financial Times it was technically possible and even probable that uranium had been extracted from exported ore, while stressing there is no direct evidence. The national mood is neither denial nor alarm but a wary insistence on checking, which is itself new.

Zambia – Three Days to the Copper Vote

Reform seeks its receipt

Zambians vote on Thursday for a president and parliament, with President Hakainde Hichilema seeking a second term against a fragmented opposition led by Brian Mundubile. The country is Africa’s second-largest copper producer and the world’s eighth, and copper supplies about 70% of its export earnings.

Hichilema steered the country through a punishing debt restructuring after it became the pandemic era’s first sovereign defaulter. The question this week is whether voters feel any of it in their own lives.

Stability without the receipts

The previous 1.7 billion dollar programme with the International Monetary Fund expired in January, and investors treat a successor as the real test of continuity. Standard Chartered expects this year’s deficit near 5.0% of output, more than double the government’s 2.1% target, partly because a record maize harvest obliges the state to buy heavily from farmers.

Drought has also undercut a power system that leans on hydro, forcing cuts that stall industry. Zambia’s temper is that of a country asked to be patient for five years and now being asked, politely, for proof.

South Africa – A Speech Against Violence, and Eleven Dead

Seventy years after the march

President Cyril Ramaphosa marked Women’s Day at the Union Buildings on Sunday, seventy years after thousands of women gathered there to protest against apartheid pass laws. He condemned those who try to justify abuse, saying how women dress or behave can never be an excuse.

He called on men and boys to take a stronger stand and on communities to stop turning away. He also urged more women into science and engineering.

The same weekend, in Cape Town

Eleven people were killed in three separate mass shootings in the city. Three men died in Khayelitsha, five in Langa, and three at the Barcelona settlement in Gugulethu, where two others were wounded.

Police have reinforced deployments and no arrests have been made, with motives still under investigation. The gap between the speech at the Union Buildings and the weekend in the townships is the country’s whole predicament in a single day.

Senegal – Six For, Seven Against

A candidacy that stalls at the first ballot

Former president Macky Sall took six votes in favour, seven against and two abstentions in the Security Council’s first informal ballot for United Nations secretary-general, held on 30 July. The polls are non-binding, and further rounds are expected through August and possibly into the autumn.

Two Africans are in the race, Sall and Uganda’s Olara Otunnu, who entered late. A former head of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa judges the continent’s chances this year to be low.

A prize Africa keeps not winning

Sall was nominated by Burundi rather than by his own country, and only secured Senegal’s endorsement later. At home the ruling party still holds him responsible for deaths during protests in 2021 and 2023.

The mood in Dakar is not wounded so much as unsurprised. A continent that supplies the world’s minerals is still waiting to supply its secretary-general.

One country is counting votes on whether its copper has paid off, and its neighbour has begun counting what has been leaving alongside the same ore — the Copperbelt, at last, taking its own inventory.

Kenya – The Arithmetic of 2027

A retreat at Naivasha

President William Ruto and Oburu Odinga led a broad-based parliamentary retreat at Naivasha, gathering legislators from across the governing arrangement. The subject is the shape of the coalition heading into the 2027 election.

Kenyan politics is already organising itself around that date. Alliances are being tested well before any campaign formally begins.

Governing and campaigning at once

The country’s mood is watchful and transactional, with everyone counting numbers a year and a half early. That leaves less attention for the cost of living that drove last year’s protests.

Kenya’s economy has held up better than many of its neighbours. Its politics is the part that never rests.

Sudan – The Students Who Kept Going

Education as refusal

Sudanese students are finding ways to continue studying through a conflict that has emptied universities and scattered families. United Nations accounts describe young people sitting examinations and resuming courses in displacement.

One of them said simply that it made him dream again. It is a small sentence carrying a great deal.

What persistence is worth

A generation losing its education is the slowest and most expensive damage any conflict does. Countries that keep teaching through disaster recover years faster than those that do not.

The mood here is stubbornness rather than hope, which may be more durable. Sudan’s students are protecting the one asset nobody can carry away.

The Bigger Picture The Copperbelt is one geological formation running under two countries, and this week it holds both of the continent’s largest stories. Zambia votes on Thursday on whether five years of reform have reached ordinary lives, with copper supplying about 70% of export earnings and a deficit heading for double its target. Across the border, DR Congo has begun testing what leaves alongside the same ore, after research alleged that thousands of tonnes of uranium were exported unmeasured for two decades. The claim is disputed by the government and by the Chinese firms involved, and Kinshasa is checking anyway, which is the part that matters. Elsewhere the day was about counting of a different kind. South Africa counted eleven dead in three Cape Town shootings on the weekend its president spoke against violence, Senegal counted six votes for Macky Sall and seven against, and Kenya’s politicians counted their numbers for an election still a year and a half away. Africa Intelligence Brief August 10: What We Are Watching

13 August – Zambia’s presidential and parliamentary elections.

Coming weeks – Whether Zambia agrees a successor programme with the International Monetary Fund.

Within 60 days – DR Congo’s assessment of health and environmental risks from uranium in cobalt exports.

Coming weeks – Whether the International Atomic Energy Agency sends a technical mission to Kinshasa.

Ongoing – Arrests, or the absence of them, after the Cape Town shootings.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is DR Congo testing its cobalt exports for uranium?

Research published on 30 July in Nature Communications, examined by the Financial Times and Lighthouse Reports, estimated that thousands of tonnes of uranium left the country as a by-product of cobalt exports over roughly two decades, most of it destined for Chinese-owned entities. The government announced on 7 August that it would test exported cobalt hydroxide, form a working group, consult the International Atomic Energy Agency and assess health and environmental risks within sixty days, while disputing the study’s methodology and noting that uranium occurs naturally alongside copper and cobalt in the region.

What is at stake in Zambia’s election on 13 August?

President Hakainde Hichilema is seeking a second term against a fragmented opposition led by Brian Mundubile, in a vote widely seen as a test of whether his economic reforms have reached ordinary households. Zambia is Africa’s second-largest copper producer and copper accounts for roughly 70% of export earnings, while a 1.7 billion dollar International Monetary Fund programme expired in January and Standard Chartered expects the 2026 deficit near 5.0% of output against a 2.1% target.

What did President Ramaphosa say on Women’s Day?

Speaking at the Union Buildings on Sunday 9 August, seventy years after the 1956 march against pass laws, Ramaphosa condemned those who attempt to justify abuse, saying how women dress or behave can never serve as a justification, and urged men and boys to take a stronger stand while calling on communities not to turn a blind eye. Over the same weekend eleven people were killed in three separate mass shootings in Khayelitsha, Langa and Gugulethu, with police reinforcing deployments and no arrests reported.

How did Macky Sall perform in the first UN straw poll?

In the Security Council’s first informal ballot on 30 July, the former Senegalese president received six votes in favour, seven against and two abstentions, a result widely read as weakening his candidacy. The polls are non-binding, with further rounds expected through August and possibly into the autumn before a single candidate is recommended to the General Assembly, and the new secretary-general takes office on 1 January 2027.

São Paulo · Nightlife

São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 10, 2026

If You Only Go to One Place Last Days: Two World-Cinema Festivals Two rare film seasons run tonight and close Wednesday. CineSesc on Rua Augusta has the first-ever complete Aki Kaurismäki retrospective — all 18 features — while Cine Belas Artes is finishing its Festival Filmes Incríveis of unreleased world cinema. Both are open tonight, both are cheap (around R$20, US$4), and both end 12 August. On a quiet Monday, this is the move.

Tonight at a Glance —Kaurismäki retrospective · CineSesc All 18 of the Finnish director’s features, first time complete in Brazil, on Rua Augusta. Runs daily to 12 August. Around R$20 (US$4). —Festival Filmes Incríveis · Cine Belas Artes Unreleased films from festivals like Cannes and Berlin, on Consolação. Final days through 12 August. Check tonight’s exact showtimes on the site. —SP2B, Day 2 · Ibirapuera The innovation festival’s content day (from 1 pm) is credential-based — the Sunday opening with Esther Perel was Platinum-only and is done. But the park’s open areas stay free to walk through all week. —Monday forró & pagode · Pinheiros / Centro / Mooca São Paulo’s Monday music tradition: forró pé de serra at Remelexo Brasil (Pinheiros, from 11 pm) and Estúdio Lâmina (Centro), plus a Monday pagode night in Mooca. Confirm the night’s band on their socials. —CCBB São Paulo · Centro Open Mondays (closed Tuesdays) until 8 pm, with free exhibitions and film sessions. A good early-evening culture stop before dinner. Confirm the current programme on the site.

Tonight, Monday 10 August 2026, is a classic São Paulo Monday — slow for clubs, but the cinemas and a handful of Monday-night music rooms keep the city alive. The standout is timing: two exceptional film seasons, a Kaurismäki retrospective and the Festival Filmes Incríveis, both end this Wednesday, so tonight is one of your last chances. SP2B rolls into its business-content day at Ibirapuera, and Vila Madalena keeps its Monday forró going.

A quiet Monday in São Paulo leans on its cinemas and Monday music rooms. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Aki Kaurismäki retrospective at CineSesc — Rua Augusta 2075, Cerqueira César. The first complete retrospective in Brazil of the Finnish master, gathering all 18 of his fiction features — dry humour, working-class characters, and that unmistakable deadpan style. It runs daily to 12 August, so tonight is a genuine last-chance window. Tickets are R$20 (US$4) full, R$10 (US$2) half, R$6 (US$1) with a Sesc card. Check the day’s specific titles and times.

Festival Filmes Incríveis at Cine Belas Artes — Rua da Consolação 2423, Consolação. The art-house festival of unreleased world cinema — 14 films from 14 countries, many straight from Cannes, Berlin and Rotterdam — is in its final days before closing 12 August. Tickets around R$20 (US$4) full, R$10 (US$2) half, with a five-film pass at R$45 (US$9). Confirm tonight’s programme on the site.

SP2B, Day 2 at Parque Ibirapuera — the innovation festival’s content programme begins around 1 pm on Monday and runs through the week. Access to the stages and talks requires a paid credential (Explorer from about R$1,180, US$232, up to Platinum at R$4,720, US$930); the Sunday Opening Night with Esther Perel was Platinum-only and has passed. Worth knowing: the park itself stays open and free, so you can still walk the grounds and catch the open-area atmosphere without a ticket. The festival is 18+.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Early evening (6 pm) — Start with a film. CineSesc on Rua Augusta and Cine Belas Artes on Consolação are a short walk apart, both in the Paulista corridor, so you can check both schedules and pick the session that fits.

Dinner (8 pm) — The Consolação/Augusta stretch is full of bars and restaurants. Grab a bite between or after screenings without moving far.

Later (10–11 pm) — For music, head to Pinheiros for the Monday forró at Remelexo Brasil (it gets going around 11 pm), to Estúdio Lâmina in Centro, or to Mooca for the Monday pagode. All are relaxed, local and danceable — the antidote to a quiet Monday.

Nightcap (11:30 pm) — Vila Madalena’s bars stay open on a Monday if the forró winds down. Keep it low-key; the big clubs are a weekend affair.

Alternative — Culture-first: CCBB in Centro closes at 8 pm, so catch an exhibition early, then move to Augusta for a late film.

Scenes & Sounds

Cinema — This is the Monday story. Two festivals in their final days: the Kaurismäki retrospective at CineSesc and Festival Filmes Incríveis at Cine Belas Artes, both closing 12 August. Nationwide, the Harry Potter and La La Land anniversary re-releases are also in cinemas this month. Where: CineSesc (Rua Augusta), Cine Belas Artes (Consolação), Cinemateca Brasileira (Vila Clementino).

Forró — Monday is forró night in São Paulo. Traditional forró pé de serra runs every Monday at a couple of dedicated houses, with dancing and a welcoming crowd. Where: Remelexo Brasil (Pinheiros), Estúdio Lâmina (Centro) — confirm the night’s band on their socials.

Pagode and samba — A Monday pagode night runs in Mooca, and samba turns up across the city midweek. Where: Bar Templo (Mooca) and neighbourhood bars — confirm the night’s act.

MPB and jazz — Small rooms like Centro da Terra (Perdizes) and Coringa (Vila Madalena) sometimes programme Monday sets. The bigger jazz and MPB houses skew to later in the week. Where: Centro da Terra, Coringa, JazzB — check listings.

Cultural and talks — SP2B’s business programme runs all week at Ibirapuera (credential required); the park’s open areas stay free. CCBB in Centro is open tonight with exhibitions and film sessions. Where: Parque Ibirapuera, CCBB (Centro).

Electronic and clubs — Not a Monday thing in São Paulo. Save the Barra Funda clubs (D-Edge, Clash Club) for Friday and Saturday. Where: Barra Funda, weekends.

Pick Your Night

See it before it’s gone: The Kaurismäki retrospective at CineSesc or Festival Filmes Incríveis at Cine Belas Artes — both close Wednesday.

Dance on a Monday: The Vila Madalena forró — social, danceable, and very São Paulo.

Culture first: CCBB São Paulo in Centro — free exhibitions, open Mondays until 8 pm.

Ideas and networking: SP2B at Ibirapuera, if you hold a credential — the business content runs from the afternoon.

Dance till sunrise: Not tonight. Save the Barra Funda clubs for the weekend.

Where to Go

CineSesc — Cerqueira César (Rua Augusta) A comfortable Sesc-run cinema on Rua Augusta with popular-priced tickets, hosting the first complete Aki Kaurismäki retrospective in Brazil. Tonight: Retrospectiva Aki Kaurismäki — all 18 of the director’s fiction features, running through 12 August. Check the day’s titles and times. Best time: Daily, roughly 1:15 pm to 9:30 pm during the retrospective. Cost: R$20 (US$4) full / R$10 (US$2) half / R$6 (US$1) with Sesc Credencial Plena. Address: Rua Augusta 2075, Cerqueira César Website: www.sescsp.org.br Getting there: Metro Consolação (green line), short walk up Rua Augusta. Good to know: Programme and tickets on the Sesc São Paulo site.

Cine Belas Artes — Consolação São Paulo’s beloved art-house cinema, finishing its Festival Filmes Incríveis 2026. A cultural anchor with a great courtyard café. Tonight: Festival Filmes Incríveis — unreleased world cinema, final days through 12 August. Confirm tonight’s exact showtimes on the site. Best time: Evenings. The courtyard café is open all day. Cost: R$20 (US$4) full / R$10 (US$2) half; five-film pass R$45 (US$9). Address: Rua da Consolação 2423, Consolação Website: www.cinebelasartes.com.br Getting there: Metro Paulista (yellow line), 10-minute walk. Good to know: Buy tickets online or at the box office.

SP2B — Parque Ibirapuera The city’s big new innovation and culture festival, spread across the park’s cultural buildings and open areas for eight days. Tonight: Day 2 — business-content programme from about 1 pm. Credential required for the stages and talks; the Sunday opening with Esther Perel has passed. Best time: The main content block runs Tuesday to Thursday; the free music and Experience Day land on the weekend. Cost: Credentials from about R$1,180 (US$232) Explorer up to R$4,720 (US$930) Platinum. The park’s open areas remain free to enter. Address: Parque Ibirapuera, Vila Mariana Website: sp2b.com.br Getting there: Rideshare best; buses from Paulista. It’s 18+ for the festival areas. Good to know: Check the app for the day’s stages and any free public activations.

Monday forró — Remelexo Brasil (Pinheiros) & Estúdio Lâmina (Centro) São Paulo’s Monday forró tradition. Remelexo Brasil is one of the city’s best-known forró houses; Estúdio Lâmina is a decades-old forrozeiro haunt near São Bento. Both keep a traditional pé de serra going every Monday, with dancing and a welcoming crowd. Tonight: Live forró at Remelexo Brasil (Mondays, from about 11 pm) and at Estúdio Lâmina (every Monday). Confirm the night’s band on their socials. Best time: Late — Remelexo runs into the early hours. Arrive earlier for a table. Cost: Remelexo cover around R$30 (US$6) in advance, R$50 (US$10) at the door, plus drinks. Card accepted. Address: Remelexo Brasil — Rua Ferreira de Araújo 1076, Pinheiros; Estúdio Lâmina — Av. São João 108, Centro Getting there: Remelexo: rideshare, or metro Faria Lima/Pinheiros. Estúdio Lâmina: metro São Bento, then rideshare out late. Good to know: No dance experience needed — locals are happy to show you the basic step.

CCBB São Paulo — Centro The Banco do Brasil’s cultural centre in a restored 1901 building in the historic centre. Free exhibitions, cinema and theatre — and open on Mondays. Tonight: Open until 8 pm with current exhibitions and film sessions. Confirm today’s programme on the site — the schedule turns over between shows this month. Best time: Wednesday to Monday, 9 am to 8 pm. Closed Tuesdays. Cost: Free, with timed tickets reserved online (bb.com.br/cultura) or at the box office. Address: Rua Álvares Penteado 112, Centro Histórico Website: ccbb.com.br/sao-paulo Getting there: Metro São Bento (blue line), short walk into the pedestrian centre. Good to know: Centro empties after office hours — use rideshare door-to-door at night.

Blue Note São Paulo — Paulista The São Paulo outpost of the New York jazz club, polished and central. A strong option for later in the week. Tonight: Typically no Monday show — Blue Note programmes shows Wednesday to Sunday. Check the site and plan for later in the week. Best time: Wednesday to Sunday. Arrive 30 minutes early — seating is first-come. Cost: Couvert from R$40 (US$8) to R$80 (US$16) depending on the act. Address: Av. Paulista 2073, 2º andar (Conjunto Nacional), Consolação Website: bluenotesp.com Getting there: Metro Consolação (green line), 200 m from the door. Good to know: Show seating is first-come; arrive early on show nights.

Casa de Francisca — Sé/Centro An intimate listening room inside the gorgeous Palacete Teresa, mixing MPB, jazz and instrumental. A hidden gem for another night. Tonight: Usually no Monday show — the Casa’s programme runs Tuesday to Sunday. Check the Instagram and plan for later in the week. Best time: Tuesday to Sunday, shows around 8 pm or 9 pm. Cost: Couvert around R$30 (US$6) to R$60 (US$12). Cash and card accepted. Address: Rua Quintino Bocaiúva 22, Sé (Palacete Teresa) Instagram: @casadefrancisca Getting there: Metro Sé (red/blue lines), 5-minute walk. Use rideshare after dark. Good to know: Tiny room — reservations strongly recommended when it’s open.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Paulista / Consolação / Augusta: The city’s spine — cinemas, bars and jazz clubs within a short walk. Safe and well-lit, and the natural base for a Monday film-and-dinner night.

Vila Madalena / Pinheiros: Bohemian and bar-heavy, and home to the Monday forró. Walkable and lively even early in the week.

Sé / Centro: Historic core with CCBB and hidden gems. Grand by day, very quiet after dark on a Monday — use a rideshare.

Ibirapuera / Vila Mariana: Leafy and upscale around the park, which hosts SP2B this week. A more relaxed, residential side of the city.

Barra Funda: The club district — empty on a Monday, alive at the weekend. Home to D-Edge and Clash Club.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Weekend-led scene — São Paulo’s big queer club nights, including the Barra Funda parties, are Friday-and-Saturday affairs. Mondays are quiet on that front.

Everyday-friendly spaces — The Augusta corridor and Vila Madalena bars are broadly mixed and welcoming any night. For a Monday, that’s your best bet; save the dedicated club nights for the weekend.

Money & How Paying Works Cinema tickets: Festival films run around R$20 (US$4) full, with half-price (meia) at R$10 (US$2) for students and others. Bring ID for meia. Couvert artístico: Music bars add a per-person music charge, not a tip — usually R$20 (US$4) to R$40 (US$8). It will be on your bill; ask before you sit. Cash, card and Pix: Cards and Pix are widely accepted, but carry R$100 (US$20) to R$200 (US$40) in cash for smaller bars and street vendors. Tipping: 10% is standard and often added as ‘serviço’. Check before you double-tip.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: The last trains leave between midnight and 12:30 am, depending on the line. Check the ViaQuatro and Metrô SP apps before you rely on it.

Rideshare: 99 and Uber are reliable and widely used. Wait in a lit, busy spot, especially leaving Centro late.

Centro at night: The Sé and República areas are very quiet after dark on a Monday. Stick to lit main roads and take a rideshare door-to-door.

Phone awareness: Don’t walk with your phone out on quiet streets. Duck into a bar to check maps or call a car.

Augusta and Vila Madalena: Both stay busier and better-lit early in the week, but keep the usual city awareness late at night.

Frequently Asked Questions

I’ve just landed at GRU tonight. Can I still do something?

Yes — aim for a late film. CineSesc and Cine Belas Artes both run evening sessions and are about a 40-minute rideshare from the airport, in the well-connected Paulista corridor. For something livelier, the Vila Madalena forró runs late.

Can I just show up to SP2B tonight?

Only to the park itself, which stays open and free. The festival’s stages and talks require a paid credential (from about R$1,180, US$232), and Monday is a business-content day. The Sunday opening with Esther Perel was Platinum-only and has passed.

Do I need to speak Portuguese?

For the films, many are subtitled world cinema, so no. At the forró, the music and dancing do the work — a smile and a willingness to try the step are all you need.

What’s the dress code on a Monday?

Casual everywhere tonight. Comfortable clothes for the cinema and the forró; jeans are fine. Bring a light layer for air-conditioned screening rooms.

Sources: sescsp.org.br (Kaurismäki), cinebelasartes.com.br, sp2b.com.br, ccbb.com.br

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — August 10, 2026

If You Only Go to One Place Samba do Trabalhador at Clube Renascença Monday looks quiet on paper, but Rio’s samba world is wide awake. Moacyr Luz’s Samba do Trabalhador has run every Monday for two decades at the Renascença Clube in Andaraí — gates from around 4:30 pm, samba from 5 pm. It is the most Carioca thing you can do on a Monday, and it’s cash-only, so come prepared.

Tonight at a Glance —Samba do Trabalhador · Andaraí The city’s most famous Monday roda, led by Moacyr Luz. Gates ~4:30 pm, samba from 5 pm, ends around 9 pm. About R$30 (US$6), cash only. —Roda de Samba da Pedra do Sal · Saúde Free open-air samba at the birthplace of Carioca samba, in the old port’s “Pequena África”. From about 7 pm on the stone steps. Bring cash for beer tokens. —CCBB Rio · Centro Open Mondays (closed Tuesdays) until 8 pm. Catch “Vik Muniz: A Olho Nu” before the port fills up — a strong culture warm-up in the historic centre. —Lapa The nightlife heart is quiet on a Monday — the big houses (Rio Scenarium, Circo Voador) run later in the week. Good for a low-key boteco nightcap under the Arcos, not a big night out. —Jazz TribOz in Lapa is the city’s dedicated jazz room, but it runs Wednesday to Saturday — not tonight. Note it for later in the week.

Tonight, Monday 10 August 2026, is a classic Rio Monday — slow on paper, but the samba is the whole point. The city’s two great weekly rodas run as they always do: Moacyr Luz’s Samba do Trabalhador in Andaraí and the free open-air roda at Pedra do Sal in the old port. Add an early exhibition at CCBB and you have a full, unhurried evening. They sit in different parts of the city, so realistically you pick one roda and commit.

Rio’s Monday samba rodas draw a devoted weekly crowd. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)
