Wilson pointed to the two regional joint ventures — Guyana — CAM Motors — an automotive operation supporting ATL-represented brands in Guyana; and Trinidad and Tobago — Spectra Motors and LAFAST Motors — supporting ATL-represented brands in Trinidad and Tobago.

“Our customers remain our most important concern and the hub helps to ensure that vehicles are backed by trained teams, recognised retail standards, manufacturer-supported warranty processes and consistent after-sales care,” Wilson emphasises.

Executive Chairman Stewart explains the vision:

“Many people look at the Caribbean and see one region. We see distinct markets, each with its own culture, economy, currency, regulations and way of doing business. That understanding has been built over decades, and it’s what makes the ATL Automotive Caribbean hub so powerful.

“By connecting these economies under one umbrella, we’re creating greater scale, stronger partnerships, better support for our dealer network and new opportunities for global automotive brands. It’s a model that benefits everyone — our manufacturers, our dealer partners, our Jamaican-based regional team and, ultimately, the customers we all serve.

“It’s proof that world-class regional businesses can be built from Jamaica, creating value not only for our company but for the wider Caribbean economy.”

In sum, according to Wilson, the hub works alongside its dealer partners, supporting where they need it most, sharing best practice and providing additional resources that help them grow while always respecting that they know their local market best.

“We do the hard work behind the scenes, ensuring every brand is represented to the highest standard in every market,” says Wilson, unable to hide his passion for the job.

World.title: Who should get the Reggae Icon Award?
World.content:
Bob Marley, the Third World’s biggest reggae megastar

At last Thursday’s Independence Grand Gala, Busy Signal and Wayne Wonder joined Sizzla Kalonji, Capleton, Beres Hammond, Leroy Sibbles, Derrick Morgan, Rita Marley, Morgan Heritage, Third World, Ken Boothe, Toots Hibbert, Dawn Penn, Melody Makers, Byron Lee and the Dragonnaires, Shaggy, Grub Cooper, and Sanchez, as recipients of the culture ministry’s Reggae Icon Award.



In this article shared with the Jamaica Observer, Dr Leo Gilling, criminologist, Diaspora strategist, journalist, philanthropist and policy analyst, questions what exactly does the award measure and why a slew of apparently deserving artistes were leapfrogged by some of the current recipients.

Following is part one of a lightly edited version of the article:

Let me begin with what this article is not.

This is not an argument that Sanchez, Wayne Wonder, Busy Signal, Sizzla Kalonji, Capleton, Beres Hammond, Leroy Sibbles, Derrick Morgan, Rita Marley, Morgan Heritage, or Third World et al are undeserving of national recognition.

They are accomplished artistes who have made significant contributions to Jamaican music. My question is different.

If Jamaica has established qualifications for determining who should receive the Reggae Icon Award, do those qualifications adequately explain who is selected — and, just as importantly, who is selected first? That distinction matters.

An award does more than recognise achievement. A national award helps establish a standard. It tells younger artistes, the music industry, Jamaicans and the wider world: This is what we mean when we call someone a Jamaican music icon.

If Jamaica creates a national award intended to represent the highest standard of musical excellence, then the first recipients should help define that standard. The pioneers should establish the benchmark.

Subsequent generations should have something meaningful toward which to aspire. If you create a benchmark, you should begin with the benchmark.

The five qualifications

The qualifications publicly associated with selection for the Reggae Icon Award can be summarised in five broad areas:

1. Pioneering Foundation & Evolution

The artiste should have played a foundational role in originating, developing, or evolving Jamaican genres such as ska, rocksteady, reggae, dancehall, or dub.

2. Authenticity & Conscious Message

The artiste’s work should demonstrate cultural grounding, positive or uplifting messages, social consciousness, spirituality, national pride, or advocacy for social justice.

3. Global Ambassadorship

The artiste should demonstrate sustained international impact and help expand the global footprint of Jamaican music.

4. Longevity & Artistic Consistency

The artiste should demonstrate decades of artistic excellence, influential recordings and resonance across generations.

5. Community & Nation-Building Impact

Consideration is also given to mentorship, charitable activity, youth development and other contributions to Jamaican communities.

At first glance, these appear to be reasonable qualifications. But something interesting happens when we actually apply them.

For purposes of analysis, I assigned each qualification a maximum of 10 points, producing a possible total of 50.

These are not Government of Jamaica scores. They are my analytical application of the qualifications and are intended to encourage discussion about how the criteria operate when applied consistently.

Artiste Pioneer / Evolution Cultural / Conscious Global Longevity Community Total /50

Rita Marley – 9 10 10 9 10 48

Leroy Sibbles – 10 9 9 10 8 46

Beres Hammond – 8 9 10 10 9 46

Derrick Morgan – 10 8 9 10 8 45

Sizzla Kalonji – 8 10 9 9 9 45

Capleton – 8 10 9 9 8 44

Peetah Morgan / Morgan Heritage – 8 9 10 9 8 44

AJ Brown / Third World – 7 9 10 9 7 42

Busy Signal – 8 8 8 8 7 39

Sanchez – 4 7 8 10 7 36

Wayne Wonder – 6 6 9 9 6 36

Reasonable people will disagree with individual scores. That is expected. But the numbers themselves are not the central argument. They simply force us to examine what the qualifications actually mean.

When viewed against those qualifications, the pattern of selections can appear erratic and inconsistent, particularly when artistes with demonstrably stronger claims to pioneering influence, historical importance and global impact remain outside the list.

And perhaps nowhere is the difficulty clearer than with the word “pioneering”. What exactly is a pioneer?

A pioneer is not simply someone who became successful, popular, or enduring. A pioneer changes the architecture of the music; introduces something; transforms something; opens a previously closed door, or creates an approach upon which subsequent generations build.

That distinction matters because if “pioneering” is one of the measures of icon status, it cannot simply become another word for longevity or popularity.

Derrick Morgan has a genuine pioneering claim because his career reaches into the formative development of ska, rocksteady and reggae.

Leroy Sibbles has one because his work as vocalist, musician and arranger intersects directly with the development of Jamaica’s early reggae sound.

But consider Sanchez.

Sanchez is unquestionably one of Jamaica’s great vocalists. His voice is distinctive. His longevity is extraordinary. Generations of Jamaicans know his recordings. But a substantial part of his career has involved interpreting songs written and previously recorded by others.

That is an artistic accomplishment. It can even be an extraordinary artistic accomplishment. But it is not necessarily pioneering. If pioneering means originating, developing, or substantially evolving Jamaican music, longevity cannot simply be substituted for innovation.

The same question arises, although differently, with Wayne Wonder.

Wayne Wonder became an important participant in modern dancehall and reggae crossover and achieved significant international success. But was he a pioneer of that evolution, or an exceptionally successful participant within it? Those are not the same things.

This distinction is important because otherwise every successful artiste eventually becomes a “pioneer”. That empties the word of meaning.

A great singer can be an icon without being a pioneer. A great songwriter can be an icon without being an international superstar. An artiste can revolutionise Jamaican music without operating a charitable foundation. And an artiste can achieve enormous international commercial success without having created a new musical form. These are different kinds of achievement. A credible national recognition system should be capable of distinguishing among them.

The historical question

Now consider something else.

The Reggae Icon Award was introduced in 2019. Reggae was not. Neither was Jamaican popular music. By the time this award was created, Jamaica already possessed more than half a century of extraordinary musical history. There was therefore already a historical backlog of giants.

Artistes had helped create ska. Others had shaped rocksteady.

Others had helped create reggae. Some revolutionised the Jamaican deejay tradition. Others developed dub. Others helped establish dancehall.

Some carried these musical forms around the world. Others influenced musical genres far beyond Jamaica. So when Jamaica established a new national award bearing the word “Icon”, there was an important question to answer from the beginning: Who establishes the benchmark?

If the qualifications emphasise pioneering, longevity, international impact, cultural authenticity and national contribution, one would reasonably expect the earliest recipients to include the artistes whose careers most completely embody those qualities.

This is why the sequence matters. It is not enough to ask whether an individual recipient qualifies. We must also ask: Who else qualifies more strongly? And: Why did one qualifying artiste receive recognition before another?

Those questions do not diminish anyone who has already received the award. They test the integrity of the selection architecture.

The fairest way to examine this is simple. Take exactly the same qualifications. Do not change them. Do not create special rules for anyone. Apply them to Jamaican-born artistes who have not received the award.

What happens when Bob Marley, Toots Hibbert, Jimmy Cliff, Peter Tosh, Bunny Wailer, Burning Spear, Marcia Griffiths, Dennis Brown, U-Roy, Gregory Isaacs, Shabba Ranks, Ini Kamoze, Eek-A-Mouse, and others are placed beside the existing recipients?

If the qualifications are sound, they should help us understand the hierarchy. If they cannot, perhaps the problem is not the artistes. Perhaps the problem is the criteria.

That is where Part II begins.

Tomorrow: Jamaica’s Reggae Icon Award – when the same test is applied to the giants

World.title: GOLDEN GIRLS
World.content:
Members of Jamaica’s women’s 4x100m relay team (from left) Natrece East, Sashana Johnson, Shanoya Douglas, and Thieana-Lee Terrelonge celebrate after winning the gold medal on Sunday’s final day of the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon. The team ran a World Under-20-leading 42.89 seconds, the fourth-fastest time ever in the age group. (Photo: Paul Reid)Paul Reid

OREGON, USA — Jamaica’s fourth-consecutive women’s 4x100m relay gold medal delivered a special moment for double silver medallist Shanoya Douglas on more than one levels, as the island closed out the World Athletics Under-20 Championships in strong fashion at Hayward Field, Eugene, Oregon, on Sunday.

The team ran 42.89 seconds – the fourth fastest in history among Under-20 women – to give Jamaica three of the top-four times ever.

Jamaica won an additional three medals on Sunday’s final day, a gold and two bronze, with Joseph Salmon in the men’s discus and the men’s 4x100m team both finishing third, for a total of eight medals at the championship — two gold, three silver and three bronze, to finish fourth on the medal table.

Douglas, who anchored the team to a World Under-20 leading 42.89 seconds, was part of back-to-back gold medal-winning teams, after her role in Lima, Peru, last year, told the Jamaica Observer, “The gold really means a lot for me because I wanted to continue the streak to four straight. This is what we are know for, winning gold medals in relays and it meant a lot to be able to continue that streak.”

Douglas, who came into the championships as the world leader and favourite in the 100m and 200m, was upstaged by American Mia Maxwell in both finals and after a quick reflection, hinted at her disappointment having not topped the podium in the individual event, “knowing that I’d broke the streak in the 100m,” she said.

She was part of two changes to the team that ran in the semi-finals. Along with lead-off runner Sashana Johnson and powered by strong legs from Theianna-Lee Terrelonge and Natrece East on the second and third legs, Jamaica held off Switzerland, who took the silver in 43.36 seconds and Belgium, who ran a national under-20 record 43.91 seconds for third.

With 100m silver medallist Gary Card and Nyrone Wade back from the winning team two years ago, the men’s team finished third in 39.01 seconds with Kyle Bodden leading off and Sanjay Seymore on anchor.

The USA, with men’s sprint double champion Tate Taylor on anchor, ran a Under-20 world record 38.16 seconds to take the gold, with Great Britain second with an Area Under-20 record 38.90 seconds.

There was drama in the men’s discus throw final with the lead changing hands no fewer then six times in the final two rounds, which saw the Jamaicans, Salmon and Kamari Kennedy, move into the first two spots before dropping to fifth and sixth places.

When the smoke settled, Salmon, the world leader, was third with 64.37m and Kennedy fourth with a massive new personal best of 64.18m, which also sees him ranked fourth in the world.

American Simon Rosselli won with a national Under-20 record of 66.39m coming into the final round with Estonia’s Sten-Erik Iir taking silver with a personal best 65.42m, also in the final round.

Jahvanie Tyrell was eighth in the men’s 400m hurdles with 53.23 seconds, after running a lifetime best 49.98 seconds in the semifinals on Saturday.

Shevaughn Thomas failed to finish the women’s 400m hurdles final.

Both 4x400m relay teams also finished down the track. The women’s team of Daniellia Dixon, Kristen Herbert, Davine Dickenson and Kevongaye Fowler were sixth in 3:34.28, while the men’s team of Nishawn Walker, Jabari Matheson, Jason Pitter and Jabulani McLeod were fifth in 3:05.71 seconds.

World.title: UK approves its second weight-loss pill while EU access lags
World.content:
However, with the arrival of the first GLP-1 pill Wegovy (semaglutide) from Danish competitor Novo Nordisk — which launched in the U.S. and U.K. this year and is soon expected in some EU countries — demand for the more-convenient tablet is expected to rise.

Novo Nordisk has been attempting to reach as many patients as possible with its pill to capture market share, said CEO Mike Doustdar last week.

Doustdar also said the company would soon launch in Germany at its chosen price, ignoring pressure from the U.S. administration to raise prices in Europe.

Washington has been pressuring EU countries to pay more for medicines to offset pharma revenue losses from lower U.S. drug prices. The U.K. is the only country to agree to pay more for medicines via a bilateral deal with the U.S.

Foundayo's arrival in the U.K. will initially provide competition in the private market. A decision on whether the National Health Service will cover the pill is not expected until Nov. 18, and will be made by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.

World.title: Europe’s scorching summer is erasing its economic growth, says report
World.content:
The biggest drag is expected to come from people struggling to work in extreme heat. Triodos estimates lost labor productivity alone could shave around 0.6 percent off EU GDP, while agricultural output could fall by between 3 and 7 percent.

“At first sight this might seem modest, but it is exactly the expected economic growth for the EU this year,” said the bank of the overall €180 billion blow.

And the summer is not over. France and Britain are bracing for their fifth heat wave of the season this week, with temperatures nearing 40 degrees Celsius in southeastern France and 36 degrees forecast in the U.K.

The bill is already mounting beyond GDP. POLITICO estimated at least 14,000 excess deaths across the six hardest-hit European countries during the record-breaking heat wave from mid-June to early July.

Drought has also hammered Europe’s energy system: Low water levels in the Danube in recent weeks have forced sharp cuts at Hungary’s Paks nuclear plant and pushed Romania to blast apart a rock to divert water toward its last operating reactor. Vessels on the Rhine and Danube have had to sail only partially loaded.

In Austria, meanwhile, drought has caused an estimated €1 billion in agricultural losses, according to Austrian Hail Insurance, after some regions received more than 75 percent less rain than normal since mid-June.

Triodos warned against treating this summer as a freak event, saying extreme heat “might become structural” as the planet warms. But governments can soften the damage through irrigation, insulation, cooling and shifting working hours, said the bank.

“Every year adaptation without mitigation is a year borrowed against a hotter baseline.”

World.title: Moldovan president condemns Russia over killer drone crash
World.content:
Maia Sandu participates in a press conference in Warsaw on Jan. 26, 2026. | Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images

Chișinău has recalled its envoy to Moscow after two incidents in recent weeks.

Moldovan President Maia Sandu has blamed Russia’s war in Ukraine for a recent drone crash in the southeast of her country.

A drone crashed and exploded in the village of Crocmaz on Sunday, causing a fire that damaged several properties but caused no casualties. After conducting preliminary analysis on the fragments, local police said it could be a “missile-like drone.”

“I strongly condemn the latest violation of our airspace,” Sandu wrote on X, adding: “This is a direct consequence of Russia’s war, and it endangers us all.”

World.title: Farage demands sacking of Lowe aide as price of Reform-Restore talks
World.content:
On Monday the prospect of the two warring factions signing a make-up pact seemed to be at an impasse.

Farage used a press conference in Westminster to publicly state a new condition for holding discussions with “that party,” as he referred to Restore. Lowe must, he said, kick out Restore’s co-founder — a move Lowe has already rejected.

“I’m always happy to meet people and talk to people — within reason,” Farage said when asked by POLITICO what his conditions for entering talks with Lowe would be.

Leader of Restore Britain Rupert Lowe speaks to the media in Wigan, England on June 18, 2026. | Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images

“But I do think it’s fair to say that there are one or two people in the orbit of the upper echelons of that party who, if I sat down and talked to, I think our members and our voters would be utterly shocked that I’d done it,” he added.

“So we can talk to Rupert Lowe — that’s fine. But when you have co-founders, etcetera, putting out what I would call the ‘old theory’ — the old theory that we probably haven’t heard in this country since 1936 — and you have other adjacent publicly-supportive people demanding that all Jews be removed from the country, just as an example…

“So the condition I would put on it is those people would have to be out of the inner circle — and I think that for me would be the only way we could sensibly proceed.”

World.title: Meloni, Frederiksen unite to condemn ‘uncontrolled immigration’ after Ceuta crisis
World.content:
In response to the Ceuta crisis, which reignited Europe’s long-running debate on illegal migration, Denmark and Italy had sent a joint letter to the European Commission demanding immediate action at the EU’s external borders. The letter was co-signed by 20 other European heads of state and government.

Italy has since been one of the harshest critics of Spain’s left-wing government and its migration policies, with Rome announcing border controls for travelers arriving from Spain on Friday.

Meloni and Frederiksen argued that the adverse effects of illegal migration — “rising crime rates, growing pressure on public services, and an erosion of citizens’ trust” — were indisputable.

“For too long, ordinary people … have paid too high a price because of uncontrolled immigration,” they said.

“We are both proud of Europe’s Christian cultural heritage and want to protect it. We expect those who come to our countries and choose to make Europe their home to respect our values and not seek to impose ways of life on us that we do not share,” they said.

World.title: EU conservative chief demands migrant return hubs in Africa
World.content:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and her right-wing government are among the harshest critics, with Rome introducing border controls for travelers from Spain on Friday and sparking retaliation from Madrid.

Weber echoed proposals made last week by EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner, arguing that countries outside the bloc could be offered closer trade ties, economic collaboration and legal migration opportunities in exchange for accepting the installation of return hubs.

“Migrants who have no right to remain must leave Europe — no ifs, ands or buts!” he wrote, adding that returns must no longer depend on the political will of individual member countries.

Weber called for expanding the EU’s border and coast guard agency Frontex to 50,000 operational personnel, working alongside national forces and monitoring member countries’ compliance with the bloc’s border rules.

Weber also rejected internal border controls within Europe as a long-term solution. “They may be necessary in exceptional situations. But they do not address the root cause of the problem … There can therefore be only one answer: strong, joint European protection of the external border.”

In early June, the European Parliament and European Council announced new EU rules on migrant returns, including removals to countries outside the bloc in return hubs.

Weber also argued that the Ceuta crisis, which left around 100 dead, was the result of unilateral national action and said that the Spanish government’s “political signals” have had “an immediate impact on migration routes.”

World.title: Drought declared in 'almost three-quarters' of England, UK government says
World.content:
Some 71.3% of England is in drought, the UK government said on Monday, after the nation experienced its driest July on record, with a fifth heatwave and scant rain forecast for the week ahead.

 

Parks and fields that are usually green at this point in the year were parched and yellow, according to AFP news agency photos, as river levels dwindled and farmers battling low crop yields warned of possible food shortages.

"Almost three-quarters of England is now in drought as conditions worsen following a dry start to August," the environment department said, as parts of the central Midlands and northeast England joined other areas of the country experiencing prolonged dry weather.

"All regions of the country are experiencing pressure on their water resources," the department said, with "nowhere" in the UK having a "normal" status.

The Department of Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA) said most of England is experiencing a "flash drought," which develops quickly and is the result of very low rainfall and high temperatures.

A person walking through Primrose Hill as temperatures are expected to reach up to 33C in parts of the UK, 9 August, 2026 AP Photo

It is the third drought Britain, usually known for its unpredictable wet weather, has experienced in five years. More than 50% of England was declared to be in drought at the end of July.

Britain was also facing its fifth heatwave of the 2026 summer that has seen multiple temperature records being broken.

As much of Europe braces for another heatwave and prolonged dry conditions, scientists warn climate change is making extreme weather events more intense and frequent.

England and Wales both experienced the driest July on records, the UK's Met Office weather agency announced earlier, with England recording just 10% of its usual long-term average rainfall.

"There are warnings of more dry weather and another heatwave on the way, with temperatures tipped to reach the mid-30s in some places," DEFRA said.

The government has imposed irrigation restrictions on farmers and introduced a hosepipe ban in some regions, with more than 27 million people living under water-use restrictions.

There are now 45 million people living in a drought area, according to official figures. The total population of the United Kingdom is estimated at 69.3 million.

"We know the hot and dry weather is taking a real toll on farming and there will be long-lasting impacts on our environment," said the Environment Agency's Tony Grayling, who heads the National Drought Group.

World.title: Road rage: Which countries have the most aggressive drivers?
World.content:
Italy is a world-renowned holiday destination, with wonderful art, iconic scenery and top-class food.

 

However, one metric that appears to leave much to be desired is its roads, and particularly its drivers.

Italy is the country with the most aggressive drivers, according to the respondents of a recent global survey, with 23% of drivers claiming they experienced erratic or reckless behaviour in the country.

Second place may not be the most obvious, though: the UK is usually pictured with rolling green hills and some of the world's most comfortable cars, yet it ranked second in the poll by car rental platform Discovercars.com, with 11% of drivers saying they endured aggressive attitudes there. London in particular emerged as one of the most mentioned cities.

ars in a traffic jam at a cross roads in Rome, Friday, Nov. 14, 2025. AP/Gregorio Borgia

What are the most annoying driver behaviours?

The US comes in third place with 9%, followed by France and Australia with 5% each.

In joint fifth place, 4% of survey respondents said they had experienced the most aggression on the roads in Spain, with another 4% for Turkey.

The most annoying behaviour tends to be failing to indicate at turns (56%).

Tailgating also annoys drivers (46%), even more than slow driving in the overtaking lane (43%) and sudden braking (20%).

Which countries were voted as the most polite?

Perceptions of a country's politeness differ depending on whether its citizens are on or off the road, although there are still some common trends.

Italians also scored poorly in another poll on manners, ranking among the countries least associated with politeness in general: 24th out of 25 countries according toa poll by financial services company Remitly. Only Austria fared worse.

Firmly at the top of the chart is Japan, where bowing is still considered a sign of respect. It was followed by Canada and then the UK in third place.

The same poll asked respondents to reflect on their own behaviour and determine whether they would consider themselves polite and whether they treat strangers with respect.

Interestingly, Japanese people gave themselves one of the lowest rankings, albeit still high (8.73/10).

Brazil and Chile are the nations that most see themselves as the most polite in the world overall among the surveyed nations, giving themselves an average score of 9.46. The Indians came next (9.41), followed by the Swedes (9.40) and the French (9.40).

World.title: Russian intelligence op aimed at discredting Sweden, EU, NATO disrupted, Säpo says
World.content:
The Swedish Security Service (Säpo) said on Monday it had thwarted a Russian intelligence operation aimed at discrediting Sweden and which involved an "agent" working in a foreign diplomatic mission in Sweden.

 

The counter-espionage agency said in a statement it had "gathered information on, and taken measures against, a Russian intelligence operation aiming at influencing Swedish decision-making and discrediting Sweden, NATO and the EU."

According to Säpo, the "intelligence operation has been planned and directed by the Russian foreign intelligence service SVR for some time."

It did not identify the diplomatic mission where the agent allegedly involved worked.

"One of the aims of the operation was to gather information on Swedish decision-making in order to enable the Russian intelligence services to conduct influence operations concerning polarising issues, with the goal to undermine Swedish decision-making and discredit Sweden, NATO and the EU," Säpo said.

The NATO flag is hoisted on the patrol ship HMS Carlskrona (P04) setting sail from the naval port in Karlskrona, 4 February, 2025 AP Photo

Christoffer Wedelin, Säpo's deputy head of operations said that, upon learning of the operation, "the Swedish Security Service took action to protect vital Swedish assets and counter continued impact."

In 2024, Sweden ended two centuries of military non-alignment and joined NATO, spurred into the alliance by Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Säpo has repeatedly pointed to Russia, along with China and Iran, as the main intelligence threats to the country.

World.title: Solar power output set to fall during eclipse
World.content:
Portugal's grid operator Redes Energéticas Nacionais (REN) expects it will have to tap additional energy reserves to offset the loss of solar power generation caused by Wednesday's eclipse.

 

In the statement REN published on its website this Monday (source in Portuguese), the company says that "additional reserves from hydro and/or thermal generation will have to be mobilised" to mitigate the impact the phenomenon will have on the balance between energy consumed and generated in the National Electricity System (SEN), as well as the deviations the eclipse will cause in the interconnection between the Portuguese and Spanish grids. In neighbouring Spain, the eclipse will be 100% in a large part of the territory, while in Portugal it will be "almost total", ranging from 92% in the Algarve to 100% in the municipality of Bragança. The village of Guardamil is considered the best place in Portugal to see the eclipse in full.

According to REN's statement, the phenomenon, which will occur between 18:30 and 20:30 on Wednesday 12th, "will lead to an estimated loss of solar generation of 450 MW", which will represent around 7% of consumption and 45% of the solar output of the National Electricity System forecast for this time slot (average values). REN further indicates that "compared with the peak solar output forecast, the impact of the eclipse is estimated at around 15%".

For these figures, REN considers only centralised solar production and that recorded/measured by the company, excluding the solar energy generated by households for self-consumption. However, the impact that the drop in this household production will have on demand is factored into the consumption forecasts for that day.

The company says that "preparations for this event have been carried out in coordination with the other European transmission system operators, in particular through the Short Term Adequacy (STA) load-coverage assessment service, which ensures the balance between electricity generation and consumption over a seven-day horizon".

At the level of the European synchronous area, REN says the approximate loss of generation is estimated at 9,700 MW.

REN also points out that the phenomenon will occur in the late afternoon/early evening, a period when solar power generation is already declining, and so the impact will be smaller.

Solar power generation in Portugal reached an important milestone in July, the first month in which this energy source was the most used, accounting for 19% of consumption. Renewable sources represented 53% of total energy consumption.

World.title: From Tuscany to Moldova: The best winery restaurants in Europe revealed
World.content:
Forget the usual winery tasting with a perfunctory cheese board.

 

Some vineyards are now serving up destination-worthy dining too, pairing seriously good food with equally impressive wines and views.

Wine Enthusiast magazine has rounded up its favourite winery restaurants around the world, from laid-back vineyard lunches to ambitious tasting menus worth planning an entire trip around.

The publication’s list is made up of 57 wineries globally, and 22 are in Europe – with six in Italy alone – meaning a significant chunk of the best spots are relatively close to home.

Italy

Italy is world famous for its wide variety of wines and excellent cuisine, so it’s unsurprising that it appears six times on this list.

Tuscany is arguably the most famous wine region in the country, and four of the six – Osteria di Brolio and Il Ristoro di Castello di Ama in Chianti and Ristorante Campo del Drago in Montalcino and Indigeno in Montepulciano – are located there.

However, look in less well known areas and you’ll still find vineyards with food on a par with their beverage offerings.

La Veduta is located above the hills of Irpinia in the Campania region in the country’s southwest. It serves up handmade pasta and produce from the local countryside, best enjoyed with wines made from Fiano, Greco, and Aglianico grapes.

Near Verona, you’ll find Locanda Costasera, a winery restaurant which has a ‘wine first’ philosophy – meaning that food is paired with wines, rather than the typical other way around.

The rustic spot is the perfect place to try a Corvina-Merlot wine blend served with flavoursome tubetti pasta.

Portugal

Portugal’s Alentejo region is a trending destination right now – and that extends to its vineyards.

The vineyard attached to Malhadinha Nova restaurant serves modern wines and that’s reflected in the eatery's menu alongside traditional Alentejo cuisine. Many dishes use ingredients grown and raised on the property, including black Iberian pigs.

A growing number of vineyards are turning their tasting rooms into proper dining destinations, too David Köhler/Unsplash

Over in the Douro region, restaurant Bomfim 1896 is well and truly inspired by local food. Set on the riverside in Pinhão, open kitchens serve everything from smoked eel to slow-roasted baby goat.

At Mesa de Lemos in Dão, things are very modern indeed, from the building’s floor-to-ceiling glass to the menu.

Chef Diogo Rocha ensures that each plate served is focused on one single ingredient, including pandora fish from the Algarve and pineapple from the Azores.

France

France is famous for its wines of all varieties and colours as well as its eats.

Chez Jeannette in Provence has a menu with dishes which are inventive but not pretentious, like amberjack with white asparagus and acacia flower vinegar. Dishes use ingredients from the wine estate’s organic garden as well as nearby farms, ensuring the freshest foods.

In the Bordeaux region, La Grand’Vigne is one of the fancier restaurants on this list.

The restaurant boasts two Michelin stars and is renowned for its elegant French cooking and long, complex tasting menus.

England

The south of England is currently going through something of a golden age of vineyards, thanks to warmer weather and similar growing conditions to more traditional vineyard locations on mainland Europe.

Chalk at the Wiston Estate in West Sussex has capitalised on the popularity of the vineyard’s sparkling wines and leaned into English cooking. Expect dishes ranging from mackerel with horseradish and elderflower to Devonshire brill accompanied with samphire.

Hambledon in Hampshire is considered England’s oldest commercial vineyard, and its restaurant is well worth a visit.

The menu is seasonable and, while staples like guinea fowl and chalk stream trout may remain on the menu for the whole year, they’ll be served with asparagus, peas, broccoli sprouts and wild garlic in the spring and summer, and with pickled onion and chestnuts in the autumn.

Spain

While Spain is famous for its many wine varieties, its two vineyard restaurants on this list are located in Ribera del Duero in the north.

Refectorio, a Michelin-starred restaurant, pairs Ribera del Duero region wines with tasting menus.

Set in a former 12th-century abbey dining hall, the menu draws on eats from the past, serving up dishes including pickled partridge and alboronía aubergine stew.

Also boasting a Michelin star is Ambivium at Pago de Carraovejas. Each course in each tasting menu is paired with a specific wine from the vineyard’s cellar, and diners can enjoy their feast overlooking the picturesque vines beyond.

Other winery restaurants to visit in Europe

Beyond the better-known wine destinations of Italy, France and Portugal, Wine Enthusiast’s list also includes a handful of less obvious European picks.

Austria, Germany, Greece and Hungary each have one winery restaurant on the list, offering plenty of reasons to look beyond the continent’s more established wine regions.

There’s also an entry from Liechtenstein, the tiny Alpine country better known for its mountains than its wine, while Moldova makes an appearance too.

Georgia also features, and it actually has one of the world’s oldest winemaking traditions and is increasingly gaining attention from travellers interested in wine.

The list’s selections reveal that Europe’s wine map extends well beyond its most famous names and the fact that there’s only one restaurant from each of these countries in the ranking means they might be tempting for travellers who prefer their wine trips with a bit of discovery involved.

Alcohol can be dangerous for health so please drink responsibly.

World.title: Firefighters struggle to put out three wildfires in southwestern Spain
World.content:
Firefighters struggled on Monday to control three large wildfires in southern Spain that has forced the evacuation of around 800 people due to shifting winds and difficult terrain, officials said.

 

More than 600 firefighters backed by 26 water-dropping aircraft were battling the blaze which broke out last week in the Andalusian province of Huelva, said the region's minister for emergencies, Antonio Sanz.

"We are facing an extremely difficult, complex and dangerous wildfire, with the weather conditions continuing to offer us no respite. It is a long-distance race full of obstacles," he said.

"We have to be realistic: there is no forecast that the fire will be brought under control any time soon. There are still hours and probably days of intense work ahead."

Crews worked through the night, carrying out controlled burns and creating mechanised firebreaks, but authorities said rugged terrain and weather conditions had slowed progress.

A house and belongings destroyed by a wildfire are photographed as the fire continues to spread near Pelayos de la Presa, 28 July, 2026 AP Photo

More than 20,000 hectares of land are currently enclosed by the fire, but authorities stressed this figure refers to the area contained within the fire line and does not mean all of it has burned.

Officials on Monday ordered the evacuation of the municipality of El Madrono, which has a population of around 300 people, bringing to about 800 the total number of evacuees.

Crews are also battling blazes in Castellón and Segovia. All three fires have been graded level two for severity.

Spain is enduring a tough summer for wildfires, with around three dozen blazes having forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people, especially in the centre of the country.

One that raged in July in the Avila region near Madrid was considered the biggest Spain had seen in recent history, laying waste to some 50,000 hectares.

Early in July, another sweeping blaze caused 14 deaths in Almeria province in Andalusia.

Europe has suffered a succession of heatwaves and droughts this year, which scientists say have been aggravated by human-generated climate change.

World.title: At least 73 confirmed dead after major earthquake rocks Colombia and neighbours
World.content:
At least 73 people were killed and dozens of buildings collapsed in cities across western Colombia on Monday after a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck the South American nation.

 

The quake trapped residents under debris, leaving more injured and forcing people to evacuate their homes as far as the capital of Bogotá.

The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people in the Choco region about 250 miles west of Bogotá, the US Geological Survey and Colombia’s counterpart reported.

The USGS said it struck at a depth of 107 kilometers and was also was felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama, though minimal damage was reported there.

Local officials confirmed that at least 40 people were killed in the Risaralda region, where the hard-hit city of Pereira is located, and 27 people in the Valle del Cauca region, where Colombia's third-biggest city, Cali, is located. At least three of those killed in Valle del Cauca were children, the governor said.

Authorities also confirmed four people were killed in Choco and two more in the city of Manizales in the Caldas region. Many more people across the country were injured.

The quake left cities across the west of the country ravaged.

Residents and rescue workers search through the rubble of a collapsed building after an earthquake struck Cali, 10 August, 2026 AP Photo

A mix of residents and search teams picked through the rubble of collapsed buildings amid concerns by authorities of aftershocks.

Colombia's interior minister said more than 20 municipalities across the country had been hit.

Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, said he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city from his home in hills of the city as buildings collapsed. Residents in the city and rescue workers were searching the rubble for survivors.

“My entire house shook,” he said. “I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake.”

Colombia's Geological Service said on Monday that it had been “the highest magnitude earthquake registered in Colombia in the last decade” and that it had been followed by two 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude aftershocks.

Authorities also reported that flights were suspended in the airports of Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago y Buenaventura and Pereira.

People stand outside their homes after a quake was felt in Bogotá, 10 August, 2026 AP Photo

The earthquakes left many in the Andean nation unnerved after two back-to-back quakes devastated neighbouring Venezuela in late June, destroyed hundreds of buildings and killed more than 5,000 people.

At the same time the quake brought down buildings in Colombia, desperate families in Venezuela continued to search the ruins for the bodies of their loved ones.

In Pereira, photos and videos published by local media showed pieces of the airport ceiling falling down on travellers taking shelter and screaming, and people running through rubble in a panic.

Pereira's mayor, Mauricio Salazar, told a local radio station that at least 18 people had died and that many more were trapped under “a massive quantity of collapsed buildings.”

In nearby Manizales, a city nestled in the coffee-producing mountains of Colombia, one of the towers of the neo-Gothic cathedral collapsed and fell on the nave. Jorge Eduardo Rojas, the mayor of Manizales said two people had died in the city “because of the quake” and asked residents to stay outside in case of aftershocks.

Patients are evacuated outside a hospital after an earthquake struck Cali, 10 August, 2026 AP Photo

Authorities in the rural state of Choco, the epicentre of the quake, reported injured people and damaged buildings in the capital, but provided few details.

In Cali, a city 2 million people, Mayor Alejandro Eder said that residents were trapped in at least 19 buildings that had collapsed.

Small earthquakes, known as “temblores,” are common in central and western Colombia, but those above 6.0 magnitude are rare.

In 1999, a 6.2 magnitude quake near the city of Armenia, killed more than 1,100 people.

Colombia’s newly inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said on Monday that he had personally taken charge of the government’s response to the emergency in San José del Palmar following the earthquake that struck the country.

“You are not alone. The state is present and taking action,” he said.

World.title: Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy
World.content:
The launch of the Yeni Party in Turkey promises to energise the country's struggling opposition. But while some polls show it leading, it remains vulnerable – already beset by arrests it says are "politically motivated".

Advertising

In a glitzy video, set to pumping music and shared widely across social media, Ozgur Ozel launched the Yeni Party – "New Party" – vowing to usher in a new era in Turkish politics and end President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s long rule.

Ozel founded the New Party after a court removed him from leading the main opposition party, the Republican People’s Party (CHP).

His rival, former party leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu, 77, who lost every election during his decade in charge of the CHP, replaced him.

Many in the country believe Erdogan played a role in the removal of Ozel, as his popularity grew thanks to tireless campaigning.

Riding the wave

The New Party is settings its sights beyond the CHP’s usual supporters.

"It covers the whole political spectrum in Turkish political life," explains Ozel's advisor Ilham Uzel.

"There are critical elements like democratisation, rule of law, secularism and a pro-Western approach, so we maintain these main pillars. But it is not confined to social democracy; we reach out to every section of Turkish society, including Islamists and conservatives, nationalists and liberals. We have Kurdish supporters."

The New Party is riding a wave of excitement. Ninety-one out of 135 CHP parliamentary deputies have defected to its ranks, joined by dozens of mayors and it is swiftly becoming the main opposition in parliament.

Turkey opposition worries that Europe is sacrificing democracy for security

Some polls show the party soaring above 30 percent, leaving Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party behind, while the CHP’s support has collapsed.

The New Party’s broad approach is finding fertile ground. "Even those who still support the governing coalition, the AK Party and MHP, are unhappy with how things are or how politics is practised, especially regarding economic issues. So there is a push towards change," says political commentator Sezin Oney.

"There is a yearning to change things at the grassroots, and the New Party may be the only party that can represent a new way of doing politics. But they have to live up to it, of course."

Corruption charges

Erdogan has remained in power for more than 20 years partly by exploiting divisions within the opposition, which is made up of conservatives, hardline secularists, and both Kurdish and Turkish nationalists.

The New Party has a key advantage over the strongly secular CHP, whose history is linked to past policies targeting Turkey’s large Kurdish minority and religious conservatives.

"CHP is identified with many bad experiences that the Kurds and conservative people had in past decades," said Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

"If you look at what Ozgur Ozel says during his speeches, you may clearly see the Yeni Party doesn’t have the baggage of CHP."

Erdogan has also often exploited the CHP’s history, painting it as anti-religious and hostile to Kurdish minority rights. The New Party faces the tricky task of keeping CHP loyalists on board while reaching new supporters.

But for now, simply staying out of jail may be the most pressing concern for its representatives.

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Several mayors who joined the New Party have been arrested on corruption charges, widely seen as politically motivated. In the past two years, 26 opposition mayors and hundreds of officials have been imprisoned on corruption allegations, compared to two mayors from Erdogan’s AK Party.

"They are cracking down on our party – every other day, mayors are arrested," says Uzgel. "They filed another charge against our leader. Nobody is safe in this authoritarian regime. So Mr Ozel is on the spot, definitely."

Ozel is protected by parliamentary immunity, but Oney warns he may be running out of time.

"Ozgur Ozel might be imprisoned himself once his immunity is removed by a parliamentary vote, that's a possibility. The only immunity he can have is the immunity bestowed upon him by the people. So only public opinion is protecting him. How much can it protect him? We'll see."

With parliament about to break for summer until October, Ozel has a brief window to strengthen his party and rally public support.

World.title: Colombia: Dozens killed after large earthquake rocks region
World.content:
A powerful earthquake, measured at magnitude 7.4, has struck Colombia, killing at least 73 people. Cities including Cali, Pereira and Manizales were among the hardest-hit.

A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning.

Around five hours after the quake struck, officials around the country had reported at least 73 deaths, 67 of them just in two of the worst-hit states. Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities.

The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast.

The mayor of Cali said that 'at least 20 structures' collapsed in the quake Image: Reuters TV/REUTERS

What is the latest?

The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside.

"Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin."

Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, later said that at least 27 people had died in the quake.

Officials in Risaralda said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor.

And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira.

Residents in Cali tried to rush to safety in the aftermath of Monday's earthquake Image: Santiago Saldarriaga/AP Photo/picture alliance

The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were four dead and 69 wounded in her district as of late morning local time.

Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined.

"Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list.

Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency in San Jose del Palmar following the earthquake that struck the country.

"You are not alone. The state is present and taking action," he said.

What do we know about the quake's size and location?

The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well.

The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border.

One of the towers at the Cathedral of Manizales was damaged by the quake Image: John Jairo Bonilla/AP Photo/picture alliance

The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south.

The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter.

The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors .

Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela.

USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake.

The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier
