In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). The nominee, Mateusz Szpytma, has served as deputy head of the IPN since 2016, including when it was under the leadership of Karol Nawrocki, who last year was elected president of Poland with the support of the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. Szpytma’s candidacy has been opposed by most of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, who argue he helped politicise the IPN under the former PiS government. However, some more conservative elements of the coalition joined the opposition in supporting Szpytma, giving him a majority in the Sejm but not the Senate. Senatorowie nie wyrazili zgody na powołanie Mateusza Szpytmy na Prezesa Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej – Komisji Ścigania Zbrodni przeciwko Narodowi Polskiemu — Senat RP 🇵🇱 (@PolskiSenat) August 6, 2026 The IPN is a body tasked with researching, documenting and educating about Poland’s tumultuous and tragic 20th-century history. It also has the power to prosecute crimes relating to the periods when the country was under Nazi and communist rule. The institute was led by Nawrocki from 2021 until August last year, when he became president of Poland. Since then, the IPN has been without a permanent head. Last October, the IPN’s council nominated Karol Polejowski, another of the institute’s deputy heads, to be its new president. But he was rejected by the Sejm, which, along with the Senate, must approve the choice. In April, the council instead recommended Szpytma, whose candidacy was approved by the Sejm last month. He received support mainly from opposition parties, including PiS and the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). However, in a rare split within the ruling coalition, one of its junior members, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), also backed Szpytma, as did some MPs from the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050). That was enough to give him a majority. By contrast, the main ruling party, Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), and The Left (Lewica) opposed his nomination, citing a letter signed earlier this year by 170 academics, who described Szpytma as “one of the faces of IPN’s politicisation” under the former PiS government. However, PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, who also serves as Poland’s defence minister and deputy prime minister rejected that characterisation and said that PSL had backed Szpytma because of his work commemorating historical figures from the agrarian movement in which PSL is rooted. In a rare split in the ruling coalition, MPs from two parties, PSL and Poland 2050, voted with the opposition in the Sejm for a new head of the Institute of National Remembrance. However, PM Donald Tusk says their choice will be rejected by the Senate https://t.co/0CGmbsNp4F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 However, it was widely expected that Szpytma’s candidacy would be blocked by the upper-house Senate, where even the PSL and opposition combined do not have a majority in the 100-seat chamber. That was confirmed in a vote on Thursday, when 50 senators were opposed to Szyptma and only 38 were in favour, with one abstention. “We voted against further politicisation” of IPN and “against tolerating financial irregularities”, wrote the speaker of the Senate, Małgorzata Kidawa-Błonska of KO. The latter comment was likely a reference to a report by the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) last year which found that the IPN had, between 2022 and 2025, failed to properly manage tens of millions of zloty in spending, including various violations of regulations on the use of public funds. Szpytma told journalists that he was not surprised by the result of the vote, saying he believes his connection to Nawrocki, who is an ardent opponent of the current government and has vetoed a record number of laws, is the reason why he lost. Nie zgodziliśmy się w Senacie, by człowiek Karola Nawrockiego został prezesem IPN. Zagłosowaliśmy przeciw dalszemu upolitycznianiu Instytutu. Przeciw tolerowaniu nieprawidłowości finansowych. Pan Szpytma nie wprowadziłby żadnych zmian w funkcjonowaniu IPN. — Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska (@M_K_Blonska) August 6, 2026 The IPN plays an important role in Polish public life, including in commemorating, investigating and prosecuting crimes that took place during the Nazi-German and Soviet occupations of Poland in World War Two, as well as during the decades of communist rule afterwards. Under Nawrocki’s leadership, the IPN accelerated the process of demolishing remaining Soviet monuments in Poland, often prompting criticism from Russia. It has also been closely involved in the exhumation of victims of the Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Poles during World War Two. During PiS’s time in power from 2015 to 2023, the IPN was accused of becoming increasingly politicised, using its activities to support the historical narratived promoted by the government. In 2021, Israel protested after a former far-right activist was appointed to head one of the IPN’s local branches. Russia has criticised the "sacrilegious" demolition of a Soviet monument in Poland, calling it a “flagrant violation” of a bilateral agreement. But Poland's @ipngovpl says it was a "propaganda object" that had to be removed under a "decommunisation" law https://t.co/73T99ZlPqU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Polish state energy giant Orlen posted a record profit in the first half of 2026, as turmoil in the Middle East boosted earnings in the fuel sector, despite Polish government measures to cushion the rise in consumer prices. Orlen has also this year seen its highest ever proportion of revenue from foreign markets. The results come amid a political dispute over a government plan to impose a windfall tax on excess profits from fuel sales, aimed at recouping billions spent on consumer subsidies. Orlen would be the biggest target of the tax, but the plan has been obstructed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. W pierwszym półroczu Orlen zarobił na czysto 15,8 miliarda złotych. Trzy razy więcej niż przed rokiem.https://t.co/qJS81csI0H — TVN24 BiS (@TVN24BiS) August 6, 2026 On Thursday, Orlen reported consolidated net profit of 15.9 billion zloty (€3.7 billion) for the first six months of the year, almost tripling from the 5.7 billion zloty recorded in the same period of 2025. Revenue rose to 152.2 billion zloty from 134.4 billion zloty. CEO Ireneusz Fąfara acknowledged that the figures came amid exceptional market conditions. Energy prices jumped globally in March, after the US and Israel began to attack Iran and Tehran responded by blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a key export route. Fąfara noted that, despite this, Poland had maintained some of Europe’s lowest fuel prices. He said that Orlen had prioritised fuel availability and competitive domestic prices while taking advantage of stronger margins abroad, where it brought in an “absolutely record level of revenue from foreign markets”. In the first half of 2026, foreign markets accounted for 35.7% of Orlen’s revenue, up from 33.8% a year earlier. The bulk came from Germany, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Austria, where Orlen operates petrol stations, as well as from trading activities in markets such as the Netherlands and Switzerland. Pierwsze półrocze 2026 roku ORLEN zamyka rekordowym zyskiem z rynków zagranicznych. Wynik netto całej Grupy w II kwartale wyniósł 7,7 mld zł. Wypracowane wyniki finansowe pozwoliły na wypłatę rekordowej dywidendy dla akcjonariuszy oraz dalsze finansowanie największego programu… pic.twitter.com/ohcxksuv4G — ORLEN (@GrupaORLEN) August 6, 2026 Orlen has expanded rapidly in recent years, as it has swallowed up other state-owned energy firms and sought to diversify away from its traditional focus on oil towards gas, renewables and hydrogen. In March this year, Orlen’s market valuation rose to its highest ever level of €35.2 billion, up from €7 billion in early 2022. As a result, it overtook the market capitalisation of Russian energy giant Gazprom. Mateusz Czyżkowski, an analyst at brokerage XTB, attributed Orlen’s record profits this year to “skilful balancing between geopolitical conditions and local pressures”, including government-imposed fuel price caps that squeezed margins. “The global commodities market in the second quarter of 2026 was strongly buoyed by tensions between Iran and Israel and ongoing disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz…This significant geopolitical premium boosted profits in [Orlen’s] Upstream & Supply segment,” he wrote in a note. The announcement of record profits comes as Orlen finds itself at the centre of a political dispute over the government’s proposed windfall tax, which would introduce a 60% levy on excess profits from liquid fuel sales. The measure was expected to raise around 4 billion zloty, which would have offset most of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by, among other things, cutting VAT and introducing a maximum daily price. However, although the tax was approved by the government’s majority in parliament in July, President Nawrocki refused to sign it into law, instead referring it to the constitutional court for review – a process that has no time limit and can take years. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 According to government calculations, Orlen would account for around 60% of the tax base if the measures eventually come into force. However, at his press conference on Thursday, Fąfara emphasised that the company supports the windfall tax. “We have viewed this solution positively from the very beginning. I believe it is in the interest of the company, our customers, and the country,” he said. However, Fąfara rejected suggestions that Orlen could unilaterally reduce pump prices by sacrificing margins. “We cannot lower prices in defiance of the market and global prices…If we lowered prices below parity, there would be a shortage of fuel,” he warned, adding that artificially low prices would encourage speculative exports and fuel tourism. Prices at petrol stations jumped today in Poland after the government ended the last of the support measures introduced to cushion consumers from the energy crisis caused by the war in Iran. Some places saw prices rise by as much as 14%https://t.co/mUfWUyDMle — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 1, 2026 Prime Minister Donald Tusk used Orlen’s record profit announcement to reiterate criticism of the Nawrocki for obstructing the windfall tax. “Taxing such extraordinary profits made by oil companies, not just Orlen, was intended to bring down prices at petrol stations. That is precisely what Karol Nawrocki blocked. Remember this when you’re tanking up,” Tusk wrote on social media. Nawrocki’s office has, however, rejected the idea that an increased tax on fuel companies would somehow reduce fuel prices, arguing that, if anything, it would have the opposite effect if companies pass some of the costs onto consumers. Zysk Orlenu w pierwszym półroczu był wyższy od zeszłorocznego o 10 miliardów! Opodatkowanie takich nadzwyczajnych zysków koncernów paliwowych, nie tylko Orlenu, miały służyć obniżeniu cen na stacjach. To właśnie zablokował @NawrockiKn Pamiętajcie przy tankowaniu. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) August 6, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: New Polish opposition group proposes paying parents “salary” to encourage more births
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. New Polish opposition group Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which recently broke away from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, has proposed the idea of paying a “parental salary” for the first three years of a child’s life. The idea is part of a package of proposals to tackle Poland’s dire demographic situation released on Friday by Development Plus in its first major policy announcement since leader Mateusz Morawiecki announced that the group would soon become a political party. 3600 zł miesięcznie na dziecko do 3. roku życia – jedna z wielu propozycji @RozwojPlus dla demografii! Pensja Rodzicielska wynosząca równowartość płacy minimalnej, czyli obecnie około 3600 zł netto miesięcznie przez pierwsze 3 lata życia dziecka. To ponad czterokrotnie więcej… pic.twitter.com/253pwcskNK — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) August 7, 2026 The proposed parental salary would amount to 3,600 zloty (€837) per month, the equivalent of the minimum wage after taxes. It is 4.5 times more than the current child benefit payment of 800 zloty per month that all Polish parents of children under 18 receive. Development Plus says that the parental salary could be combined with income from other work that parents undertake and that it would include contributions towards their pensions. It would end once a child turns three, after which parents would have access to normal child benefit payments. The group says that, for now, the idea is just a proposal, based on expert analysis of how to tackle Poland’s demographic crisis, and that it now wants to “refine it through dialogue with Poles” rather than “imposing top-down provisions”. Poland has long been grappling with a shrinking, ageing population. Last year, the number of births fell to a new post-war low of 238,000, while deaths totalled 406,000. That marked the 13th consecutive year in which more people died than were born in Poland. The country’s fertility rate – meaning the average number of children that are born to a woman over her lifetime – fell to a new record low of 1.068 in 2025. That is one of the lowest figures anywhere in the world and well below the so-called “replacement rate” – the figure needed to ensure that the population does not decline – which is generally defined as 2.1. Poland’s fertility rate, already one of the lowest in the world, fell to a new record low of 1.07 in 2025, deepening concerns over the country's shrinking and ageing population https://t.co/OMGC1MpA5l — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 28, 2026 Successive Polish governments have introduced various measures intended to boost the birth rate, though so far without clear success. The former PiS government, with Morawiecki as finance minister and later prime minister, introduced and expanded the current child benefit programme. While there was a brief bump in births after it was launched in 2016, numbers subsequently continued their downward trend. After PiS lost power in 2023, the current government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, continued the child benefit programme and also introduced new payments to support parents who return to work and restored funding for IVF treatment, which was previously cut by PiS. When announcing the proposed parental salary on Friday, Development Plus also outlined seven other proposed new policies to ease Poland’s demographic problems. One would allow workers to have a portion of their contributions go towards their parents’ pensions. Another pledged to provide better maternity care, including access to anaesthesia, a private hospital room and dedicated midwife, prenatal testing, and infertility treatment. Other policies promised more flexible working arrangements and mortgage repayments to prevent people from having to choose between a family or a career, as well as school hours and after-school care that “adapt to the lives of families, not the other way around”. Development Plus also proposed “granting parents the right to represent the voices of their minor children”. However, they provided no details of what this would mean in practice. Dzieci to nasza przyszłość! To fundament bezpieczeństwa Polski i polska racja stanu. Jak sprawić, by Polaków rodziło się coraz więcej? Oto strategia demograficzna dla Polski Stowarzyszenia @RozwojPlus🇵🇱➕. pic.twitter.com/1hiQPNuL47 — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) August 7, 2026 Development Plus was founded as an association by Morawiecki in April this year. That immediately prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. Matters came to a head last month, when PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński demanded that all the party’s lawmakers sign a pledge of loyalty and commit to leave any political associations they are part of. Morawiecki and his allies refused to do so, prompting Kaczyński to declare that meant they had effectively resigned from the party. Last week, Development Plus announced it had formed its own separate parliamentary caucus with 40 MPs in the Sejm, the most powerful lower house of parliament. The move immediately made it the third-largest group in the parliament, while also meaning PiS was no longer the biggest. On Monday this week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”, following PiS’s shift in a more hardline direction over recent months. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has called for Ukrainian men of conscription age who are not legally working to be deported to Ukraine. The policy, which continues a recent hardening of PiS’s position towards Ukraine and Ukrainians as it competes with the far right for support, was condemned by government figures, who called it “absurd” and “disgusting”. 🇵🇱 Bezpieczeństwo obywateli powinno być priorytetem każdego rządu. Potrzebne są zdecydowane działania wobec osób przebywających w Polsce niezgodnie z prawem. 👉 Udostępnij! 🔥 Ku nowemu rządowi! pic.twitter.com/m8MctmmPXd — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) August 6, 2026 On Thursday, PiS, which has recently been hit by falling support in the polls and the defection of a large breakaway group of more moderate MPs, held a policy convention at which it presented ideas it wants to implement if it returns to power after next year’s parliamentary elections. “One of [our] government’s first, most significant decisions will be to deport men, Ukrainians of military age, who are not legally working in Poland,” announced Tobiasz Bocheński, a deputy leader of the party. “They will have the opportunity to fight for their homeland, so that the horrors of this war can quickly end,” he continued. “Because for Central and Eastern Europe to be secure and free, Ukraine must win.” Bocheński denied that the policy was inhumane, noting that, in 2022, when PiS was in government, “Poles, like no other nation in Europe, opened their hearts, their homes and their wallets to women, children, the elderly and disabled people fleeing Putin’s bombs”. Poland was the primary destination for refugees fleeing Ukraine in 2022. Almost one million of them remain in the country, alongside hundreds of thousands of other Ukrainian immigrants, many of whom arrived before 2022. They are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group. In their announcement of the proposed policy, PiS gave no details of how it would work in practice, nor on what legal basis Ukrainians who are legally resident in Poland and have not violated any laws would be deported. News website Interia, which had reported on PiS’s plans shortly before they were officially announced, notes that data from Poland’s labour ministry show that only around 11,000 Ukrainians are registered as unemployed in Poland. The figures are not broken down by gender, but most are believed to be women. However, PiS’s policy would also apply to Ukrainians in the so-called grey economy, where people work informally without registering or paying taxes, reports Interia. Military-age Ukrainian men in other European countries should not receive social benefits, says Poland's foreign minister, @sikorskiradek. "There should be no financial incentives for avoiding the draft" https://t.co/5TcTqyDa6X — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2024 PiS’s plan was immediately criticised by government figures, with interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka calling it “an absurd idea” and “pure demagoguery”. She noted that over 95% of Ukrainian men of conscription age in Poland are working legally and paying taxes. “Without these people, many key sectors of the Polish economy would simply grind to a halt,” wrote Gałecka. “Stop the incitement.” Deputy interior minister Maciej Duszczyk, meanwhile, told broadcaster TVN that, among the Ukrainian men not working, many are wounded soldiers in Poland for treatment and rehabilitation or fathers caring for disabled children. Deportations are a “purely political, disgusting idea”, he added. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński wrote that, “when [PiS] was in power, they couldn’t even deport those who were breaking the law, and now they’re supposedly going to deport everyone without rhyme or reason”. Since taking power, the current government has increased deportations of foreigners who are in Poland illegally or broke the law while in the country. Last year, it carried out over 9,000 deportations, up from 7,200 in 2023, the last year that PiS was in power Absurdalny pomysł @pisorgpl ws. deportacji Ukraińców to czysta demagogia! Ponad 95% mężczyzn w wieku poborowym legalnie pracuje w 🇵🇱 i płaci podatki (dane ZUS).@OficjalnyJK zapowiada deportacje. A jak miałoby to wyglądać w praktyce? Patrole sprawdzające dokumenty na ulicach?… — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) August 6, 2026 During the conference on Thursday, PiS emphasised its tough approach to migration more broadly, saying that it would “create a new, restrictive system for foreigners” that would track each immigrant in the country. “Every foreigner will have their own individual account,” and if they commit any offences or fail to abide by any administrative obligations, “the information will be immediately entered into the system, and the deportation process will begin”, said Bocheński. “The only good migration is the return of Poles from abroad,” declared the party on social media. 🛡️ Bezpieczne granice to bezpieczna Polska. Skuteczna ochrona granic i walka z nielegalną imigracją to obowiązek każdego odpowiedzialnego państwa. 👉 Udostępnij! 🔥 Ku nowemu rządowi! pic.twitter.com/rRPZpmXi5U — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) August 6, 2026 In fact, it was during PiS’s time in power from 2015 to 2023 that Poland saw the largest wave of immigration in its history, and one of the largest anywhere in Europe. In every year between 2017 and 2022, Poland was the EU member state that issued the highest number of first residence permits to immigrants from outside the bloc. There are now over two million foreigners registered as living in Poland, making up just 5% of the population. Around three quarters are Ukrainians (1.55 million), with the next largest groups being Belarusians (139,300), Indians (26,100), Georgians (22,200), Russians (19,500), Vietnamese (15,100) and Turks (14,500). The number of foreigners with residence permits in Poland has reached two million, making up just over 5% of the country’s population, new government data show. The largest national group by far are Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians and Indians https://t.co/SI09WtR7hR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 26, 2026 While in government, PiS welcomed Ukrainian migrants and refugees and was a strong supporter of Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. However, since going into opposition, it has taken an increasingly tough line. That has reflected a broader shift in Polish society, with a variety of polls showing rising negative sentiment towards Ukraine and Ukrainians. Recent months have also seen a rise in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland, including a number of high-profile incidents. Meanwhile, two far-right parties that have long taken an anti-Ukrainian stance, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have soared in the polls, placing pressure on PiS to toughen its own position. One Confederation MEP, Stanisław Tyszka, mocked PiS’s latest policy announcement. “PiS wants to heroically deport hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians whom they themselves let into Poland,” he wrote. “Comedy.” The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland invokes emergency grid capacity powers for second time in three days amid heatwave
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s power grid operator, PSE, has, for the second time in three days and third time this summer, invoked emergency measures to ensure supply amid an ongoing heatwave. Before this summer, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced. However, following a meeting with PSE and other state energy officials, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has assured Poles that, despite “a very difficult period”, the “situation is under control” and power supplies are secure, thanks in part to the growth of renewables in recent years. ❗️PSE ponownie ogłaszają okresy przywołania na rynku mocy❗️ To już 3. raz w tym roku, kiedy operator sięga po to narzędzie. W historii zdarzyło się to tylko 5 razy, wliczywszy 3 przypadki tegoroczne, co pokazuje wyjątkowość roku 2026 dla energetyki. pic.twitter.com/DbCPnpyae4 — Jakub Wiech (@jakubwiech) August 6, 2026 PSE has called on contracted electricity generators to increase output and large consumers to cut use to help balance the grid on Thursday between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m., as temperatures have this week approached 40°C (104°F) in many parts of the country. The same measures were introduced on Tuesday, as the heatwave pushed up electricity consumption, partly due to increased use of air conditioning and refrigeration. Participants in Poland’s capacity market are paid for maintaining standby capacity and fulfilling their obligations when called upon by the operator. According to PSE, the mechanism is “a remedial measure” used when the generation capacity available to the operator falls significantly below the required safety level. Previously, the measures were invoked in June this year, amid another heatwave that saw Poland hit its highest-ever recorded temperature of 40.5°C. But before that, they had only been used twice since being introduced in 2018. Temperatures in Poland have reached the highest level on record, with a figure of 40.3°C (104.5°F) recorded this afternoon, as the heatwave that has hit Europe this week moves eastwards https://t.co/eRhRxiuCGq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 28, 2026 Poland’s weather institute IMGW issued heat warnings on Thursday for 13 of the country’s 16 provinces, with daytime temperatures forecast to reach between 33C and 38C. High temperatures and prolonged drought conditions have also pushed water levels in many rivers to extremely low levels, with the Vistula, Poland’s longest river, only 5 centimetres above the historic low of 4 centimetres it fell to in Warsaw last year. Some other parts of the river have hit all-time record lows, reports Polsat News. One result has been a disruption of cooling supplies to Poland’s power sector. State energy firm Enea this week announced reduced operations at two of its coal-fired plants that are cooled by water from the Vistula. Around 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of capacity (just over 1% of Poland’s total) has gone offline. On Wednesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk convened a meeting of a government crisis team, including PSE’s deputy president, to discuss the current heatwave and its potential impact on the power sector. However, afterwards he assured that “the situation is under control” and that the fact that Poland now has “a lot of energy from solar panels and wind turbines makes our system relatively secure”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Poland’s renewable sector has expanded rapidly over the last decade. Last year, it provided just over 29% of the country’s power, with onshore wind supplying 14% of the energy mix and solar 12%. Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021. Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined. World.title: Polish top court confirms withholding funds from opposition PiS party over campaign finance irregularities
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s top administrative court has upheld a decision by the finance ministry to withhold state subsidies from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party due to campaign finance irregularities. The decision was welcomed by the government, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying that there will be “no money for grifters”. PiS, however, argues that the money is being withheld for political reasons and accuses the authorities of “Russian standards”. Naczelny Sąd Administracyjny oddalił w środę kasacje ws. dotacji i subwencji dla PiS. – Miażdżący dla PiS wyrok podtrzymany! – stwierdził szef MF Andrzej Domański https://t.co/bcL18WbiYf — OKO.press (@oko_press) August 6, 2026 The dispute dates back to August 2024, when the National Electoral Commission (PKW) rejected PiS’s financial report for the previous year’s parliamentary election campaign after identifying around 3.6 million zloty (€838,000) in unauthorised expenditure. As a result, the PKW ordered that PiS should lose 10.8 million zloty from the state subsidies that political parties in Poland receive based on their level of electoral support. The party would normally have received 25.9 million zloty based on its 2023 election result. The decision triggered months of legal wrangling, with PiS arguing that the funding should be restored after the Supreme Court upheld its complaint against the PKW’s decision. However, finance minister Andrzej Domański refused to release the money, saying there were unresolved legal doubts over the ruling. The finance minister has refused to comply with the electoral commission's decision to pay out subsidies to the opposition PiS party He says there are "legal doubts" over the issue. But PiS says he is obliged to pay and will be held criminally responsible https://t.co/ZwIZRqn5tp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 9, 2025 Those doubts stem from a broader dispute over the controversial and contested judicial reforms implemented by PiS when it ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023. The chamber of the Supreme Court that ruled in PiS’s favour was created as part of those reforms. It has previously been found to not be a legitimate body by both the European Court of Justice and European Court of Human Rights because it contains improperly appointed judges. After the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling, the PKW initially said it would not recognise the decision until the chamber’s legal status was clarified. Two weeks later, however, it reversed that decision and approved PiS’s financial report. Domański still declined to restore the subsidy, arguing that the PKW’s resolution was internally contradictory. While it approved the payments, it also stated that the chamber’s ruling should come from a body recognised as a court and that it was not determining whether the chamber met that standard. PiS challenged Domański’s decision. However, its case was initially rejected by a lower court in June last year, and that decision has now been upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), which is the final court of appeal for administrative issues. The NSA found the minister had acted lawfully in withholding the funding. It also said the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling had no legal effect because it had been issued by a body that was not a properly constituted court, reports news website OKO.press. The ruling was welcomed by Domański, who called it a “crushing blow to PiS” and said that “yet another PiS lie has been exposed”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk, meanwhile, wrote on social media: “Just as we said, there is and will be no money for grifters.” Tak jak mówiliśmy, dla przekręciarzy pieniędzy nie ma i nie będzie. https://t.co/4Kqexj6NoC — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) August 5, 2026 The PKW’s decision to cut PiS’s funds was made after it found that government resources – including from the justice ministry, Government Legislation Centre (RCL) and Research and Academic Computer Network (NASK) – had been used to support the party’s election campaign. However, PiS has always argued that the decision was a political one, implemented at the behest of the new Tusk government in order to undermine the main opposition party. Radosław Fogiel, a senior PiS lawmaker and former party spokesman, said that the new NSA ruling “does not change the essence of the matter: it unlawfully deprives the main opposition party of the subsidy to which it is entitled. World.title: Prague Plans 1.9 Billion Crown Reconstruction of Kasárna Karlín
World.content:
Prague plans to invest around CZK 1.93 billion, including VAT, to transform Kasárna Karlín into a mixed-use complex with shops, offices, student housing and space for cultural and artistic activities.

The city acquired the former military complex in 2023 and has since been working on plans for its long-term redevelopment.

Prague City Council has now approved the next step, allowing the city-owned Trade Centre Prague (TCP), which manages the site, to launch a tender for the preparation of the reconstruction project.



Construction is scheduled to follow between 2027 and 2032, with the investment financed from Prague’s municipal budget.

The first stage will focus on the complex’s main building. A separate building in the courtyard, currently used by the Karlín Barracks Cultural Center, will be addressed in later phases.

Deputy Mayor for Territorial and Strategic Development Petr Hlaváček said the reconstruction should open the site to the surrounding neighborhood while preserving its historic character and protected architectural elements.

One of the main changes will be to improve access to the courtyard, which currently has just one entrance and is largely hidden from the surrounding streets.

Adam Zábranský, Prague’s councilor for property, transparency and legislation, said new passages from the street would lead into the complex, with shops and services occupying the ground floor. The arcade running alongside these commercial spaces would form part of the new circulation system through the site.

The upper levels could eventually accommodate student housing, studios and offices. Zábranský also mentioned the possibility of using some of the space for businesses such as a technology park.

The exact future use of many of the rooms has not yet been decided. According to Zábranský, the project should therefore prioritize flexible layouts that can be adapted for different purposes over time.

The initial investment will focus in particular on replacing and upgrading essential infrastructure, including water, electricity and waste systems, as well as preparing the commercial areas on the ground floor. Work on the upper floors is expected to come later.

World.title: Czechia Sees Lyme Disease Surge With 90 New Cases a Day
World.content:
Lyme disease cases are rising sharply across the Czech Republic, with more than 8,000 infections recorded since the beginning of the year.

Health officials warn that the summer peak may not have arrived yet.

A total of 8,108 cases were reported through the end of July, according to data from the Czech State Institute of Health (SZÚ). July alone accounted for 2,792 infections, meaning that roughly one in three cases recorded so far this year occurred during the month.



Doctors registered an average of about 90 new cases each day in July.

The figures are significantly higher than those seen in previous years. Between January and July, the Czech Republic typically recorded between 1,500 and 2,000 Lyme disease cases.

Part of the increase may be linked to a change in the way infectious diseases are reported.

The number of tick-borne infections depends on several factors, including tick populations and seasonal weather conditions. Climate change is also playing an increasingly important role.

The highest numbers of Lyme disease infections have so far been reported in the Central Bohemian and South Moravian regions.

The risk is not limited to forests and countryside. Prague’s parks and wooded areas can also provide suitable conditions for ticks.

“Prague’s parks and forest parks create a specific microclimate where ticks thrive, so the risk of infection is real for residents even during an ordinary walk,” said Martina Marešová, head of the anti-epidemic department at the Prague Hygiene Station.

Early treatment can prevent complications

One of the most recognizable signs of Lyme disease is an expanding red rash that develops around the site of a tick bite and may have a paler area in the center.

Anyone who develops such a rash should seek medical attention rather than waiting for it to disappear.

The most common form initially affects the skin. If left untreated, the infection can progress and cause further skin problems. More serious complications can involve the nervous system, heart or eyes.

World.title: Shella Radio Visualizes Struggling Culture Scene At National Gallery
World.content:
A radio tower installation at Prague’s National Gallery is showcasing local efforts to preserve alternative culture as the Czech government seeks to cut funding to the arts and other public sectors.

Created by members of Prague-based Shella Radio, the tower is adorned with fabrics and relics of previous parties hosted in Ankali & Planeta Za, a nightclub that has faced closure due to financial problems.

“We believe in the idea of this radio as an amplification of voices that are often neglected in other spaces,” Shania Rodriguez, a Prague-based DJ and Shella radio host, said in an interview. “Here, they can be vocal about the issues and problems within our system and also share ideas of change.”



Many artists and curators say the environment for cultural organizations has grown more challenging due to financial cuts by the new right wing government led by Andrej Babiš.

The planned budget for this year shrank by 3.9 billion crowns – an almost 20 percent decrease from the previous year, according to the Czech Ministry of Culture. The cuts sparked widespread backlash across the country in April, and many took to the streets.

Shella, an Egyptian Arabic slang word meaning “a group of friends who do things together,” hosts political talk shows, electronic music club nights, and summer markets featuring local artists.

“The idea behind our installation was to be able to transmit parts of our identity that have been fundamental in Shella Radio’s trajectory,” Rodriguez said. “This DIY approach gives us the freedom to customize and handcraft our installation and studio space using materials from our temporary home: Ankali.”

The installation is part of the Necessary Wishes exhibition at the National Gallery which brings together more than 50 collectives and artists.

The event is free of charge and ends on September 13.

By: Lili Anna Lempek, Adam Pohořilský, Milena Gevorgyan, Isabella Fattore

World.title: Where to See the Partial Solar Eclipse in Prague and Across Czechia
World.content:
Skywatchers in the Czech Republic will have two reasons to look up on the night of August 12.

A partial solar eclipse will be visible in the evening, followed by favorable conditions for watching the annual Perseid meteor shower.

The eclipse will be visible across Czechia shortly before sunset, with the Sun low over the western and northwestern horizon. In Prague, the partial eclipse is expected to begin at about 7:19 p.m., reach its maximum at 8:12 p.m. and end around 8:27 p.m.



At the height of the eclipse, the Moon will cover about 86 percent of the Sun’s disk in Prague, making the event particularly noticeable if skies are clear.

The eclipse will look different depending on where observers are located. The farther east they are, the later the eclipse will begin and the less of it will be visible. In eastern Czechia and much of Slovakia, the maximum phase will take place after sunset, when the Sun is already below the horizon.

The event will be a partial eclipse in Central Europe, while a total solar eclipse will be visible in parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain. Astronomers and eclipse enthusiasts are expected to travel to those areas to experience totality.

A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, blocking part or all of the Sun from view. In Czechia, the eclipse will be especially low on the horizon, so observers will need an unobstructed view toward the west and northwest.

Several Czech observatories are preparing public observing events. A list of locations and other information about the eclipse is available through the Czech astronomical website astro.cz.

Perseid meteor shower will follow

The same night will also offer good conditions for watching the Perseids, one of the most prominent annual meteor showers.

The shower will reach its peak during the early hours of August 13, when the Moon will be only a few hours past its new-moon phase. With virtually no moonlight in the sky, faint meteors should be easier to spot.

The Perseids are active from July 17 through August 24, but the best opportunity this year will come during the night of August 12-13.

Under dark skies and favorable weather, observers away from cities could see between 50 and 80 meteors per hour.

Light pollution will be the main obstacle for anyone hoping to see large numbers of meteors. The best locations are well away from major cities, ideally several dozen kilometers from strong sources of artificial light.

World.title: Non-Alcoholic Beer Sales Rise by More Than 25% in Czechia
World.content:
Beer remains a staple of the Czech shopping basket, but new sales data from online supermarket Rohlík shows that drinking habits are gradually changing.

Traditional lagers still dominate, while non-alcoholic beer is recording the fastest growth among the main beer categories.

The category has grown by more than a quarter over the past year, with Birell among the brands driving the increase. Birell sales alone are up by almost 20%.



Together with flavoured beers and radlers, non-alcoholic beer now accounts for close to one-third of all beer sales on Rohlík.

Beer from small and regional breweries is also gaining ground, with sales increasing by more than 11%.

The biggest decline is being recorded among craft beers grouped by style, including IPA and APA. This is currently the only major beer segment experiencing a year-on-year drop.

Czech brands continue to dominate the market. More than nine out of every 10 beers sold through Rohlík are from domestic brands.

Imported beers, however, are growing at a faster rate. Their sales have increased by 18% year-on-year.

Beer sales peak at the weekend

Friday is the busiest day for beer sales, with roughly twice as much beer sold as on Monday. Friday and Saturday together account for almost two-fifths of the category’s weekly sales.

Orders containing beer also tend to include significantly more items than orders without beer, suggesting that customers often buy it as part of a larger meal or weekend shop rather than as a standalone purchase.

Seasonal patterns have also shifted. Beer sales during this year’s summer months have reached levels comparable with the December Christmas peak.

World.title: Explore Holašovice: A UNESCO-Listed Gem with Its Own Stonehenge
World.content:
For over 20 years, the South Bohemian village of Holašovice has held a place on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

Located approximately 16 kilometers west of České Budějovice, this village is famed for its picturesque houses, built in the distinctive Peasant Baroque style.



The first recorded mention of Holašovice dates back to the late 13th century. The village has a rich and storied history, marked by events such as the Hussite wars and a devastating plague in the 16th century that significantly reduced the local population.

The iconic houses that now define Holašovice were constructed in the latter half of the 19th century, reflecting the Baroque, Rococo, and Classical influences prevalent in South Bohemian architecture of that era.

The village’s ethnic composition underwent significant changes during and after World War II. Following the establishment of the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, the Czech residents were forced to leave Holašovice, and the village was annexed to the Third Reich.

After the war, the German population was expelled, once again altering the village’s demographics.

Lada’s Pond and the Czech Stonehenge

Despite its turbulent past, Holašovice has retained a unique atmosphere that continues to attract visitors.

In addition to its charming houses, tourists can explore the local chapel and the picturesque Lada’s Pond, which, along with a statue of a water sprite, seems to be straight out of a painting by Josef Lada.

Just outside the village lies a unique stone circle, often referred to as the “Czech Stonehenge.” This site was designed to channel negative energy away from the human body, offering visitors a chance to experience its reputed healing properties.

World.title: Prague 7 Plans Floating Swimming Pool on the Vltava in Holešovice
World.content:
A floating swimming pool could be built along the Vltava River in Prague’s Holešovice district, near U Vody Park.

Prague 7 City Hall is considering using a section of the waterfront near the Port 7 development for the project.

The municipality hopes the pool could be ready within three years, although the cost has not yet been determined.

The project is still in its early stages. The district is currently looking into whether it could obtain older or unused pontoons and adapt them to create the swimming facility.



One of the main questions is where the pool water would come from. Prague 7 is considering both the Vltava and the municipal water supply.

The aim would be to use this data to determine when swimming in the river is considered safe. Čižinský has suggested introducing a simple traffic-light system similar to those used in cities such as Copenhagen and Amsterdam, allowing swimmers to see whether conditions are suitable.

According to Čižinský, the Vltava generally has good enough water quality for swimming, although conditions can deteriorate after heavy rainfall.

Recent measurements support this concern. Prague hygiene officials have been monitoring the water at Branická beach since the beginning of this year. The water has generally received a rating of two on the five-level scale used by hygienists.

The Holešovice proposal is not the first plan to introduce a floating swimming facility on the Vltava.

A similar idea was included in an earlier proposal to transform Prague’s riverfront. The project near Vyšehrad envisaged a large floating structure measuring 69 by 7.5 meters, with a swimming pool and a smaller paddling pool. A second connected vessel would have provided facilities for visitors.

The proposal was later put aside. In 2025, Prague property councilor Adam Zábranský of the Pirates said the investment was not among the city’s priorities.

World.title: Construction Disrupts Prague Tourists and Businesses During Peak Summer Season
World.content:
Construction projects across Prague’s historic center are proving a pain for tourists and locals alike who say the clumps of dirt, building supplies and equipment block popular sites and make it difficult to move around one of Europe’s most visited cities.



Heading down Národní to the Charles Bridge or going for a beer near the Vltava river now looks more like a vast construction site where tourists need to look out for more than the cobble-stone streets and baroque spires.

“It’s their first time here too, [they’ve] never seen it and now it’s torn up,” said Sherryl, a tourist visiting from the United States with her friends.

A major source of the disruption are upgrades to the public transport system. The central tram route delivering travelers to the heart of the city near the Národní Divadlo stop has been shuttered for weeks.

The disruption has taken a heavy toll on surrounding businesses like Aggeo, an Italian grocery store along the corridor. Its manager, Irena Kumpová, noted a sharp drop in foot traffic from travelers and regular local customers, who stroll by the National Theater on their way to gaze at the artist David Černý’s famous Kafka head.

“I’d rather stay closed… it’s a catastrophe,” remarked Kumpová.

With tourism growing every year in Prague, the widespread construction is making its mark this summer. So far this year, 1.7 million people have visited Prague, marking the strongest start in 15 years, according to Prague City Tourism and the Czech Statistical Office.

Tram services are suspended through the city center, clogging the streets and forcing many to find another way to work or home. For businesses that rely on heavy foot traffic during the busiest months of the year, that means less earnings.

“I have a table outside, but mainly just to signal to people that we’re open, but no one sits there right now,” said Kumpová.

The reconstruction is part of Prague’s broader effort to modernize its transport network, including long-term investments such as the future tram connection to Wenceslas Square and the expansion of Metro Line D as the city seeks to expand public transport.

Not everybody minds the disruption. The loud machines, dusty air, and obstructed sidewalks offer a certain charm for some who view the construction as part of the sightseeing experience.

“Despite the construction, it’s still beautiful,” said Raluca Costachescu, a traveler from Romania.

Written by: Mae Bryant, Bilyana Spasova, Milica Petrušová, Zuzana Kormančíková, Zhanna Bekiryan

World.title: Budapest public safety operation ‘a success’, says ministry, civil guard patrols come to help public safety
World.content:
The Interior Ministry has deemed the 30-day public safety operation in Budapest a success, the ministry said on Monday. The operation was launched in mid-July after reports from local government leaders and residents, with police involvement.

Budapest public safety operation ‘a success’

The operation’s results suggest that Budapest’s public safety issues have complex roots, meaning law enforcement measures alone cannot resolve them, according to the ministry’s statement. The underlying social and health-care challenges require the involvement of affected areas and experts, making information-sharing critical so that all stakeholders can take effective action in their fields, it added.

The ministry noted that the 30-day intervention significantly improved the situation and provided valuable experience for developing long-term, sustainable solutions. Key elements of these solutions include continued enhanced police presence at 19 locations across the capital and mobile police patrols at nearly 100 sites, the statement said.

During the operation, 154 people were detained, 118 were taken into custody, 80 misdemeanour reports and 72 criminal complaints were filed, and 154 on-the-spot fines were issued. So far, 1,600 police officers have worked 11,000 service hours across 97 locations as part of the programme.

A meeting on Monday was attended by Gabor Posfai, the interior minister, Gergely Karacsony, Budapest’s mayor, Norbert Baricska, Budapest’s police chief, and Kriszta Bodis, the government commissioner for national social policy.

The operation was launched after several local leaders, including district mayors, reported a significant deterioration in public safety in parts of the capital, particularly linked to drug use.

Civil guard from outside capital helping to boost Budapest public safety

Civil guard patrols from outside the capital are serving in Budapest from the first week of August until the third week of September on weekends as part of a programme launched last week by the National Civil Guard Association, the association said on Monday.

If you missed: Chilling details emerge about how Japanese mother Megumi was brutally murdered by foreigner ex-husband

The initiative, dubbed One Day for Budapest’s Public Safety, aims to strengthen the capital’s public safety and improve the sense of security for residents and visitors through the visible, coordinated and preventive presence of civil guard patrols, the statement said.

In the first phase, between Aug 7 and 20, guest civil guards are patrolling with their local counterparts at sites designated by the police, primarily in the outer districts. From Aug 21 to Sept 20, they will participate in joint actions alongside police officers. On the first weekend, a total of 23 civil guards from Bács-Kiskun, Fejér, Heves, Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok, Nógrád , and Pest counties performed duties in the capital.

World.title: Popular Hungarian singer delivers pointed political message to PM Magyar from Sziget Festival’s main stage
World.content:
Wellhello’s Sunday set at the Sziget Festival was not all about the music. At the close of the concert, Fluor Tomi, a popular Hungarian singer, used the platform to offer a few political reflections, addressing the crowd — and younger festivalgoers in particular.

Strong message to the premier from the main stage of the Sziget Festival

The day’s programme had been devoted to János Bródy, with nearly 70 performers revisiting the work of the legendary songwriter. Wellhello contributed two of Bródy’s numbers — Micimackó and Ezek ugyanazok — reworked in their own distinctive style.

By the end of the show, however, Tomi Fluor had moved beyond music. The rapper urged the audience to remain sceptical of every government and to do what they could to prevent, in his view, a repetition of the past 16 years, Blikk wrote.

His remarks were met with loud applause. Fluor has criticised the political establishment on several previous occasions, so his latest intervention did not come entirely out of the blue. What made the message particularly striking was that it was the first explicitly political statement of the concert.

Ezek ugyanazok – by Bródy (scroll down for English lyrics):

What is this song about?

János Bródy’s song depicts a “dialogue” between a child and his father, through which it becomes evident that those who overthrew the previous regime have, in time, become indistinguishable from the very adversaries they once opposed. This may be interpreted as a pointed political message — or, more precisely, a warning — from Fluor to Péter Magyar and the Tisza Party, coupled perhaps with a hope that they will avoid mirroring the figures they sought to replace.

Check out the lyrics below:

Just as forty years ago there were hard times too,

But they never cared about Kondratyev cycles, it’s true.

For the strong always feel they cannot go wrong,

Father, don’t tell me these are the same ones.

When entropy rises and stirs up everything,

The services kick in so the noise won’t ring.

And the arse‑lickers once again get their place,

Father, don’t tell me these are the same ones.

Here you can be beautiful, but not wise, faith’s a must,

And everyone who doubts becomes an enemy, a distrust.

And hypocritical coat‑turners preach about right,

Father, don’t tell me these are the same ones.

Slowly, individual experience falls out of memory’s store,

Rewritten by new data sent out from the centre’s core.

And those who adapt to every system come along,

Father, don’t tell me these are the same ones.

As always, around the idol the dance starts anew,

An invisible chain again weaves our lives through.

And the eager fools and the timid compromisers appear,

Father, don’t tell me these are the same ones.

And when at last the house collapses on them, credit gone,

They blame someone else for what they themselves have done.

And law and justice serve obediently, no log,

Father, don’t tell me these are the same ones.

So, my dear son, my sweet daughter, engrave this well:

In this fair land more than alcohol causes hell.

They’ll come and proclaim what great Hungarians they are,

But know this: these ones are always the same, by far.

Father, you said it: these are the same ones.

Oh, somewhere it’s like this: as it was, so it will be,

Father, you said it to me.

There are places where it’s like this: as it was, so it will be,

Father, you said it to me.

World.title: Young women collapse one after another at Budapest concert: police investigate as victims recount same story
World.content:
Police have launched an investigation into suspected drug possession following a series of medical incidents during DJ Balázs Sebestyén’s show (DJ OTI), Telex reported on Monday, citing the Budapest Police Headquarters. Several women fell ill during Saturday’s concert, amid media reports that GHB – known in Hungary as “gina” – may have been slipped into their drinks. When combined with alcohol, the drug can cause paralysis of the central nervous system.

Young women collapsed one after another at Budapest concert

In response to questions from the newspaper, Budapest police said investigators had already interviewed several witnesses and were seeking to establish the full circumstances of what happened. One young man posted on Sunday that his sister may have been drugged without her knowledge during the party. Shortly afterwards, a 39-year-old woman described in a video how she had collapsed almost immediately after drinking from her glass, MTI wrote.

The organisers of the Sziget Festival also responded to the reports on Sunday evening. They said that the DJ OTI production was not part of the programme of the Sziget Festival. They added that they were “deeply outraged” by the accounts circulating on social media and urged anyone affected by a similar incident to contact the police. The organisers added that they would assist the investigation.

Sziget Festival opens its gates today. Photo: Facebook/Sziget Festival Official

They also said their catering outlets had worked for years with the same tried-and-tested, reliable subcontractors, who served festival-goers safely and to a high standard.

Treated as drug users in the detox unit

In his post, the participant of DJ OTI’s concert said that while he was waiting at the on-site detox unit, at least 18 young people were taken there in connection with similar incidents. He condemned the way both his sister and he were treated, saying they had been made to feel as though they were responsible for what had happened.

Hungary’s National Ambulance Service responded to criticism on social media by saying it took seriously concerns about both patient care and communication, and would therefore review the circumstances surrounding its operation.

Illustration. Photo: Daily News Hungary

The service said that, alongside professional medical care, it was essential for its staff to treat every patient and relative appropriately and with empathy. “We believe it is important to learn from such feedback, identify the causes of any potential mistakes or shortcomings, and improve our procedures wherever necessary,” it said.

Ambulance arrived after two hours

We also reported on the case yesterday. Enikő, the 39-year-old woman mentioned above, said she had asked someone to bring her a drink from the VIP area because the queue was so long.

She then collapsed, something she said could not have been caused by alcohol. A young doctor and his wife tried to keep her conscious. Had her husband and the couple not been there, “anything could have happened” to her, she said. According to Enikő, the ambulance did not arrive for another two hours.

There were a lot of people at Balázs Sebestény’s Budapest concert the day before yesterday. The venue was the same as Sziget Festival’s. Photo: Facebook/DJ OTI

If you missed: Georgian tourist attempted to rape Hungarian teenager – but Chinese neighbours stepped in just in time

Several people on social media suspected that GHB may have been added to the women’s drinks, although this has not yet been confirmed. GHB is a synthetic drug, meaning it can only be produced in a laboratory. It is a colourless, odourless liquid and is known as a “rape drug” because of its association with sexual assault. It is often added to the drinks of young women, but its use carries serious risks: it can cause respiratory failure and, in the worst cases, death, Blikk reported.

Source: Pixnio.com

The drug can be detected in the blood for only four to five hours and in urine for between eight and 12 hours. Specialised, expensive toxicology tests can, however, detect it in hair months later.

If there is even a suspicion that someone has been given GHB, an ambulance should be called immediately and the person taken to a safe place and placed in the recovery position.

World.title: Chilling details emerge about how Japanese mother Megumi was brutally murdered by foreigner ex-husband
World.content:
Megumi, a Japanese mother of two, was brutally killed by her former Irish husband – but police initially believed his account of what had happened. The Budapest Chief Prosecutor’s Office has charged a 45-year-old Irishman with premeditated murder and is seeking a lengthy prison sentence after he allegedly disguised the killing of his former wife as a domestic fire, prosecutors told Hungary’s MTI news agency on Monday. The tragedy provoked widespread outrage over the police’s victim-blaming statements and serious failures, which led to disciplinary consequences for several officers.

Prosecutors say murder was carefully planned

Prosecutors said they would seek a 17-year prison sentence if the defendant made a full confession. They are also seeking a custodial sentence followed by his expulsion from Hungary, and asking the court to rule that he should not be eligible for parole, MTI wrote.

According to the indictment, the Irishman, who lived in the Netherlands, decided to kill his Japanese former wife the next time he travelled to Hungary to see their children. He allegedly planned to make her death appear to have been caused by a household fire. The crime was committed on 29 January in 2025.

The case arose after the victim applied to the guardianship authority in March 2024 for permission for the children to settle in Japan, as well as seeking arrangements concerning their choice of school and parental custody. Prosecutors say the man decided to kill his former wife in order to avoid a protracted administrative process – and any subsequent court proceedings – and to prevent a decision that might have gone against him.

Japanese mother Megumi had no chance of survival – yet police believed the Irishman’s story

The defendant travelled to Hungary on 27 January 2025, and stayed at the former family flat in Budapest’s fifth district. On 29 January, after their son had left for school, he took their daughter to a swimming pool, leaving his former wife alone at home.

He took a change of clothes with him, changed, and began making his way back to the flat. On the way, he also put on a hood and a helmet. When he returned to the flat, he allegedly attacked and killed his former wife. He then placed her body on the sofa and arranged a wine bottle, tea lights, cigarettes and cigarette ends nearby.

The suspect, David A., returning to the building his ex-wife lived in – moments before the brutal murder took place. PrtScr: YouTube/PoliceHungary

In an attempt to destroy evidence of the crime, he set fire to the furniture and left the flat. While walking around the area, he discarded the clothes he had changed into and put his original outfit back on. He then went to a wellness centre before returning to the flat in the early afternoon. When he opened the door, the influx of fresh oxygen caused the fire he had lit earlier to flare up more fiercely. Ten minutes later, he reported the blaze.

Police arrested the man on 3 February 2025. He has been held in pre-trial detention since 6 February. At the request of the Chief Prosecutor’s Office, the court extended the detention after charges were brought.

Murder sparked widespread outrage

Megumi’s killing caused widespread outrage at the beginning of 2025, with several civil liberties and women’s rights organisations examining the police’s role in the case.

If you missed – Ex-husband charged with Japanese woman’s murder in Budapest: Arson, death list, and a chilling history of threats

In 2022, Megumi had reportedly complained about her former husband, saying that he had kept her in fear and had even threatened to kill her, warning that she would “die in agony”.

A small area of the city centre of Budapest. Photo: Karácsony Gergely/Facebook

Police failed to act on the complaint. They also carried out a cursory investigation following her death and for days accepted the Irishman’s version that the fire had been caused by smoking in bed.

Megumi’s friends said on social media that she did not smoke. In response, they received patronising and mocking replies from the member of staff running the police’s official social media account.

The case led to an internal investigation. Several officers were removed from their posts, the employee responsible for social media was dismissed, and even the chief of police in Budapest’s fifth district was replaced.

A march was organised for the murdered Japanese woman in Budapest

World.title: Have Orbán’s former allies abandoned him? He may be seeking international posts that offer protection
World.content:
By this time next year, former prime minister Viktor Orbán could hold a senior international position after Tisza’s two-thirds election victory closed off his prospects in Hungarian politics – at least for now. One post would allow him to pursue his childhood passion; another could provide diplomatic immunity in the event of criminal proceedings in Hungary.

Is Viktor Orbán’s political career over?

Former prime minister Viktor Orbán turned 63 this year. If we take the comparison literally, he has two years left before reaching Hungary’s official retirement age. He spent virtually his entire active life as a member of parliament, from 1990 to 2026, including 20 years as prime minister – from 1998 to 2002 and again from 2010 to 2026. During four parliamentary terms, he governed with what was effectively a two-thirds majority.

But Tisza secured a two-thirds majority in the 2026 election. Following the shock defeat, Orbán also resigned his parliamentary mandate – despite the fact that it would have taken him neatly to retirement age – because he did not want to face his challengers in the National Assembly. Péter Magyar’s government has also passed a constitutional amendment preventing him from serving as prime minister again.

The age of Péter Magyar has dawned after Orbán’s crushing April defeat. Photo: Facebook/Forsthoffer Ágnes oldala

The only exception would be a fresh two-thirds victory for Fidesz. At present, however, that appears highly unlikely: support for the former governing parties has fallen below 20 per cent among most reputable polling organisations.

He committed himself for a year

Orbán is currently leader of Fidesz, the largest opposition party, but he has given no indication that he intends to withdraw from public life. Although there is resistance to him within the party and rumours of a possible breakaway civic party, he was nevertheless re-elected as leader with 97 per cent of the vote at July’s leadership congress.

He agreed to serve for one year, saying that he wanted to put the party back in order, rejuvenate it and transform it. That period would also be long enough for him to assemble an international portfolio of his own.

Orbán could launch an international career – and pursue his passion

During the year available to him, Orbán could use his extensive international contacts – and powerful supporters – to begin a new international career, if the information obtained by investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi is accurate.

Former prime minister Viktor Orbán with Fidesz MP Zsolt Németh during the 35th Bálványos Summer University and Students’ Camp. Photo: MTI/Veres Nándor

One possible destination is Fifa. According to Panyi, Orbán held talks with the leadership of football’s world governing body in the United States during the 2026 World Cup about a possible position. The exact role is unknown, but the post of Fifa vice-president may have been discussed.

Orbán was subjected to a barrage of attacks in Hungarian domestic politics because he was not in the country when, in his view, the new government dismantled the foundations of the rule of law – namely by removing the president of the republic elected by Fidesz.

To secure the position, however, he would need allies. One of the European vice-presidencies at Fifa is currently held by Sándor Csányi, president of the Hungarian Football Association and OTP Bank. His mandate expires during the 2027 election cycle.

There are plenty of obstacles

Orbán would nevertheless face several hurdles. If he wanted to join the Fifa Council as Hungary’s candidate, he would first have to secure the presidency or a vice-presidency of the Hungarian Football Association. He would then need to win the backing of UEFA’s member associations.

It was no coincidence that Orbán and Csányi appeared at the same American football event during the World Cup. Orbán watched the semi-final between Spain and France in Dallas with members of his family, while Sándor Csányi was seated close to Fifa president Gianni Infantino.

Will Fidesz split soon? A poll suggests the breakaway faction would have a strong chance

The UN could offer an easier route

The other possible route is the United Nations – specifically, according to Panyi, a position as a deputy secretary-general. An analysis by Portfolio.hu noted that Orbán would “merely” need to cultivate a good relationship with the future secretary-general and secure the support of figures such as President Trump and Argentina’s President Javier Milei.

Trump and the former prime minister last November in Washington. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

The latter could prove important because one of the leading contenders to become the UN’s next secretary-general is Rafael Grossi, the Argentine head of the International Atomic Energy Agency.

The greatest attraction of the deputy secretary-general scenario, according to Mr Panyi, would be diplomatic immunity. We have reported that Orbán could find himself in serious trouble if János Hajdu, former head of Hungary’s Counter-Terrorism Centre and Fidesz’s current security chief, refuses to accept responsibility for ordering the raid on the Ukrainian “gold convoy” and the unlawful assault on the money couriers, instead pointing the finger higher up in his testimony.

Questions have also been raised over the castle built on the Hatvanpuszta estate, as well as the enrichment of Orbán’s father, the elder Győző Orbán.

Viktor Orbán filmed in Serbia with MOL executive and controversial Hatvanpuszta estate architect

The claims were firmly denied by Bertalan Havasi, Fidesz’s director of communications, who dismissed the reports as “fake news”. A separate report has likewise described the proposed UN appointment as a possible route to diplomatic immunity for Orbán.

Viktor Orbán shares his plans after politics: family, football, teaching

World.title: Alert: A WWII bomb may have been stolen from the Danube in Budapest
World.content:
Budapest police have asked for help from the public in locating an object, thought to be a Second World War explosive device, that resurfaced in the Danube but disappeared before officers arrived.

Bomb disappears from drying out Danube in Budapest

A man reported finding a rusted object resembling a shell in the Danube in Budapest’s 22nd district on Monday, during historically low water levels which had revealed several objects in the riverbed. However, police only found the empty site upon arrival, the statement of the city’s police headquarters said.

Based on photographs taken by the finder, officials cannot rule out that the device is a Second World War artillery grenade, the statement said.

Authorities warned the public against moving, disassembling or transporting the object. Even decades-old devices embedded in soil or water can remain dangerous and should only be handled by bomb disposal experts, the statement said.

The police have launched an investigation on suspicion of misuse of explosives, the statement added.

World.title: Why Hungary’s cheapest shop may have closed – and shoppers are already furious
World.content:
Hungary’s cheapest shop has refused to explain why it has been closed for several days, citing “technical reasons” – an explanation that few people believe. Most suspiciously, all of the company’s European shops have reportedly shut, with “technical issues” cited in each case. Some commentators already believe the Budapest outlet will not be closed for merely a few days – which might be understandable in the event of a technical problem – but for much longer. Its staff have reportedly already been dismissed.

Hungary’s cheapest shop – with compromises

Until 1 August, Basket Plusz, the Mere group’s only Hungarian shop, regularly posted videos advertising a range of cheap products. The Russian-backed group’s Budapest outlet, located in the city’s 18th district, opened at the beginning of December last year, just in time for Christmas, and marketed itself as Hungary’s cheapest shop – a claim that, judging by customers’ experiences, appeared to be justified.

That came with serious compromises. The store relied on B- and C-tier brands, contracts that favoured suppliers – who were paid only for goods that had actually been sold – and a stark, warehouse-like appearance. The premises, crammed with pallets and resembling a Metro-style warehouse more than a conventional supermarket, offered a poor shopping experience but undoubtedly helped to keep prices down.

Some customers, however, complained that the products they bought were not as good as comparable items sold by other retailers.

Another explanation for the closures

The sole Hungarian outlet closed last week, citing technical problems. Its Facebook page has not been updated since, and reports suggest that the small number of employees working in the quasi-warehouse-style shop have already been sacked.

The technical explanation appears particularly suspicious when viewed alongside similar reports from Slovakia and the Czech Republic.

The Russian MERE discount chain. Photo: mere.ws

Világgazdaság reported that Mere’s Slovak shops – where the chain also arrived last December – as well as its Baltic and Czech outlets, had also ceased trading. Technical reasons were cited in those cases, too. The real explanation, however, may be the EU’s sanctions package adopted at the end of July, which placed Sergei Schneider, one of the owners of the group behind the Mere, Svetofor and MyPrice chains, on a sanctions list.

The Czech Republic even froze the family’s shares after the sanctions came into force. As a result, they cannot sell their holdings or receive dividends.

Is the group withdrawing or merely going dormant?

In Lithuania, the authorities are investigating whether the newly opened Ola shops are linked to the Russian group and whether they represent an attempt to evade sanctions. Previously, 30 shops closed in the country and 250 people were sacked.

According to Világgazdaság, the central question is whether the closures signal the group’s withdrawal from Central Europe or are merely temporary measures.

The Russian MERE discount chain. Photo: mere.ws

Hungarian customers have expressed their anger over the closure in Mere-related Facebook groups, while hoping that the shop will reopen soon. Although some accept that the closure may be the result of sanctions, many believe that neither the EU nor the government led by Péter Magyar should drive out what they regard as a promising initiative.

If you missed: Is shopping abroad really cheaper? Why are Romanians and Bulgarians outspending Hungarians? New study provides answers

Why was the owner of a food company sanctioned?

The sanctions against Sergei Schneider came into force on July 23 and include an asset freeze, a ban on financing and the suspension of the company’s operations.

The stated reason is that the Russian businessman’s corporate empire plays a significant role in sustaining Russia’s domestic economy and therefore contributes indirectly to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
