World.title: The official David Crisafulli calls direct (just don’t say he bypasses Dale Last)
World.content:
Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: the Fraine Train, emerging external recruitment allergies, Core bargaining heats up, and more tea on 1WS coffee. David Crisafulli has been busy courting public servants since ascending to the premiership in a bid to shut down Labor’s supposed scare campaign warning of Newman-like mass sackings. But beyond his own department chief Damian Walker, there’s another bureaucrat the premier has a close working relationship with – Natural Resources and Mines director-general Graham Fraine. Queensland Natural Resources Minister Dale Last, Premier David Crisafulli, and Last’s department director-general Graham Fraine. File / Supplied Circus whisperers, who spoke anonymously to discuss internal matters, said Crisafulli is known to call Fraine directly when it comes to the resources and mines portfolio.



Some experienced government staffers said it was unusual for a premier to speak with a DG directly rather than going through the minister, who in this instance is Dale Last. However, multiple contacts said they weren’t surprised, given Fraine is widely viewed as an effective operator. Public servants and former government insiders have dubbed him as a Mr Fixit, though current colleagues have said “Ideas Man” is perhaps more apt. Circus likes the ring of “Fraine Train”, and our analysis of cabinet diaries outlines the significance of his role. Fraine appears in Crisafulli diary entries three times without Last. The full trio have clocked up 12 formal entries together. A spinner for the Premier denied Crisafulli bypasses Last. Their only attributable response to questions was: “Labor’s siloed way of working is why we ended up in so many crises; we are absolutely all working together to deliver better outcomes for Queenslanders.”



But the reliance on the experienced Fraine comes at a pivotal time for Crisafulli – and Last – who are aiming to kick-start the critical minerals mining and production industry, which will be a focus of trade talks when the Premier travels to the US later this month. Related Article Critical minerals The Nordic country’s pitch to Queensland for multibillion-dollar industry And what of Fraine’s meeting with Dave Davies from Gina Rinehart’s Hancock Prospecting and Last’s chief of staff Ally Foley back in December, discovered during our recent diary crunching efforts? The department regularly engages with stakeholders in its role helping the sector, a spokesperson said. Given this often involves commercially confidential matters, they declined to say more. An allergy to listing top roles? Mackie appears to make it two from two



Friday delivered news of maybe the worst-kept secret since State Development chief John Sosso’s departure – the appointment of Public Sector Commissioner David Mackie as his successor, again. Another recurring element, just one month after Sosso’s move was made public? This government’s apparent newfound allergy to independent external recruitment for directors-general. Under directives for the recruitment and selection of these roles, Premier David Crisafulli is responsible for deciding the process, including whether a competitive advertised approach is taken. Queensland Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie and Public Sector Commissioner David Mackie at the latter’s wedding in April, in which Bleijie acted as a celebrant in a “private capacity”. Facebook / Jarrod Bleijie This is despite the landmark 1989 Fitzgerald Inquiry report suggesting all director-general appointments be conducted through an external, transparent, merit-based recruitment process.



A number of initial post-election appointments were, as was that of Local Government Department boss Bronwyn Blagoev after the departure of predecessor Linda Dobe. Related Article Public service Misdirected or misleading? Health boss in hot water over estimates show But, with Michael Drane’s permanent elevation at Youth Justice in July, Mackie’s sideways shift seems to make it two from two recent department head hirings to not have involved a wider search. From August 17, Mackie will lead the major department driving infrastructure projects and economic development under Deputy Premier (and his wedding celebrant) Jarrod Bleijie. And despite suggestions from some of our columnist comrades, word reaching the Circus tent – along with annual report crunching – says there’ll be no skin off his $700,000-plus salary.



We’re certainly not suggesting Mackie (or Drane) are not suitable. But without hearing from a wider range of applicants, who knows if they’re the best. We sent questions to Crisafulli’s office and have heard only crickets about the process taken – but we’ve seen no evidence it was externally recruited. At estimates hearings last month, Mackie said direct appointments allowed consideration of “whether or not it would be wasteful to go to market”. During that same line of questioning, Crisafulli said they could save tens of thousands of dollars – “a lot of money”. All eyes now are on the recruitment of a permanent police commissioner, and the now acting heads of the Public Sector Commission, Queensland Corrective Services, and Customer Services. State and union Core Agreement talks approaching the pointy end



Among the remaining workplace deals still being wrangled by the Crisafulli government, the State Government Entities Certified Agreement is a big one. It’s politically sensitive, with 13 unions at the table, representing a large proportion of the public sector workforce. Hence, the “Core Agreement” label. Another factor likely to complicate Core Agreement talks for the workplace deal covering a vast array of public servants across the state: the looming State Wage Case. Matt Dennien Circus has been keenly awaiting any hints of things heating up, which emerged in the form of a brief July 31 update posted online. In its telling, after 15 central meetings and 40 entity-specific ones, the government floated an offer on June 30 “to achieve early resolution” and replace the deal set to expire that day.



“On 31 July 2026, Together Queensland, Industrial Union of Employees, advised it did not accept the fair and reasonable Offer Government made to unions,” the update read. “As a result, the Offer has now lapsed and negotiations will continue.” Also lapsing, according to the government, is the offer of backpay to July 1. Circus has sung out to Together for their side of things, but is aware of another factor likely to complicate things: the State Wage Case which sets minimum wage and award rates a number of collective agreements can’t drop below. With some of those already overtaking or nipping at the heels of workplace deals, the QCU and Together are again chasing a repeat of the federal Fair Work Commission’s 4.75 per cent June lift to awards it oversees, to apply from September 1. The state is trying to inject as much context into the case as it can, to ensure the “fair and reasonable” increase is a little closer to the up-to-3.5 per cent year-one lift in its wages policy.



In one affidavit filed for the state, Office of Industrial Relations executive director Shane Donovan said while a 4.75 per cent lift to awards would directly benefit the less than 2000 workers reliant on awards or the minimum wage, it would also indirectly boost pay for those in up to 29 of the state’s collective agreements – including six in arbitration. In another, deputy under-treasurer Matt Bonaventura put the cost of any such lift at about $93 million in the 2026-27 financial year. Bonaventura warned this could lead to further cost implications through next year’s boost to awards then applying to a higher base, and used boilerplate talk copied from last year about the pressure such wage increases place on government service delivery and fiscal objectives. There was also a nod to the precarious position of the state’s credit rating. Circus wonders if the curtain of secrecy drawn over an uncertain $6.8 billion in planned savings might play more of a role in that than a slight ripple in the $40 billion wages bill. New coffee machines landing, but 1WS tea supply answers still in the mail



Brewing news last week about the lack of tea stock in the Tower of Power, perhaps unsurprisingly, has seen many more Circus folk come forward to spill the proverbial hot beverage. By all accounts, it’s been a masterclass in muddled messaging from all involved – but we’ve used our powers for good to try to get to the bottom and read the leaves on what’s really going on here. Electronic payment options? In 2026? After fielding an image of one laminated sign warning of the removal of tea, milk and sweeteners from all 1 William Street kitchens as of August 1, we’ve now also seen one all-staff departmental email saying similar. Both informed readers they would need to supply their own from here on, and sheeted blamed for the decision on the building – not the department.



This had all been explained as related to a changing of the automatic coffee machine guards from the old coin-operated fleet whose funds fed the supplies, to new ones with electronic payments enabled. Technology! (One director-general even told staff last week not to panic and pointed them to the sole remaining relic on level 40. Luckily, we hear, a stampede did not ensue.) Well, Circus has now seen photographic evidence of the fancy new machines installed, along with signs seemingly from 1WS building management thanking people for their patience. We’ve also dropped them a line to see if they can’t shed more light on the situation – and had to push back when we were pointed to the Right to Information website. Best put the kettle on. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email us on m.dennien@nine.com.au or james.hall@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The art of the deal: Victoria to pay millions more than host cities overseas to bring NFL to Melbourne
World.content:
Exclusive SportNFLCity life The art of the deal: Victoria to pay millions more than host cities overseas to bring NFL to Melbourne Bridget McArthur August 10, 2026 — 8:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victorians could pay up to 11 times more than other international host cities to bring American football to Melbourne next month after beating NSW and Western Australia for the sporting privilege. The state government announced in February last year that it had secured Australia’s first-ever in-season NFL game, signing a “two-plus-one” multi-year contract – two confirmed games over four years, with the possibility of a third. Sports Minister Steve Dimopoulos has called the deal “one of the biggest returns on investments Victoria has ever seen”. However, figures obtained by this masthead suggest Victoria is expected to pay between $10 million and $15 million per NFL game, substantially higher than what was paid for matches to be held in Germany and Brazil. Berlin paid about $7.4 million per NFL game, with the first taking place late last year. Getty Images Speaking in parliament earlier this year, shadow industry minister Richard Welch put the cost at $15 million a game – a figure that aligns with what the NSW government said the NFL put to it, according to a source familiar with negotiations who spoke to The Australian Financial Review last year – which would see the state spend $45 million in a three-game scenario.



The government has not confirmed or denied this figure, but comments made by Dimopoulos in a recent podcast interview indicate it is in the ballpark. Referencing the commercial benefits of the deal, he told the Armchair Experts podcast last month: “If you were to buy that advertising on digital and media right across the world, [it would be] over $32 million. Now that’s well and truly a great head start to our investment”. Related Article Exclusive

NFL 2026 ‘Here to stay’: The numbers behind the NFL’s major Australian gamble If $32 million is a great head start to covering Victoria’s investment, the total amount spent is likely to be higher. However, if one assumes that figure as an absolute minimum, and divides it by three games – though only two are currently assured – Victoria must be paying at least $10.6 million per game. When this masthead contacted Dimopoulos to confirm these figures, a spokesperson said all financial details were commercial in confidence and could not be discussed. By comparison, the German city of Frankfurt paid just $1.3 million a game, while Berlin paid $7.4 million, and Sao Paolo in Brazil paid $7.5 million. The only overseas host to pay more than Victoria was Ireland, which paid $17.8 million for a single game in Dublin.



A spokesperson for Berlin’s department of sport estimated the NFL was contributing about $78.5 million of its own money to take the put on the games in the German capital. The department spokesperson and a spokesperson for the Frankfurt mayor’s office said no additional financing for the events had been provided by the German federal government to either city. Sao Paulo’s municipal government did not respond in time for deadline clarifying whether the federal government had contributed funds. In Ireland, a government spokesperson confirmed it had approved an allocation of up to $17.8 million to host a single game in Dublin last year, and said the investment had covered the licence fee, infrastructure works, security, transport services, city-activation events and a once-off contribution to venue-related costs. When this masthead put the public spending estimates to the NFL and asked why Victoria is set to pay significantly more per game than other international host cities, a spokesperson for the league did not dispute the figures, saying only it did not comment on financial matters. “The NFL has a growing presence in Australia and is committed to investing in the development of the game year-round,” the spokesperson said. “Through grassroots participation including our national flag football program, youth development, strategic partnerships, and now the historic first-ever regular-season NFL game being played at the MCG this September, Australia represents a key market in the league’s global expansion plans.”



There is no doubt there is significant appetite for the game to come to Melbourne, with 100,000 fans expected to turn out to watch the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers at the MCG. Related Article NFL 2026 On one of the AFL’s biggest weekends, 10,000 US fans will paint Melbourne red When the game was announced, more than 151,000 people registered interest, and the first tranche of tickets sold out in less than half an hour. All four foreign hosts said the economic benefits of hosting the games far eclipsed the amount they had spent on them, with net profits estimated to be between $90 million and $190 million per game. While that will likely be the case in Victoria, the higher government input could reduce the expected return on investment.



Germany and Brazil have more-proven NFL markets. However expanding the sport to new markets is a key tenet of the league’s long-term strategy, and Australia has long been in its purview. NSW had previously been considered the most likely candidate to host the NFL’s Australian debut due to its sizeable fan base and ties to current players, such as former Rabbitoh-turned-Philadelphia Eagle Jordan Mailata. It was also the only state to have hosted an exhibition game in 1999, and was later assessed to host another pre-season match-up, according to the NFL’s former executive vice president of international Mark Waller, though plans were ultimately dropped. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell (middle right) commended then premier Jacinta Allan (left) for convincing him to hold Australia’s first in-season NFL game in Melbourne. Simon Schluter The NFL visited sites in 2024 and met representatives across various states, with NSW, Victoria and WA on the ultimate shortlist. States were given about three months to put together a proposal that covered hosting rights, investments, value-in-kind contributions, venue hire, and stadium operations. In October of that year, representatives from each state flew to London for a meeting to discuss their respective bids. When Victoria was confirmed as the winning host city, NSW Premier Chris Minns described the NFL’s asking price as “a king’s ransom”.



“We said no, it was just too expensive,” Minns said. “I’ve got a lot of pull on the government dollar – I didn’t have enough for the NFL game. I can only speak to my government’s priorities and where we spend your money, your tax money. We have to spend it wisely.” Dimopoulos has on multiple occasions said then-premier Jacinta Allan was eager to secure the deal, while NFL commissioner Roger Goodell commended her for having “the vision and the strength and the leadership to convince us this was the right place to play” – suggesting Victoria was chasing the league, not the other way around. A mural in Sao Paulo, Brazil, which has hosted two in-season NFL games to date. Getty Images Speaking in Melbourne this year, Goodell said the money offered was not as important as Victoria’s strong record in major events. “This community knows how to do big events,” he said in April. “They’re pros, and we felt very comfortable that they were going to deliver not just what they said but everything that was necessary to make this event successful.”



Goodell also cited the size and “tremendous reputation” of the MCG as another key factor in choosing Melbourne. Mark Waller, who laid the groundwork for the NFL’s international expansion, said Melbourne’s wider infrastructure – including public transport, accommodation and the proximity of the stadium to the CBD – was also likely to have played a part. It is a massive, tightly run logistical exercise for all involved. A local security company, which did not want to be named due to the sensitivity of corporate dealings with the NFL, said the league was bringing over its own security detail – although the Victorian government said there would still be security jobs created here. On game day, fans will be required to bring their belongings in clear bags – per NFL policy in the US. Local company HG Turf will be under the pump to get the pitch set up and packed away between AFL games – a final is potentially on the cards for the MCG the following day. In a statement provided on Monday, a spokesperson for the sports minister’s office said the NFL partnership had been transformational for Victoria, and a rise in visits by Americans and hotel bookings had already been recorded.



“The September game will be beamed live to millions of US viewers during prime time, delivering significant economic returns through the $239 million American visitors spend annually in Victoria and attracting record interest from international fans and business leaders,” the spokesperson said. “Our multi-year NFL partnership is cementing Victoria’s status as Australia’s major events capital, with Delta Airlines now offering three new direct flights per week from Los Angeles, creating year-round tourism growth and business opportunities. The LA Rams will play the San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne in September. Getty Images “This multi-year partnership is creating hundreds of jobs across Victoria – from security and hospitality to transport co-ordination and event management. The vast majority of staff delivering the game and surrounding fan activities will be local workers contracted by the MCG and MOPT [Melbourne and Olympic Parks Trust], supporting Victorian jobs and businesses throughout the event.” The NFL’s media team has been restrictive in its communications. An interview previously organised between this masthead and the NFL’s Asia-Pacific head, Brett Gosper, was cancelled. A reason for the cancellation was not provided.



A lot is on the line for the American sports giant. If it can grow a loyal fan base in Australia, it will unlock significant potential earnings from media broadcast rights, sponsorships and merchandise deals. It is also seeking to grow flag football, handing out kits to every school in Victoria, as it looks to cement the non-contact sport on the global stage, including ensuring it remains in the 2032 Brisbane Olympics after its debut in the 2028 LA Games. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Labour MP among 115,000 NZers currently on dormant electoral roll
World.content:
Labour MP Willow-Jean Prime is sounding the alarm after discovering she was moved on to the dormant electoral roll earlier this year without her knowledge.

Chief Electoral Officer Karl Le Quesne on Monday revealed about 115,000 people were currently on the dormant roll. That is about 25 percent lower than the same time in the 2023 election cycle, but Le Quesne said it was still "not good enough."

People were typically shifted onto the dormant roll if the Electoral Commission had tried and failed to get in touch them.

Voters would still be able to cast a ballot, but would have to go through the special vote process and would not be sent an EasyVote card.

Prime told RNZ she only discovered her dormant enrolment status "by chance" when she checked online in June, only to be told: "You are not currently enrolled", which she said was "misleading."

She said she had earlier been emailed and texted by the commission asking her to update her details, but she did not because they were all correct.

"I did what they told me to do, and every time I went on there, my details were correct. I hadn't moved."

Prime said the whole situation felt "a bit messy".

"My concern is: if that happened to me as a member of Parliament, how many other Māori has this happened to?" Prime said.

"This is our election. People have to have confidence in our electoral system with the changes to the electoral law from this government."

About 5000 voters of Māori descent were moved onto the dormant electoral roll since the end of March this year.

"It's hugely disappointing that thousands of Māori voters have been moved to the dormant roll, potentially without knowing and through no fault of their own," Prime said.

She was worried for people who were told they're not enrolled, as they "might not bother to vote at all."

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Le Quesne described the dormant roll as a "safety net".

In a statement to RNZ, Electoral Commission deputy chief executive for operations Anusha Guler said it would be "unusual" for someone to be asked to update their details they had not moved house, as Prime had.

She encouraged anyone in that situation to contact the commission on 0800 36 76 56.

Guler said if a person on the dormant roll turned up to vote, staff would look them up on the electronic roll and direct them to cast a "special vote" instead.

She said the main reason people ended up on the dormant roll was because they had moved house and not updated their enrolment details.

The Electoral Commission would first try to contact anyone whose mail was returned as undeliverable.

If it had an email address or mobile phone number for the voter, it would send them a message telling them their address appeared to be out of date and asking them to update their details.

After four weeks, if the voter had not responded, they would be removed from the main roll and placed on the dormant roll.

Guler said a reminder text would be sent in late August to everyone on the dormant roll for whom the commission had a mobile number, asking them to update their details.

A voter could return to the main roll as soon as they confirmed their address through vote.nz or by completing an enrolment form.

World.title: Number of teens with no qualifications higher than reported
World.content:
The number of teens leaving school with no qualification is much higher than officially reported at nearly one-in-five of last year's 70,786 leavers.

The figure has been under-reported because since 2004 the Education Ministry has counted students half-way to a level two or three NCEA certificate as if they had a qualification, even if they didn't.

Including those students took the number of school-leavers with no qualification equivalent to at least NCEA level one to 13,165 last year - 19 percent of the total number of leavers and well above the previously reported figure of 10,496 or 15 percent.

Figures provided by the ministry also showed the number of school-leavers with 30 or more credits but no qualifications grew by 150 percent from 1058 in 2019 to 2669 last year, a period in which the total number of school-leavers increased 19 percent.

Adjusting 2019's result to include leavers with 30 or more credits but no qualification took that year's percentage of students with no qualification to 13 percent.

The practice of counting 30 or more credits at levels two and three as equivalent to a lower level certificate in the school-leaver statistics was no secret - it was included in the definitions used for each level of achievement - but it was a surprise to principals spoken to by RNZ.

Papakura High School principal Simon Craggs said he had no idea about the methodology and he did not agree half a level two or three certificate was equivalent to a level one certificate.

"For getting level one, particularly up until recently, you needed to have 80 credits so it's actually a lot hader to get level one than it is to get level two or three currently in terms of the number of credits accumulated," he said.

Papakura High School principal Simon Craggs. RNZ / Luka Forman

But Craggs said completed achievement or unit standards carried some value, even if students did not have a full NCEA certificate.

"A prospective employer can look at the things that a student is able to do and that's one of the strengths of the NCEA system," he said.

"Something that we've been advocating strongly for in the new qualification is that there is a list of what students can do and it's more strengths-based rather than they just passed or failed."

Steve McCracken from the Post Primary Teachers' Association (PPTA)'s secondary principals council said counting qualifications in the way the ministry did for its statistics way would make a big difference to schools' results - but they were not allowed to do that and it would not be true.

"I don't think it would be accurate would it, it would be a little bit of falsification of information really," he said.

"It's not right and it's not accurate so it needs to be rectified."

McCracken said schools relied on the ministry's figures to benchmark their own performance so it was important they compared like with like.

He said changing the interpretation of the results made a big difference to the school leaver figures.

Chair of the PPTA's Secondary Principals' Council, Steve McCracken. Supplied / Whangaparāoa College

"That's a significant increase isn't it in terms of people leaving without any formal qualifications," he said.

The ministry's data and insights general manager Grant Pollard said the practice was historical.

"The decision on that methodology was made at the time to reflect the transition in school quals. So 2002, NCEA level one was phased in as the primary qualification for Year 11 students replacing School Cert," he said.

Asked if the ministry decided at the time that 30 or more credits at levels two or three represented as much learning as a lower-level certificate, Pollard said it was possible to infer that but he could not definitively say why the decision was made.

He said the ministry would consider if it needed to change the methodology given a new qualification would be introduced from 2028-2030.

"We do need to look at it going forward," he said.

World.title: Uni students skipping meals and classes to keep on top of bills
World.content:
A Wellington student is doubting that pursuing a degree is a smart move as she skips meals because she can't afford to eat.

A student association survey of 1238 students at Te Herenga Waka - Victoria University Wellington found many were skipping meals and missing classes as they worked to pay rent and bills on top of their studies.

Thirty-three percent of the students who responded to the survey said they had skipped a meal in the previous week because they couldn't afford to eat.

Pyper-Alex Adams is in her third year at Victoria University - studying Psychological Sciences.

She said a part-time job and a casual position on top of her full-time studies helped keep her rent paid, but she often skimped on meals - especially when shifts were sparse.

"If I get offered shifts that's great but I don't have any shifts this week, I don't have any shifts next week. I've actually had to apply to the student hardship grant to help with my power bill this month because I don't know if I'm going to be able to pay it without any shifts from my second job," Adams said.

She said she was starting to question whether a tertiary qualification was really a smart move.

"It makes me just want to drop out of university. I am barely able to afford rent. We're cold all the time because we're only using the heat pump during free power. I'm skipping meals.

"I'm going to university to try and get a degree. To maybe have a job someday - if I can get one in this country - but I'm seeing people my age that are doing so much better without the degree - which is the thing that we're all told in high school to do, right?" Adams said.

300 level student Pyper-Alex Adams. RNZ / Bill Hickman

Third-year maths and statistics student Cam Dickson was trying to be creative to find his way around the high cost of living.

"You know people talk about chicken and rice? We're not doing chicken and rice, we're doing beans and rice. I'm moving away from fresh fruit and vegetables because they're not super accessible right now. Going heavy on the carbs - on the cans - on the box stuff," Dickson said.

Dickson is one of the nearly 38 percent of students surveyed who said they had missed classes because they couldn't afford public transport costs.

"I don't have public transport in the wiggle room. I've got no way to own a car, to pay for the fuel. I'm very constrained to where my feet can get me and sometimes that's not university," Dickson said.

At the lower entrance to Victoria University, a billboard advertising open days asked whether people were 'Ready to experience Wellington like a Victoria University student?'.

Cam Dickson said many students' experience of the slogan might be different to what the advertisers imagined.

"It means to be cold a lot of the time. Sometimes it means to be hungry. Sometimes it means to be damp. Sometimes it means to just kind of struggle to get by and I wouldn't really recommend anyone that experience," Dickson said.

At the lower entrance to Victoria University, a billboard advertising open days asked whether people were 'Ready to experience Wellington like a Victoria University student?'. RNZ / Bill Hickman

The situation appeared to become more acute for students in their later stages of study.

Seventy-eight percent of third year students said they had considered heading overseas for better job opportunities - eight percent higher than respondents from across the entire survey population.

President of the Victoria University Students Association and Masters student, Aidan Donoghue, said the intense competition for work was changing how students approached their degrees.

"It's so competitive that you must be a straight A student. You must have X amount of internships. You must have all these extra curricular activities at this point just to put your name out there," Donoghue said

He had a message for people who saw today's student poverty as the same rite of passage experienced by previous generations.

"Students aren't just complaining. It's just as expensive as it was then but twenty years of inflation on top. Plus stagnant wage growth, plus competitive working environment. All the bad things of university that you have experienced have gotten worse over decades of compounding interest," Donoghue said.

World.title: Police didn't know child victim's name in reopened abuse case, documents reveal
World.content:
A review into how police handled 40 child protection complaints has already triggered nine reports of suspected abuse or neglect. A series of documents obtained by RNZ reveal NZ Police did not know the name of a child victim whose case they had reopened, and that Oranga Tamariki was unaware of the major investigation until media began asking questions. National Crime Correspondent Sam Sherwood reports.

Eleven days before Oranga Tamariki was told of a major police investigation that involved the re-opening of 40 child protection complaints, police sought their help to identify a child linked to one of the cases under review.

Five days later, on 30 June, Oranga Tamariki (OT) replied saying it would grant access to the information request but, because of high demand, expected to provide the information by December.

Police responded saying they were "taking another look at an older file we believe holds risk for both police and OT".

"It has come to our attention because of a sensitive matter which I can't elaborate on at this time."

Internal police emails reveal the request was urgent because investigators needed information that would help identify the victim including the names and details of children placed in a person's care.

Police warned that waiting until December for the information "is going to create significant problems in addressing this risk".

The documents do not reveal what action, if any, OT took in response. It was not until 6 July that the agency was formally told about what Police had dubbed Operation Hark.

More than 100 pages of emails released to RNZ under the Official Information Act reveal how Oranga Tamariki first learned of the investigation, its scramble to assess dozens of affected cases, and senior staff's concern the agency could be "a bit over reliant on police's view" in the Child Protection Protocol process.

RNZ can also reveal that nine reports of concern have been created as a result of the NZ Police and Oranga Tamariki review of the identified cases.

Detective Inspector Kevan Verry. Screenshot

The information request

Operation Hark began after concerns were raised in May about Detective Inspector Kevan Verry's handling of a historical sexual abuse case in Northland that had sat for a couple of years with no investigation. The initial case sparked a further review where another 13 cases were identified as requiring re-investigation

Police also carried out a rapid review of about 1000 files which were under Verry's oversight, with a further 40 cases identified for re-investigation. A team of specialist child protection and adult sexual assault investigators had been pulled together to work on the re-opened cases.

On 25 June, police sent the information request to Oranga Tamariki. Five days later they got a response from OT saying they would grant their request.

"As we are currently receiving more requests than anticipated, we are experiencing delays in processing these."

OT said it would supply the information by 7 December.

A police staffer, whose name is redacted from the OIA, sent an email that went to Detective Superintendent Uraia Vakaruru and another staff member asking if they had any way of fast-tracking the request.

One of the recipients asked what the file related to and said they would follow up with their contact at OT.

The staffer replied with information about the case (this information is redacted in the OIA).

"I have attached the IR that I submitted to OT - I did request a lot of information from them but the most important part was the names and details of children placed in her care as that would help us identify the victim."

One of the staff then emailed a staff member at OT saying they were taking another look at an older file "which we believe holds risk for both police and OT".

"It has come to our attention because of a sensitive matter which I can't elaborate on at this time.

"What I can say is that this IR relates to [redacted] so there is obvious risk and additional scrutiny attached to this."

Police asked for the request to be "escalated in the priority queue".

"The estimated response time of December 2026 by OT is going to create significant problems in addressing the risk."

Oranga Tamariki deputy chief executive Thomas Ronan. supplied

The 'heads up'

On 6 July, OT chief social worker Nicolette Dickson sent an email to six staff including deputy chief executive Thomas Ronan and national commissioner North Alison Cronin advising them she had just been contacted by an assistant commissioner at NZ Police who was managing a "conduct issue" relating to one of their Child Protection Protocol (CPP) investigators.

"It appears that this information in quite significant detail has been leaked to media…" Dickson said.

An urgent meeting was being set up for OT and police staff that afternoon.

"One of the key issues for me is that the CPP process is a joint process and we will need to assure ourselves that we took appropriate steps for at least the 30 cases where gaps have been raised.

"We can be a bit over reliant on police's view in the CPP process so we will need to check we took appropriate steps from a child safety/wellbeing perspective."

Ronan later emailed Assistant Commissioner Tusha Penny asking to have a chat ahead of a meeting that was planned for later in the week as OT needed to do "some assessment work off the back of it".

Penny cc'd in Assistant Commissioner Corrie Parnell who was in charge of investigations and asked him to have someone forward details relating to each child protection case to OT.

Later that evening, a member of police's media team emailed OT's media team with a copy of a statement that would be sent to media about Operation Hark.

The statement included a line that said police were "working with Oranga Tamariki, IPCA and other agencies, as we progress this matter".

OT chief of staff Stephanie Short replied in an internal email querying the line about working with OT and asked whether that referred to the meeting that was scheduled to take place later that week or the initial call that Dickson received earlier that day.

"I'm also concerned from our minister's office perspective about what and when we knew about this issue when the police media response indicates we are working together."

On 7 July, an email was sent to a group of OT staff about the operation in Te Tai Tokerau relating to concerns about CPP work.

The staffer who sent the email - whose name is redacted - said they had told chief advisor Simon Harding that the group of staff would be happy to be part of any work OT undertakes to look at the cases that have been identified so far.

"I noted we will have been across lots of these and we have noted some cases where delays occurred or decisions to not take actions.

"I will let you know when I hear more, it is great to see police moving to address the concerns and responding publicly as a team we have seen how serious things have been up in TTT for some time."

That morning RNZ approached OT with questions about Operation Hark.

Ronan emailed police and said they were getting a few media requests and hoped to get the case details from police "as soon as possible".

A police staffer said they had two staff assigned to sorting the information and hoped to have it completed by the following day.

In a separate email exchange on 7 July, Harding emailed some staff about the list of cases that was coming on 8 July and said they would need a "structured spreadsheet or template" to use to inform the reviews.

He then listed a series of possible things to cover including did OT know, and what actions OT took.

"Possibly something about what the Police told us? (unsure about this one, I am getting at the potential issue we may find of Police telling us things are fine when there is insufficient information to take that at face value, or perhaps that was about prosecution and we used it as the reason to close without considering safety and wellbeing more broadly? This could instead be a consideration under other areas)."

Harding also suggested questions around safety.

"I.e. is there evidence to show we considered safety risks and (if needed) either addressed them or were satisfied they were addressed? Are you worried about child safety after taking a look??"

Nine reports of concern

Ronan told RNZ OT had completed a review of all cases identified by police as potentially impacted and which involved children, all of whom were under 18 at the time of reporting to police.

"We did not identify any cases requiring urgent intervention to keep children safe.

"However, we continue to work with police locally to consider each case, share information, and determine any further actions required."

Asked how many of the CPP cases required further action by OT, Ronan said the agency had worked with police on most of the cases identified thus far to determine what further response was appropriate. This included engaging with children and families.

"Nine reports of concern have been created as a result of the police and Oranga Tamariki review of the identified cases," he said.

A report of concern is a notification to Oranga Tamariki about suspected abuse, neglect, harm, or wellbeing concerns for a child or young person.

RNZ also approached police for comment on the OIA including why the victim's name was not known and why Oranga Tamariki was not informed of the investigation before 6 July.

In response, Detective Superintendent Keith Borrell said police had made specific enquiries with OT "during an early and sensitive stage of our investigations".

"During the initial assessment phase of Operation Hark we were working to understand the scale of the situation. We have shared more fulsome information once it was appropriate to do so with OT."

World.title: A 'living room for the city': Nelson pub at risk of closure under council civic centre plans
World.content:
A popular Nelson pub in a 100-year-old former church could face closure under one of the city council's multi-million dollar options for a new library, community hub and civic centre.

The council is [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/regions_nelson/808899/consultation-opens-for-multi-million-dollar-community-hub-and-library-in-nelson proposing three options: developing the current Civic House and the adjourning Savings Bank and State Advances sites at a cost of $73.3 million; or building a new hub, library and civic space in Collingwood Street for $74.1m, or in Church Street for $88.2m.

Under the Collingwood Street option, The Free House would be replaced with a new building.

The pub, which was established in 2009, has become a regular meeting place for many groups including knitters, singers, backgammon players and mountainbikers, among many others.

The Free House opened in 2009 in an old Reformed Church. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Owner Eelco Boswijk said he was aware of plans to develop the land adjacent to The Free House, but news the land the pub was on was also included in one of the council's options came as a bit of a surprise.

"It was only when we saw the pictures that the council put out that it was like, 'oh, okay, we're well included' but it is what it is and people have to decide which one they want, if they want anything at all."

Boswijk said the idea for The Free House came after he and former co-owner Mic Dover couldn't find anwhere in Nelson to get a decent beer.

"All the pubs were tied basically and we were lamenting the fact that there were craft breweries popping up all over New Zealand and we couldn't get the beer in Nelson."

The Free House owner Eelco Boswijk. RNZ / Samantha Gee

The pair ran beer fetes once a quarter at Founders Park, all the while hoping someone would see there was a market for craft beer and open a pub or change their taps, he said.

When the former Reformed Church on Collingwood Street came on the market, Boswijk and Dover decided to have a go at it themselves.

In the last 17 years, it had become a community hub, a neutral space that welcomed everyone, he said.

If the Collingwood Street option was chosen, he hoped there was scope for The Free House to be integrated into the design in some way.

"There are two other options on the table and they may well get chosen so there's no point in getting terribly worked up just yet."

The Nelson City Council's options for the combined Community Hub, Library and Civic Space. Supplied / Nelson City Council

'A nugget of gold', a 'living room for the city'

Jenny Smith started the Free House Knitters about five years ago, in a bid to make a hobby that was often solitary more social.

"We didn't want to meet anywhere where there's a room charge or a minimum drinks requirement or anything like that and The Free House was just always very accommodating,.

"It's just a great living room for the city, there's so many special interest groups that meet here and you always see your friends here too, even if you're not planning anything."

Fellow knitter Gera Verheul said people often asked if they could join the group and anyone was welcome.

The pub reserved a table by the fireplace for the knitters, and put a bright light so they could see what they were doing.

"It's so much more than a pub, like on Tuesdays when we're here, you'll see in the corner there's a bunch of backgammon players, they're always here, live musicians will come and play music, the mountain bikers love it here, artists, all sorts of people come here."

The Free House Knitters meet fortnightly at the pub. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Verheul said she was all for a new library, but not in place of The Free House.

"This is an institution, there's an inner city garden here, we can sit outside, there's greenery, this building is an old church from the 1900s.

"We've got to hang on to these things, we don't want everything big and new and modern."

Carolyn Phillips and usually one if not two of her brothers have been meeting at The Free House every week since it opened. The three grew up in Jamaica, but now live in Nelson.

Their group, known as The Jamaicans, had grown to include many others and every Thursday, they gather play dominoes.

"[It's] a great Jamaican tradition, very noisy, as you will hear, lots of banging and crashing and yelling and several glasses of beer and or wine, but such fun."

Chris, Carolyn and Christian Phillips, who are in a group known as The Jamaicans, play dominoes every week at The Free House. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Phillips said she couldn't believe it when she heard one of the council's options for a new civic building could mean the end of The Free House.

"What do you mean you want to take this down to build a community centre? This is a community centre, I meet so many people here, so many people I know and so many people I don't know, which I think is one of the healthiest aspects of it.

"Why aren't you taking some derelict place that nobody goes to or some bit of empty land or some horrible concrete box that is an eyesore? There must be other places.

"To me, it would be like removing a nugget of gold from this city and I think this city is under stress anyway as it is."

David Montgomery started the Nelson Shanty Club about six months ago and it found a home at The Free House.

"Every month we get together and over the course of a couple of hours and probably a few drinks, sing some sea shanties together.

"We do kind of impose shanties on [pubgoers] a bit for the evening, but a lot of them really enjoy that, get involved in singing and singalong, so it's brilliant."

Nelson Shanty Club meets once a week at The Free House, with anyone welcome to join in and sing. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Whakatū Ultimate Frisbee Club member Jim Risner said for at least seven years, a group of players had been heading to The Free House after their Thursday night games.

"One, it's got a great selection of beer which always changes, two, the staff are great and three, I do like the decor, but that's why I stay, that's not why I come."

Risner said the pub was part of Nelson's history and world famous outside New Zealand.

"A couple years ago, it was in a guidebook. Tourists would be reading that from overseas that come here to the pub, you can't replace that, you can't tear it down."

Three locations, one decsision

Deputy mayor and city revitalisation taskforce chair Pete Rainey said the council been grappling with how to address the ageing library and council building for some time.

Plans to build a $46m library on the banks of the Maitai River were shelved in 2022 after the severe flood event caused millions of dollars worth of damage to the community, with the cost also considered unaffordable in the current economic environment.

That same year, the council building Civic House was served two earthquake-prone notices, despite strengthening works undertaken in 2021.

"This term of council we've taken it head on and given real thought to what we can do about both of those issues and that's when we came to the decision to go ahead with a plan to combine the facilities into one building because we think it's the most cost-effective, prudent and forward-thinking plan for the city."

Deputy mayor and city revitalisation taskforce chair Pete Rainey. VNP / Phil Smith

He said he really liked The Free House and that it encompassed many of the things he hoped that a new civic community space would too.

"A lot of the activity that happens in the Free House, the community aspects, are exactly the kind of things that I would like to see happening in a new community space that we would build for the city. Not necessarily the bar, but all of the community-facing type of activities that happen in there, are they the kind of things that we need real consideration to."

Rainey said there were multi-use facilities around New Zealand that were great examples of combining libraries with civic administration; the Te Kahu o Waipuna - Marlborough Library & Art Gallery in Blenheim, Te Ara Ātea in Rolleston and Te Whare Whakatere in Ashburton.

He encouraged people to make a submission on their preferred option.

"We need to know what people think, there's no doubt that it's tricky economic times, we certainly recognise that, but we don't think sitting still and parking the issue is the right move.

"We've got to start thinking ahead for the city for the next 50 to 100 years. This is not just about the current ratepayers and the current population of Nelson, it's about their children and their grandchildren."

World.title: Coroner finds Corrections missed risk assessment before Invercargill inmate Nukuroa Strange's death
World.content:
A Coroner has recommended changes to the way Corrections manages vulnerable prisoners as a result of the death of an Invercargill Prison inmate.

Nukuroa "Nuku" Strange, 30, died in his cell on August 4, 2022 after he was shifted out of a unit for at-risk prisoners and segregated.

Strange, who was on remand, learned he was facing a prison sentence of about eight years for 22 driving, property and firearm offences.

His partner had ended their relationship because of his likely long jail term.

In findings released on Tuesday following an inquest, Coroner Amelia Steel said Strange had attempted suicide twice since June 2022, and Corrections staff deemed him at risk of self-harm four times.

The day before his death, Strange was shifted out of the prison's Intervention and Support Unit (ISU) - special rooms allowing for close monitoring and access to specialist care - after being deemed "no risk" of suicide.

Corrections staff then put him on directed segregation, meaning he was to be kept isolated from other prisoners without any visits.

Steel found staff skipped a mandatory face-to-face risk assessment when segregating Strange, instead relying on the "no risk" assessment.

"While it is not possible to state whether an in-person review risk assessment would have altered the outcome for Nuku following his directed segregation, it represents a missed opportunity to reassess acute risk when it was formally required," she said.

Expert evidence at the inquest noted a vulnerable prisoner with plans to self-harm might say "all the right things" to staff simply to secure a transfer from ISU to standard cells where they had more privacy.

Strange had initially objected to moving to the ISU, in one instance hitting an officer with a piece of wood.

His resistance twice resulted in "planned use of force", including pepper spray, and was the reason for his segregation, the report said.

The Coroner said Strange had a long history of mental health and psychosocial vulnerability.

He had previously been incarcerated on 11 other occasions and received four sentences of imprisonment.

Visibly distressed before death

On the morning of his death, two other prisoners warned staff about Strange's behaviour.

One said they had seen him "visibly distressed" on the phone, while the other warned Strange was not well enough to be in the South Unit and said he should return to the ISU.

Strange's last phone conversations that morning were to his ex-partner and to his mother.

"He told his mother he loved her and she told him not to do anything stupid. Footage from South Unit CCTV was played during the inquest and Nuku could be seen leaving those conversations, wiping his eyes," the report said.

Strange was visited by a staff member after the phone call who said he "did not appear agitated".

He was found dead at 11.03am by a fellow prisoner cleaning cell windows, 25 minutes after his cell was locked.

New transitional units, more mental health staff recommended

Steel made five key recommendations, including the creation of new transitional units for prisoners shifting between the ISU and prison units.

"These units would extend current focus beyond the 'acute' risk and would strengthen the support available to prisoners experiencing distress," she said.

She also recommended changes to the way Corrections carries out risk assessments, saying health and medical staff should be consulted and any historical self-harm alerts should remain active on prisoners' files indefinitely.

"This reflects the unpredictability of suicide risk and its manifestation; it may assist to remove bias associated with completing the assessment may support staff to complete the assessment correctly and in accordance with policy; and it mitigates an overreliance on the prisoner's self-reporting of risk," she said.

Steel said Corrections should employ more trained mental health staff and provide more frequent training focused on suicide risk for existing custodial and health staff.

Steel said Corrections failed to act with urgency to eliminate known hazards in cells, despite being warned of the risks after a similar death in 2016.

She described the current programme as "disparate and underfunded".

Corrections responds

Following Strange's death, Corrections said it had introduced daily multi-disciplinary team meetings between custodial and mental health staff to share clinical and observational data about inmates.

All high-risk prisoners had active care and management plans, it said.

Corrections said it had also made risk assessment forms more detailed and made the presence of health staff mandatory during any planned use of force.

In response to the Coroner's recommendations, Corrections agreed to continue investigating opportunities for staff suicide training and update alert systems to ensure historical self-harm risks were kept active on files.

Corrections said it was not feasible to consult health staff on all risk assessments but it would look to mandate it in "defined, high-risk" situations, such as any recent self-harm or suicide attempts or recent placements in the ISU.

In response to the recommendation for new transitional units, Corrections said it was "restricted by available funding and budget allocations", and such a move could have unintended consequences.

"A step-down unit could still be quite isolating, or could promote socialisation with other vulnerable at-risk people," it said.

Corrections said it had taken steps to create a more therapeutic environment in the mainstream unit and the ISU, including more rehabilitation programmes, new paint and decorations and new furniture.

Invercargill Prison was recruiting more mental health nurses and counsellors, Corrections said.
