World.title: Southland road closed overnight after serious crash
World.content:
A Southland road will remain closed overnight after serious crash northeast of Invercargill.

Police said one person is in hospital with serious to critical injuries following the two-vehicle crash at Mabel Bush, which was reported about 5:35pm.

The intersection of Grove Bush Woodlands Road and Rakahouka Hedgehope Road will remain closed overnight, ahead of a scene examination on Tuesday morning.

World.title: Council pushes Ohakune's water restoration another 24 hours
World.content:
The Ruapehu District Council is now saying another 24 hours will be needed before Ohakune's water network is safely back online.

The council had earlier been confident supply would be restored around 5pm on Monday.

But it says if the pipeline that carries water from its source to the treatment plant is repressurised too quickly, it could fracture, and cause even longer delays.

The outage was caused during repairs on Friday to the raw water pipeline damaged by the 5.9 magnitude earthquake near Taumarunui on 25 July. The work resulted in an airlock preventing raw water from reaching the treatment plant, leaving central North Island town without a reticulated water supply.

The town's water reservoir was down to 12 percent on Saturday morning.

RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

On Monday morning the district's mayor said the problem was more serious than originally thought and could not confirm when the town would have water again.

But Ruapehu District Mayor Weston Kirton later told Midday Report that there had been a reassessment of the conditions and water would be back on by 5pm, with experts coming in from all around the country.

Ruapehu Mayor Weston Kirton discusses Ohakune water issues Midday Report Download MP3 4m

'Extremely technical and challenging situation'

Earlier on Monday afternoon the council's chief executive Clive Manley said it was still aiming to get water back by 5pm on Monday.

He said at the time service contractor Veolia was able to locate hidden valves and was installing new ones to help release trapped air from the system.

"Restoring the supply has been complicated by sections of the raw water pipeline being buried and located in heavy bush, making valves difficult to find.

"Veolia has developed a plan for recharging the water network that includes introducing water from the treatment plant end of the system."

One of many closure notices in Ohakune today. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Additional staff and resources were brought in from Whanganui, Auckland and Central Hawke's Bay to help with the repairs, he said.

However later on Monday afternoon Manley said another 24 hours would be needed and water was expected to be back around 5pm Tuesday.

He said if the pipeline that carried water from its source to the treatment plant was repressurised too quickly, it could fracture, and cause even longer delays.

"A slower, controlled approach is therefore needed to protect the repaired infrastructure and safely restore the town's water supply."

"This has been an extremely technical and challenging situation. We have been working to keep the community fully informed as new information becomes available, but the situation and expected restoration time have continued to evolve as work has progressed."

Council's water services contractor, Veolia, had confirmed that the airlock affecting the raw water pipeline had been resolved.

Evie Story says she's been bathing 18-month-old Thea by using bottled water during Ohakune's outage. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

The council said emergency water supplies were available from Ruapehu District Council's office at 37 Ayr St and people could reuse water bottles at this same location.

It said port-a-loos were located at the council's office; Thames Street opposite the Powderhorn; Goldfinch Street / Shannon Street; and the rear carpark of the Ohakune i-SITE.

"We are contacting schools to let them know about this situation. We expect schools will make the decision to close, but that is their decision to make."

Residents were asked to keep all taps inside their properties turned off while network restorations where ongoing.

A water truck in Ohakune supplying drinking water. RNZ / Kate Pereyra

Mayor had been unsure when water would be back

Kirton had first told Morning Report it had been more difficult to fix the piping than had been initially thought.

"We've found the leak, we've actually fixed the leak, we've then tried to flush the system out and it's not working that well... and so we're obviously working hard to overcome that problem."

Kirton had said there was about 5km of concrete piping that was about 70 years old and may have been affected by the earthquake.

But it was in difficult-to-access terrain which was hard to flush out, he said.

Angelina Reyes has filled up water bottles from the council-supplied tank in Ohakune. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

"As soon as we get on top of the airlocks then we'll be able to manufacture the water and then open the systems up for the town, but it's certainly concerning."

The water had previously been expected to be back on by Monday afternoon, but Kirton told Morning Report that was no longer the case, and he did not want to speculate on when it would be back on.

Weston Kirton says it will take longer than initially expected to get the town's regular water system fixed. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

The water plant was brand new and the issue was actually getting the water to the plant, he said.

The emergency situation was worsening and they would be dealing with that this morning, Kirton said.

"It could well be that we have an emergency situation to actually get water from elsewhere, through tankers or the like."

It would take longer than expected to get the existing plant up and running, he said.

Colin Young fills a water bottle. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

It may be necessary to put an emergency water system in place before Ohakune's regular system can be fixed, he said.

"So I can't speculate whether it's a state of emergency yet, but that's one of the considerations you know whether we call on the government for help to actually overcome the issue with our town."

There was an influx of people in Ohakune at this time of year and there were businesses that wanted to be open and operating, he said.

World.title: Former championship winning team cut from A-Leagues
World.content:
Western United has had its A-Leagues participation agreement terminated, effectively ending any flicker of hope of the troubled club making a return.

United has essentially been an A-Leagues club in name only for more than a year amid varied financial woes, which included not paying players and staff.

The club was placed into hibernation by the Australian Professional Leagues (APL) in September 2025, with A-League Men and Women players having to scramble to continue their careers elsewhere.

Ownership West Melbourne Group avoided a wind-up order from the Australian Tax Office in January by settling a $15.5 million tax debt.

Football Australia declined to reinstate the Tarneit-based club's licence in May and United again won't participate in either the ALM or ALW.

West Melbourne Group have another wind-up hearing in the Federal Court on Tuesday and on Monday the APL officially terminated their participation agreement in the A-League competitions.

Western United won the A-League Men's grand final in 2022. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

"Since the club was placed into conditional hibernation in September 2025, the APL has been in close consultation with Western United as they've worked through financial, governance and legal matters to try and rebuild the club," APL chair Stephen Conroy said in a statement.

"The APL board has since taken the decision to terminate Western United's club participation agreement.

"The club was in breach of a number of its obligations under that agreement, including its obligation to comply with the Football Australia National Club Licensing Regulations.

"It's been a difficult period for everyone connected to Western United — and we want to acknowledge the management, staff, players and especially the fans — who have given so much to the club and will no doubt be hurt by this news."

Sadness after Western United licence removal Western United fans have expressed their disappointment and sadness after the team was stripped of its A-League licence late last week.

AAP understands United still owes some of its former players and staff money.

United was granted a licence in 2018, off the back of grand promises to build its own stadium, entered the A-League Men ahead of the 2019-20 season and won the ALM championship in 2021-22.

A women's team followed in 2022-23 and reached the grand final in their first season.

United has consistently been defiant and adamant it will return to the A-Leagues.

When put into hibernation, the club claimed it wasn't a "step back".

Western United finally opened their small Ironbark Fields ground in 2024. It saw just one season of A-League football. (Getty Images: MB Media/Santanu Banik)

After the tax debt was paid in January, the club declared its ambition to seal a "strong return to the A-Leagues".

Despite the latest development, the club on Monday broadcast plans to return in a year's time under new ownership.

"Over recent months, we have worked closely with the APL on a pathway that gives the club the best opportunity to survive, rebuild and return to the A-League under new ownership," United said in a statement on Monday.

"This creates an opportunity for new custodians, new investment and a fresh start.

"The objective must now be to preserve Western United's identity in Melbourne's west and work towards a return to the A-League for the 2027-28 season.

"This should not be the end of Western United. It should be the reset that allows the club to rebuild and return stronger."

AAP

World.title: Injury could rule Socceroos defender out of Asian Cup
World.content:
Socceroos defender Cameron Burgess's Asian Cup hopes appear in jeopardy following a possible Achilles injury while playing for Swansea City.

The towering central defender played every minute of the gruelling English Championship campaign last season.

That made for 4,140 minutes, plus stoppage time, across all 46 league matches.

But there are fears Burgess's season is over after he limped off late in Swansea's 1-0 League Cup loss to Birmingham City.

In the 87th minute he challenged for a header, landed awkwardly and grabbed at his right lower leg, prompting his Birmingham opponents to check on him.

The 30-year-old, who has 29 Socceroos caps, headed to hospital for scans.

Cameron Burgess played against Türkiye and the USA for the Socceroos at the World Cup. (Getty Images: Richard Heathcote)

"It doesn't look good, but I prefer to wait for the assessment we will do," Swansea head coach Vítor Matos said.

"It could be related to the Achilles, but let's see."

If Burgess has ruptured his Achilles, he faces a significant stint on the sidelines, ending his Asian Cup hopes.

Losing Burgess ahead of tournament, to be held in Saudi Arabia early next year, is a significant blow to Australia's defensive stocks.

Burgess lost his starting spot to teen sensation Lucas Herrington during the World Cup, with coach Tony Popovic preferring a back three involving the teenager, Harry Souttar and Alessandro Circati.

But as a left-footer, Burgess is always a valuable part of Popovic's squad.

Souttar spent more than a year on the sidelines after his own Achilles tear, while wing-back Lewis Miller is on the comeback trail from the same injury, which ruled him out of World Cup contention.

Star wing-back Jordan Bos is sidelined until about October after having surgery on the left knee injured in Australia's round-of-32 loss to Egypt.

The Socceroos are next in action for friendlies against Brazil in Townsville on September 25 and Brisbane four days later.

AAP

World.title: Head aims to maintain opening spot ahead of busy 12 months
World.content:
Travis Head can envisage himself continuing to open the batting for Australia at the end of next year's Ashes.

The positive mindset of the back-to-back Allan Border Medal winner is no surprise.

Head was a revelation in home conditions in last year's Ashes series with three centuries after moving up from the middle order.

Ahead of the opening Test against Bangladesh in Darwin, the 32-year-old was asked if his order switch was short-term or whether it could work across the 20 or more Tests Australia will play in the next 12 months.

There was a sense that Head's move up the order against England was intended to counter their ultra-aggressive "Bazball".

It worked so well that the term "Travball" was coined.

Prior to the home Ashes, his stints as an opener had been short-lived.

Travis Head scored three centuries as an opener in the last Ashes series. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

Head was unstoppable on home tracks in the Ashes series, but he will face a variety of surfaces in Australia, South Africa, England and India in the next 12 months.

He says he is not worried about playing in different conditions.

"I feel like I have been adaptable in the places that I have played," Head said.

"In India and England I have opened the batting, which is a slightly different to Australia.

"Everything is going to be different, but what I have been able to do over my career is problem solve the best that I can and work through challenges — whether they are green wickets or flat wickets.

"It will look different in every Test match or every series. I am trying to be as calm and consistent as I can."

Whether Head stays an opener will depend largely on how he performs and also on the displays of the middle order.

Tweaks may be made but right now Head plans to be opening in the final Test of next year's away Ashes series.

"I think it will work," he said.

"If I have done it for [another] 20 Tests and I am sitting there in a few years and I have opened the batting the whole time … I would have done an OK job and been consistent, contributed and had a good partnership with Jake [Weatherald].

"It is a new challenge coming here and a new challenge in South Africa in a month's time and I am looking forward to the challenge."

International cricket coach Joe Gatting has posted videos of how Head plans for a variety of scenarios and surfaces and he is expected to continue to find the best approach in all conditions.

"We have a lot of footage and we couldn't be more resourced in that space. I'll continue to do that," Head said.

AAP

World.title: Geelong Cats board holds crisis meeting over concussion deal
World.content:
Geelong is about to reply to the AFL's "please explain" as the Cats brace for a potential massive penalty over the secret concussion deal with Jake Kolodjashnij.

Amid speculation over the futures of Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking and AFL chairman Craig Drummond, the club board held a crisis meeting on Monday to work out its response to the league.

Also on Monday, Geelong captain Patrick Dangerfield said the club had "buggered up", but strongly defended Hocking.

Pressure has been mounting on Geelong and the AFL since it emerged last Thursday that the Cats struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij, who had a history of concussion.

Drummond apologises AFL chair Craig Drummond issues a statement apologising for his part in the Jake Kolodjashnij concussion contract saga.

"We acknowledge this has been a challenging time for Jake, our club and Geelong supporters," Cats president Grant McCabe said in a statement on Monday.

"The board has met this morning to discuss our response to the AFL's letter. That will be submitted by end of day Tuesday, 11 August.

"This will provide the club with the chance to detail the actions it took in navigating this complex matter. We welcome this opportunity.

"The club remains committed to providing our players with the highest standard of care and support."

Hocking was Cats chief executive and Drummond was the club president when the deal was struck two years ago with Koladjashnij.

The Geelong defender signed a waiver that meant he effectively took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to indemnify the club and its medical staff from potential court action.

On the weekend Hocking defended the club in a radio interview and argued there was not a lot they would do differently.

"As a leader it's really important to take ownership and just lead through this. It's not easy to do, but I wouldn't change too much — we are a really good football club," he said.

"I know there are people out there who say culturally we are maybe not as strong as we have been, but we do so much right and occasionally there might be one or two per cent we don't get right.

"In this case that will be proven, I would suggest, that will be proven with the 'please explain'. We don't get everything right."

Drummond also released a statement in which he apologised over the deal. He added he would not be involved in the AFL's assessment and deliberation of the Kolodjashnij situation.

On Monday, Dangerfield told Fox Footy that Hocking was one of the most "placid" people he had met and gave him his full support.

"He's a man of the highest integrity … we're lucky to have him," Dangerfield said.

But he acknowledged mistakes had been made.

"Clearly there were some parts that we buggered up as a club. We can be better," he said.

AAP

World.title: WNBA player claims 'white privilege' saw her ejected after foul
World.content:
DiJonai Carrington of the Chicago Sky has been ejected after being called for a Flagrant 2 foul on Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever.

Minutes after the eviction on Saturday (local time), Carrington posted on social media the words "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever.

Cunningham, who is white, was shooting a fast-break lay-up in the first quarter when Carrington, who is black, came from behind and hit her in the head and neck, knocking her to the court as the shot went in.

Cunningham said she thought the foul in the 90–86 Indiana win was "absolutely" intentional.

"Clearly I think it was unnecessary," Cunningham said.

"I've never really spoken to her and I have no beef with her, but I guess she has some pent-up stuff."

DiJonai Carrington had little to complain about, most suggested. (Getty Images: Michael Reaves)

Fever coach Stephanie White had a different view of the play.

"It was a hard foul," White said.

"I don't think that DiJonai intentionally came out to get her across the neck like she did, but it did happen, and I thought it was the right call."

Cunningham got up immediately, charged toward Carrington and pushed her as she was held back by a teammate.

"I popped up," Cunningham said.

"I'm not going to let anyone just do that to me. I think everyone knows that. I think that's why she did it, because she wants attention."

Sophie Cunningham had to be held back after popping up after the foul. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/Melissa Tamez)

The play was reviewed and upgraded to a Flagrant 2 after the referee said there was wind-up, impact and follow-through on the foul.

Sky coach Tyler Marsh said he had not seen a replay of the play, but that seeing it live, he thought Carrington was making a play on the ball and that he did not believe it warranted a Flagrant 2 foul.

"I haven't looked at that play since, so I really don't know if it was justified or not," he said.

"But, that's what I thought in the moment."

Marsh was then asked about Carrington's social media post.

"I have to get back to you on that because I'm just now hearing about that," he said.

"So yeah, we'll handle that."

But Cunningham had plenty to say about the post.

"I think the league is taking care of that," she said.

"This has nothing to do with race. Last year, I did the same thing and I got kicked out. And I deserved to be kicked out. There's no reason even to play that card."

In the third quarter, Fever star Caitlin Clark was assessed a technical foul after she made contact with a referee when she was forced out of bounds.

WNBA champs rubbish claims of Clark jealousy The outsized spotlight on Caitlin Clark has prompted some to suggest others in the WNBA are jealous of her, but two champions of the league say that is nonsense.

The technical was Clark's eighth of the season, triggering a one-game suspension for Indiana's next game if not rescinded by the league.

"She said I ran into her," Clark said in a post-game television interview.

"I've already watched it on the tape, so we'll let the league decide. But it wasn't intentional or anything, so I'm hoping it's getting rescinded,"

A few hours after the game, Clark got her way. The WNBA rescinded the technical foul.

Cunningham has frequently come to Clark's defence after physical play by opponents and has become one of the higher-profile players in the league this season.

AP

World.title: Brazilian footballer falls in tunnel after scoring disallowed goal
World.content:
Brazilian footballer Jacy Maranhão was rushing to meet a sea of his supporters, ball in hand and jumping with joy, before he fell down a dark tunnel.

The Corbita defender had just put his club 2-0 up against Chapecoense in the first half of a game in the Brazilian Serie A.

But just as he found his footing again and dusted himself off from the fall, the referee halted the game.

On review, the Video Assistant Referee (VAR) found the 29-year-old's goal was offside.

Jacy managed to continue playing into the first few minutes of the second half before being substituted with an injury.

The incident was not the first time a footballer had fallen foul of the tunnel at the Estádio Major Antônio Couto Pereira.

Loading...

Almost a decade earlier, Cameroonian forward Diederrick Joel Tagueu-Tadjo ran to the same end of the pitch, jumping over the same advertising hoardings before falling into the now-infamous Corbita tunnel.

But unlike Jacy, his goal was not ruled out, and he managed to finish the game against São Paulo.

But according to Brazilian journalist Leonardo Mendes Jr, there was a striking similarity to the two incidents.

"There's one detail that makes it even more unbelievable," he posted on social media.

World.title: Chiefs sign premiership winger To'o away from Panthers
World.content:
Four-time premiership-winning winger Brian To'o has become the sixth player to sign with the PNG Chiefs for their inaugural NRL season in 2028.

The signing of the Penrith Panthers flyer, who has represented NSW in State of Origin and Samoa in Test matches, was announced by the Chiefs on Monday.

To'o has signed a three-year deal to join the Chiefs, with 2027 to be his final year with the Panthers.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

"Brian is an exceptional rugby league player, but this signing is about much more than football," PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson said.

"The PNG Chiefs will be a club proudly built in Papua New Guinea but with a strong Pacific identity.

"Across our region, family, culture, community and rugby league are deeply connected, and Brian represents those values every time he takes the field.

"He is fiercely proud of his Samoan heritage, incredibly close to his family and understands what it means to represent something bigger than yourself.

"That is exactly the kind of person we want wearing the Chiefs jersey."

To'o has been a key component of the Penrith Panthers dynasty, which won four consecutive premierships from 2021–2024, were grand finalists in 2020 and made last year's preliminary final.

The Panthers are on top of the NRL ladder in 2026, seeking a fifth title in six years.

To'o has played 151 matches for the Panthers since making his debut in 2019, scoring 99 tries to date.

He has played 17 Origins for the Blues, and 11 Tests for Samoa.

"Brian is an exceptional player, but he's an even better person. He's a great teammate, a devoted family man and someone who brings so much energy and positivity to our club every day," Penrith coach Ivan Cleary said.

"He's been a huge part of what we've built here and we're looking forward to sharing one more season with him before he begins his next chapter."

The Chiefs have now signed six players to its maiden roster, but have already secured key talent.

Former Penrith five-eighth Jarome Luai, who won four premierships with To'o, was the club's marquee signing earlier this year.

Alex Johnston, the all-time leading try scorer in Australian premiership rugby league, was a key outside back signed along with NSW Origin representative Zac Lomax.

Sydney Roosters utility Connor Watson and Englishman Matty Lees have also been signed.

World.title: Yeo learns fate on pec in seismic moment for Panthers
World.content:
Penrith's premiership charge has received a massive boost, with Isaah Yeo a chance to play again this year after avoiding surgery on his pectoral injury.

Yeo had been at risk of missing the rest of the NRL season after he left the field in Friday's loss to the Warriors, in what shaped as a major blow for the Panthers.

But Penrith medical staff confirmed on Monday the club's co-captain would not go under the knife following scans, and could begin rehabilitation in a bid to play again in 2026.

The news will also likely come as a relief to Australia coach Kevin Walters, with Yeo expected to again lead the Kangaroos at the World Cup if he avoids later surgery.

Former Panther Apisai Koroisau missed just one week with a pectoral injury early this year, as opposed to the 10 weeks usually out if surgery is required.

Penrith has made a habit of having players play through injury to be part of premiership wins throughout their dynasty.

Almost half of their squad were walking wounded through the first title of their four-peat in 2021, which the club compared to climbing Mount Everest.

Halves Jarome Luai and Nathan Cleary both played through persistent shoulder issues in 2023 and 2024 respectively, with both requiring surgery afterwards.

Had Yeo been sidelined, it would have been a monumental blow to the first-placed Panthers, given the role he plays in both attack and defence at lock.

Ex-Panther Spencer Leniu described Yeo as the "heartbeat" of Penrith's team over the weekend, declaring his injury would be a "massive loss" for the club.

Penrith faces Leniu's Sydney Roosters in a blockbuster top-of-the-table clash on Thursday night, which Yeo would not be expected to play in.

AAP

Tech.title: What to expect from Google’s 2026 Pixel hardware launch event
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s that time of year: On Wednesday, Google is set to host its annual Made by Google hardware launch event for Pixel gadgets. Google itself has already teased new slab-style and foldable Pixel smartphones, but leaks also indicate that the company could announce updated watches, a new color for familiar earbuds, and perhaps a brand new AirTag-like item tracker.

However, unusually, Google’s event is taking place in the evening: It kicks off on Wednesday at 6PM ET / 3PM PT instead of in the early afternoon or mid-morning, like many other tech events. And this time it has a celebrity host in Trevor Noah.

Even more strange: As noted by 9to5Google, the Google Store homepage has a Pixel 11 preorder countdown that will end at 10AM ET on Wednesday — which is many hours earlier than the launch event itself. That could mean that all of the details about Google’s new devices will be officially revealed long before the company hosts the formal launch event.

Here’s what we expect to see Google announce this week. If you want to watch the event live, you can catch it on YouTube.

The Pixel 11 lineup

A leaked marketing render of the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Image: Evan Blass

Google has already hinted at its new phones while promoting the event, including shadowy glimpses of updated Pro and foldable phones. But the new smartphones could be largely iterative updates.

Google is expected to announce four new smartphones: the Pixel 11, the Pixel 11 Pro, the Pixel 11 Pro XL, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Based on leaked images, they should look largely the same as the Pixel 10 lineup, though it appears they’ll have camera bars that are black all the way across and colors that might rule.

Perhaps the most notable visual difference will be a rainbow glowy light on the camera bar, which Google has already shown off for the Pixel 11 Pro. The company hasn’t yet specified what it’ll do or what it’s called. But code in Google’s contacts app spotted by 9to5Google indicates that it will be called “HiLight” and, at least for that contacts app, HiLight can be customized with different colors to indicate when certain people call you. Presumably, the light will work in some way with other apps as well. Based on a translation of a leaked Pixel 11 Pro Fold image, HiLight will also light up when you talk with Google’s Gemini AI.

A tease from Google showing the new light. Image: Google

Inside the phones, it seems likely that they’ll be powered by a new Tensor G6 chip. It’s rumored that the new chip will use TSMC’s 2nm process, which is expected to bring performance and power efficiency gains. If it does launch with a 2nm chip, the Pixel 11 series will be the first smartphones on the market to do so, and potentially by a hair; Apple’s chip for its next Pro phones that presumably launch in September is also expected to use the 2nm process.

Google is rumored to raise the starting storage of the base Pixel 11 and the base Pixel 11 Pro to 256GB, up from the 128GB floor with the Pixel 10 and Pixel 10 Pro. However, early Pixel 11 Pro listings have stated that the Pixel 11 Pro will have 12GB of RAM. If accurate, that would be down from the 16GB of RAM found in the Pixel 10 Pro lineup.

And expect the whole Pixel lineup to have a higher starting price, as a Google VP recently told 9to5Google that the Pixel family will get pricing “adjustments” due to the memory crisis.

The Pixel Watch 5

A leaked marketing render of the Pixel Watch 5. Image: OnLeaks and The Tide Chart

We already know that Google has manufactured at least one device called the Pixel Watch 5 thanks to, uh, Borderlands creator Randy Pitchford. In a May post that included two images, Pitchford said that a friend found the watch underwater while scuba diving. But recently, Google briefly teased the watch for an August 12th launch, so we should see more soon.

Leaked renders of the Pixel Watch 5 indicate that it may come in colors including black, polished silver, yellow gold, and a brass-y color, though the overall design looks quite similar to the Pixel Watch 4. Specs obtained by MyMobiles say that the new watch comes in 41 and 45mm screen sizes with battery life rated at 30 and 40 hours, respectively, matching the Pixel Watch 4. MyMobiles says that the Pixel Watch 5 will get 64GB of storage, which is double the 32GB of storage available previously.

On the software side, marketing materials obtained by MyMobiles suggest that Gemini Intelligence — which Google revealed earlier this year for Android phones — will be a big feature for the Pixel Watch 5 this year. One apparent marketing slide calls Gemini Intelligence a “personal, proactive assistant” that can proactively surface helpful information for you. A feature called “Proactive Suggestions” will also be able to help you reply to messages by recommending “context-aware replies” based on a conversation. The marketing materials also promise that the new watch will have Google’s “most accurate sleep tracking yet.”

However, like with the Pixel phones, expect higher prices. MyMobiles reports that the 41mm Wi-Fi model may start at $399, up from the Pixel Watch 4’s $349.99, while the 45mm Wi-Fi model could start at $429, up from $399.99.

The Pixel Buds Pro 2 in a new color

A leaked marketing render of new Pixel Buds. Image: Evan Blass

Google first launched the Pixel Buds Pro 2 in 2024, but two years on, it seems as if the company is just going to launch a new color instead of refreshing the product.

An apparent marketing image leaked by Evan Blass shows new earbuds in a nice olive green color that matches other renders that Blass and others have surfaced of the Pixel 11 lineup. But the headphones themselves otherwise look just like the Buds Pro 2 — and they have apparently already appeared on a Google Play rewards page with the name “Pixel Buds Pro 2.”

I guess there’s always next year for the Buds Pro 3.

The Pixel Tag item tracker

An image apparently showing off the Google Pixel Tag. Image: 9to5Google

Google may also launch something brand new: Pixel Tag, an AirTag-like item tracker. Based on an image 9to5Google recently obtained, it has an oval shape, meaning it could look a little bit different than Apple’s circular AirTag.

Presumably, the Pixel Tag will play nicely with Android’s Find Hub network. A machine translation of a now-removed online listing said the tracker will connect with the “Find My Device” network, which was the name of the network before Google changed it to Find Hub. But detailed specs and an expected price haven’t leaked just yet.

Don’t expect Googlebook laptops or smart glasses

Some leaks for new Googlebook laptops have also cropped up recently, but when it first announced the Googlebooks, Google said they would be launching in the fall. Google is also working on smart glasses and Android XR glasses, but those are scheduled for the fall, too.

Sure, Google could throw curveballs. But that hardware will probably get full reveals at a later date.

Tech.title: YouTube is making it harder to earn money on YouTube
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Starting February 1st, 2027, creators who want to monetize their channel through YouTube’s Partner Program (YPP) will need at least 1,000 subscribers and either 8,000 qualified watch hours over the past year, or 20 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days. That’s a sizeable jump from YouTube’s current requirement of 1,000 subscribers with 4,000 watch hours in the past year, or 1,000 subscribers with 10 million Shorts views in the last 90 days. Creators will also need to maintain 10 million Shorts views over 90 days to earn money from the Shorts Creators Pool, though falling below this threshold won’t result in removal from YPP.

Additionally, YouTube says creators will benefit from an expansion of its cheaper Premium Lite subscription, which is coming to all countries where it offers Premium. YouTube splits up subscription revenue to creators based on watch time and views, with 55 percent dedicated to long-form videos and 45 percent for Shorts. “With these additional subscribers, creators can expect higher earnings: when a user signs up for Premium, partners, on average, earn more than when the user was watching ads,” YouTube says.

The requirements are changing as YouTube ramps up efforts to become more like a premium TV service alongside Netflix, HBO Max, and Disney Plus, rather than just an online platform for videos. This year, YouTube struck deals to broadcast shows from big names like Trevor Noah, and broadly rolled out a feature that allows creators to organize their videos into seasons.

Separately, there are some new requirements for creators to keep earning money from ads and subscriptions through the YPP, though. That includes maintaining either 1,000 watch hours over the past year, 1 million Shorts views, or two long-form videos or five Shorts uploaded every 90 days. YouTube’s existing policies say it will remove creators from the YPP if they haven’t uploaded a video or published content to the Posts tab for at least six months. Creators already in the program will need to accept the new terms by January 31st, 2027, to keep making money from their content.

Tech.title: Four takeaways from Mark Zuckerberg’s massive AI manifesto
Tech.content:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has a lot to say about the idealized future he now envisions for humanity co-existing with artificial intelligence — his latest essay spans more than 6,500 words on the matter. The lengthy manifesto Zuckerberg published on Monday, titled “The Future is for Everyone,” broadly lays out his beliefs about how the technology should be developed, expanded, and regulated, and how Meta is positioning itself to enable those goals.

Some points echo a similar (albeit, much shorter) public letter that Zuckerberg put out last year, heralding the importance of public access to superintelligent AI — a term for artificial general intelligence (AGI) models capable of surpassing human intelligence, which AI companies are racing to develop. Both were published with similar intentions: to pitch the supposed personal, societal, and economic benefits of superintelligent AI, and to grandstand Meta as a responsible steward to deliver that future.

Here are some of the main takeaways from Zuckerberg’s latest essay:

Sway the public on data centers

“Sustainable infrastructure development means that communities must benefit significantly from each project,” Zuckerberg said, detailing how Meta plans to resolve the ongoing PR crisis surrounding AI data center projects. This includes pledges to build energy-generating infrastructure “wherever we invest” that could potentially give low-cost energy back to the communities, and a commitment to “restore more water than we use in the watersheds where we operate by 2030.” Meta is also launching a Future Is For Everyone Fund to support local communities, and Zuckerberg says the company is providing free training and “guaranteed high-paying jobs” for skilled tradespeople in areas where Meta is building data centers.

Open AI for everyone

Meta is planning to focus its efforts on “delivering personal superintelligence to billions of people and small businesses,” arguing that doing so will empower everyone to become more entrepreneurial. Part of this involves offering the technology “for free or as affordably as possible,” and leaning into releasing more open source AI models that anyone can download. Doing so “will bring an abundance of personal agency, expression of ideas, deepening of relationships, economic and financial prosperity, improved health, and inventions we cannot imagine today,” according to Zuckerberg. He also says this will have an impact on “some aspects of the way we work,” but waves off concerns that AI will result in fewer jobs overall.

Less government oversight

Zuckerberg voices the importance of the US leading the open source AI ecosystem, citing concerns that competing models released by foreign labs “hold several advantages” because they face fewer training data restrictions. He pitches that the US needs to rethink policies around distillation and data use, arguing that while “some have tried to frame distillation as harmful,” the US will not be able to keep up if it keeps restricting AI models from learning from other models.

“I do not believe restricting access to foreign open source models is an effective solution,” said Zuckerberg. We should note here that these concerns are likely being voiced in response to the release of open-weight models from Chinese AI companies like Alibaba and Moonshot, which isn’t the same thing as being open-source, and the models Meta has released so far aren’t truly open-source either. He also espouses that access to personal superintelligence is essential for individuals to maintain their freedom, and should only be subject to restrictions “when truly required.”

But also, more government oversight

In cases where cybersecurity is involved, Zuckerberg proposes that frontier AI labs should work with the US government to help with bolstering critical infrastructure, and believes open-source AI models will improve system security over time — especially “once superintelligence enables most of the world’s code to be verifiably secure.” That plan includes pushing AI developers to share the training information of new models “for government use and review” intermediately instead of waiting until training has completed, which aligns with the Trump administration’s AI testing framework.

“This way the government will have early access to the most powerful models and an army of capable engineers to identify and patch security issues,” Zuckerberg said. “Labs should also work with law enforcement to help identify bad actors attempting to misuse their systems.”

Getting a keyboard with customizable Hall effect sensors is more affordable than it used to be, and you don’t need to compromise on quality to get a good deal. Keychron’s aluminum-clad K2 HE with a 75-percent layout is down to $103.99 (was $130) at Amazon, which matches the lowest price we’ve seen occur a few times throughout the year. The option with wood siding is $111.99 at Amazon, also 20 percent off its original price.

The keyboard can connect via USB-C, or wirelessly via Bluetooth or with a more reliable 2.4GHz connection. Its key bindings, actuation points, and much more can be configured in Keychron’s web-based tool. Or, you can flash your own firmware to the keyboard thanks to its open source QMK support.

In case you haven’t owned a Hall effect keyboard before, they’re worth considering if you’ve wanted more granular control over how much (or how little) effort is needed to press a key. What’s more, the sensors support Rapid Trigger, which primes each switch for another input long before it has been fully released, possibly letting you get the jump on opponents.
